嘉靖三十二年，復當會試天下士。禮部尚書臣德、右侍郎臣如霖以聞。于時，左侍郎臣陞遣祀承天未還，而臣如霖有二王之婚禮。廼正月乙巳，詔以吏部左侍郎臣文德知貢舉。二月癸丑，詔臣暨學士臣銑司校文。仰惟皇上取賢歛才，與圖治理，每三歲一開科，作興修飭，視庶政特重。若茲舉也，臣自上左右，臣文德自銓曹，以奉
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the thirty-second year of Jiajing [1553], it was once again time to hold the Metropolitan Examination for scholars from throughout the realm. Your servants De, Minister of Rites, and Rulin, Right Vice Minister, reported this to the throne. At that time, your servant Sheng, Left Vice Minister, had been dispatched to perform sacrifices at Chengtian and had not yet returned, while your servant Rulin was occupied with the wedding ceremonies of two princes. Accordingly, on the yisi day of the first month, an edict appointed your servant Wende, Left Vice Minister of Personnel, to oversee the examination. On the guichou day of the second month, an edict directed me, together with your servant Xian, Academician, to take charge of assessing the examination essays.

I reverently consider how Your Majesty selects worthy men and gathers talent to join in planning good government. Once every three years, you open the examinations, encouraging learning and fostering disciplined conduct, and accord this matter particular weight above the other affairs of government. For this examination, I came from attendance at Your Majesty’s side, and your servant Wende from the Ministry of Personnel, to receive…

translation_en: …under orders to conduct affairs in the examination compound. The importance accorded to this undertaking, toward which Your Majesty’s gracious intentions are directed, has increased still further. Your servant is shallow in learning and inadequate to the charge entrusted to him. Yet I reflect that no duty of a minister is greater than serving his sovereign by finding worthy men. I have fortunately received recognition from Your sagely and enlightened Majesty, enjoyed Your favor, and been promoted. Your grace is as great as Heaven and Earth, and I have no means of repaying it. If, by exhausting my heart and strength, I can obtain men fit one day to assist in accomplishing the work of government and bringing its affairs to flourishing completion, I may perhaps repay one ten-thousandth of Your immense beneficence. Thus I dared not decline or evade the charge. On the jia-yin day, together with Your servants Xian and Wende, and the Associate Examiners—Senior Compiler Yuanli; Junior Compilers Fen, Jingchun, Chun, Siqian, Tangsun, Juzheng, and Jie; Examining Editors Shikao, Kuang, and Your servant…

闕下始臣　在館局嘗購往時所
謂舉業之文觀之大抵宣德
punctuated:
大韶，都給事中臣良翰，左給事中臣思靜、臣登之，郎中臣載鳴、臣應魁，主事臣鏘，監試官御史臣南金、臣炳然，及諸執事，陛辭入院。越丙辰、己未、壬戌，合士之前後貢於有司者四千四百有竒，如故事三試之。癸酉，遵聖斷取四百人，梓其姓名與其文二十篇，彙爲茲錄，將以甲戌之旦獻諸闕下。
始臣在館局，嘗購往時所謂舉業之文觀之，大抵宣德
translation_en:
…Dashao; your servant Lianghan, Chief Supervising Secretary; your servants Sijing and Dengzhi, Left Supervising Secretaries; your servants Zaiming and Yingkui, Bureau Directors; your servant Qiang, Secretary; your servants Nanjin and Bingran, Censors serving as examination monitors; and the various functionaries took leave of Your Majesty and entered the examination compound. On the bingchen, jiwei, and renxu days, we examined, in three sessions according to established practice, the more than 4,400 candidates who had been recommended to the responsible authorities in successive groups. On the guiyou day, in accordance with Your Majesty’s decision, we selected 400 men. We had their names and twenty of their essays printed from woodblocks and compiled them into this record, to be presented at the palace on the morning of the jiaxu day.
Earlier, while serving in the Hanlin Academy, I had purchased and read writings from former times in what is called the examination style. Generally speaking, the Xuande era…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
以前其詞簡而質弘治以前
其詞雅而暢至正德間其詞
蔚以昌矣然厭棄師說而流
於詭僻鶩於怪奇者亦間有
之乃今閱多士所爲文率能
發抒所自得而實未嘗違背
經傳及逸而出於繩墨蓋我
===
皇上繼
天立極道隆
君師
敬一之箴
五箴之註士相與講誦服習已
非一時久道化成理固然也
臣自甲子迄於辛未屢爲之

punctuated: 以前，其詞簡而質；弘治以前，其詞雅而暢；至正德間，其詞蔚以昌矣。然厭棄師說而流於詭僻、鶩於怪奇者，亦間有之。乃今閱多士所爲文，率能發抒所自得，而實未嘗違背經傳，及逸而出於繩墨。蓋我皇上繼天立極，道隆君師，《敬一》之箴、《五箴》之註，士相與講誦服習，已非一時。久道化成，理固然也。臣自甲子迄於辛未，屢爲之
translation_en:
…before [the Xuande era], their language was concise and substantial; before the Hongzhi era, it was elegant and fluent; by the Zhengde era, it had become rich and flourishing. Yet there were occasionally those who rejected their teachers’ explanations and drifted into perversity, pursuing the strange and outlandish. Now, however, when I read the compositions of these many scholars, I find that they generally express insights they have gained for themselves, without actually departing from the classics and their commentaries or straying beyond established standards.
For our Emperor succeeds Heaven and establishes the supreme standard, exalting the Way as sovereign and teacher. Scholars have together expounded, recited, observed, and practiced the Admonition on Reverent Single-mindedness (Jingyi) and the Commentary on the Five Admonitions (Wuzhen zhu) for no short time. That long adherence to the Way should bring about transformation is surely natural. From the jiazi year through the xinwei year, your servant repeatedly, on this account…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
撫卷嘉歎以為人才之盛如
此凡亮工熙載之用皆將於
是乎取之而不窮竊深自慶
焉既而思曰多士之爛然在
臣目者文也其亮工熙載卓
然著於用世者行與業也自
進士之科立士豈無聲實相
===
副如唐宋璟張九齡裴度陸
贄宋李沆王旦韓琦范仲淹
司馬光歐陽修諸人者乎抑
豈無靜言庸違文有可觀而
人無足稱者乎使多士能為
文能以行業著於用世臣則
可自慶矣不然是臣欲藉以

punctuated: 撫卷嘉歎，以為人才之盛如此，凡亮工熙載之用，皆將於是乎取之而不窮，竊深自慶焉。既而思曰：「多士之爛然在臣目者，文也；其亮工熙載，卓然著於用世者，行與業也。自進士之科立，士豈無聲實相副，如唐宋璟、張九齡、裴度、陸贄，宋李沆、王旦、韓琦、范仲淹、司馬光、歐陽修諸人者乎？抑豈無靜言庸違，文有可觀而人無足稱者乎？使多士能為文，能以行業著於用世，臣則可自慶矣。不然，是臣欲藉以
translation_en:
…holding the examination papers, I sighed in admiration, thinking that with talent flourishing to such a degree, all those needed to discharge official duties and advance the work of government could be drawn from this source without exhaustion. Privately, I felt profound satisfaction.
Then I reflected: “What shines so brilliantly before your servant’s eyes is these scholars’ writing. What enables them to discharge official duties, advance the work of government, and distinguish themselves in service to the world is their conduct and achievements. Since the establishment of the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) examination, have there not been scholars whose reputations matched their actual merits—men such as Song Jing, Zhang Jiuling, Pei Du, and Lu Zhi of the Tang, and Li Hang, Wang Dan, Han Qi, Fan Zhongyan, Sima Guang, and Ouyang Xiu of the Song? Yet have there not also been those whose words were compliant but whose deeds ran contrary, whose writing merited attention but who as men deserved no praise? If these scholars can write well and can also distinguish themselves through their conduct and achievements in service to the world, then your servant may indeed feel satisfaction. Otherwise, your servant’s wish to rely upon them to…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
報
主不可得也於是又竊有深懼焉
謹因錄成恭述
德意而併及臣將
命之心以示多士書有之萬邦黎
獻共惟帝臣夫
聖人在上固黎獻所願出而有爲
===
之時也矧夫豫教素養於學
校而又設科以求之若是其
重者耶多士有感於曠世之
遭
作人之澤則夫交相戒勗以期
光贊
聖治而因以釋主司之懼者殆弗

之時也矧夫隆教素養於學
校而又設科以求之若是其
重者耶多士有感於曠世之
遭
作人之澤則夫交相戒勗以期
光贊
聖治而因以釋主司之懼者殆弗
punctuated:
報主不可得也，於是又竊有深懼焉。

謹因錄成，恭述德意，而併及臣將命之心，以示多士。《書》有之：「萬邦黎獻，共惟帝臣。」夫聖人在上，固黎獻所願出而有爲之時也。矧夫豫教素養於學校，而又設科以求之，若是其重者耶？多士有感於曠世之遭、作人之澤，則夫交相戒勗，以期光贊聖治，而因以釋主司之懼者，殆弗
translation_en:
…to repay my sovereign would be impossible. At this thought, I privately feel profound apprehension as well.

Now that this record is complete, I respectfully recount His Majesty’s gracious intentions, together with my own feelings as his servant entrusted with carrying out his command, to make them known to the assembled scholars. The Book of Documents says: “The many worthy men of the myriad states are all the emperor’s servants.” With a sage upon the throne, this is indeed the time when worthy men wish to come forward and accomplish something. How much more so when they have been instructed in advance and steadily nurtured in the schools, and examinations have also been established to seek them out—such is the importance accorded them! If the assembled scholars are moved by this opportunity unmatched in generations and by the beneficence that cultivates talent, then surely, as regards admonishing and encouraging one another in the hope of gloriously assisting the sage’s rule, and thereby relieving the presiding examiner’s apprehension, they can scarcely fail to…

translation_en:
…allow of any cessation. I, your unworthy servant, now look forward to this daily.
Xu Jie, Grand Master for Glorious Happiness, Junior Guardian concurrently serving as Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Rites, and Grand Secretary of the Eastern Pavilion, respectfully composed this preface.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Thirty-second Year of Jiajing (1553)

Directors of the Examination

Ouyang De, Grand Master for Fostering Goodness, Minister of Rites, and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Chongyi; he was from Taihe County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the guiwei year (1523).

Cheng Wende, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Personnel. His courtesy name was Shunfu; he was from Yongkang County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the jichou year (1529).

Examiners

Xu Jie, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Guardian and concurrently Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Rites, and Grand Secretary of the Hall of Military Glory. His courtesy name was Zisheng; he was from Huating County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the guiwei year (1523).

Ao Xian, Expositor-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Grand Master for Rendering Instruction. His courtesy name was Chunzhi; he was from Gao’an County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year (1535).

Associate Examiners

Quan Yuanli, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Gentleman of the Confucian Community. His courtesy name was Rude; he was from Yin County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yiwei year (1535).

Dong Fen, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Gentleman of the Literary Community. His courtesy name was Yongjun; he was from Wucheng County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the xinchou year (1541).

Qu Jingchun, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Gentleman of the Literary Community. His courtesy name was Shidao; he was from Changshu County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the jiachen year (1544).

Zhang Chun, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Gentleman for Undertaking Affairs. His courtesy name was Renbo; he was from Xinyu County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year (1547).

Kang Siqian, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Gentleman of the Literary Community. His courtesy name was Ziyi; he was from Linfen County, Shanxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year (1547).

Wang Tangsun, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Gentleman of the Literary Community. His courtesy name was Zhenzong; he was from Yin County, Zhejiang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year (1547).

Zhang Juzheng, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Gentleman for Undertaking Affairs. His courtesy name was Boduan; he was from Jingzhou Guard, Huguang, and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year (1547).

Hu Jie, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Gentleman of the Literary Community. His courtesy name was Ziwen; he was from Fengcheng County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year (1547).

Sun Shifang, Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Gentleman for Attendant Service. His courtesy name was Kecheng; he was from the Wanquan Regional Military Commission and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year (1547).

Lin Lian, Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy, with the prestige title Gentleman for Summoned Service. His courtesy name was Zhenheng; he was from Min County, Fujian, and was a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year (1547).

Zhu Dashao, an Examining Editor in the Hanlin Academy, held the prestige rank of congshi lang. His courtesy name was Xiangxuan; he was from Huating County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in 1547.

Jiang Lianghan, Chief Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Justice, held the prestige rank of wenlin lang. His courtesy name was Xizhao; he was from Jinhua County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1544.

Zhang Sijing, Left Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Justice, held the prestige rank of congshi lang. His courtesy name was Bo’an; he was from Tongzhou, Shaanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Xie Dengzhi, Left Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Works, held the prestige rank of congshi lang. His courtesy name was Ruxue; he was from Baling County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Yang Zaiming, a Secretary serving as acting Director of the Bureau of Patents in the Ministry of Personnel, held the prestige rank of chengde lang. His courtesy name was Xuqing; he was from Taihe County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

Chen Yingkui, Director of the Bureau of Waterways in the Ministry of Works, held the prestige rank of fengyi dafu. His courtesy name was Fuyuan; he was from Putian County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1538.

Bi Qiang, a Secretary in the Henan Bureau of the Ministry of Justice, held the prestige rank of chengde lang. His courtesy name was Tingming; he was from Shidai County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1544.

Examination Inspectors:

Xu Nanjin, Investigating Censor for the Yunnan Circuit, held the prestige rank of wenlin lang. His courtesy name was Tiqian; he was from Fengcheng County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1541.

Zhao Bingran, Investigating Censor for the Jiangxi Circuit, held the prestige rank of wenlin lang. His courtesy name was Zihui; he was from Jianzhou, Sichuan, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1535.

Proctors:

Liu Sijie, a Secretary serving as acting Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the prestige rank of chengde lang. His courtesy name was Yuanjing; he was from Yizhou, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Fu Xiaqi, a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the prestige rank of chengzhi lang. His courtesy name was Tinghuang; he was from Nan’an County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1550.

Officials Responsible for Printing Examination Papers:

Wang Weizhong, Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the prestige rank of fengyi dafu. His courtesy name was Daoyuan; he was from Jinjiang County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1541.

Wang Renyong, a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, held the prestige rank of chengzhi lang. His courtesy name was Ruqin; he was from Taicang Subprefecture, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1547.

Officials Responsible for the Custody of Examination Scripts:

Zhang Zihe, Assistant Judge of the Left Division of the Court of Judicial Review [the designation “Left Division” is repeated in the transcription [?]], was performing the duties of a Central Secretariat Drafter. His courtesy name was Jiezhi; he was from Cangzhou, Zhili, and was a student admitted by virtue of an official’s status.

Li Feng, Assistant Gentleman for Cultivating Service and Registrar of the Court of State Ceremonial, performing the duties of a Secretariat Drafter. His courtesy name was Guorui; he was registered in an official household of Wugong Right Guard and was a native of Shouzhou, Zhili. He was a Confucian scholar without examination status (rushi).

Officials Receiving Examination Papers

Wang Fu, Vice Prefect of Ganzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Yongqing; he was a native of Jiangdu County, Zhili, and a tribute scholar (gongshi) of the wuzi year.

Guo Luan, Magistrate of Wuding Subprefecture in Jinan Prefecture, Shandong. His courtesy name was Yunhe; he was a native of Gaoping County, Shanxi, and a tribute scholar of the xinmao year.

Zhou Lin, Magistrate of Changshan County in Quzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. His courtesy name was Renzhong; he was a native of Wujiang County, Zhili, and a tribute scholar of the wuzi year.

第壹場

四書

大哉，堯之為君也！巍巍乎！唯天為大，唯堯則之。蕩蕩乎！民無能名焉。

誠者，非自成己而已也，所以成物也。成己，仁也；成物，知也。性之德也，合外内之道也，故時措之宜也。

由堯舜至於湯，五百有餘歲。若禹、臯陶，則見而知之；若湯，則聞而知之。由湯至於文王，五百有餘歲。若伊尹、萊朱，則見而知之；若文王，則聞而知之。由文王至於孔子，五百有餘歲。若太公望、散宜生，則見而知之；若孔子，則聞而知之。

易

君子行此四德者，故曰：「乾，元亨利貞。」

天地之道，恒久而不已也。

範圍天地之化而不過，曲成萬物而不遺，通乎晝夜之道而知，故神无方而易无体。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Great indeed was Yao as a ruler! How lofty! Heaven alone is great, and Yao alone modeled himself upon it. How vast were his achievements! The people could find no words to describe them.

Sincerity does not merely bring oneself to fulfillment; it also brings other things to fulfillment. Bringing oneself to fulfillment is benevolence; bringing other things to fulfillment is wisdom. These are virtues of our nature, the way that unites the outer and the inner. Thus, whenever they are put into practice, they are appropriate to the occasion.

From Yao and Shun to Tang was more than five hundred years. Yu and Gao Yao knew their Way through seeing them; Tang knew it through hearing of them. From Tang to King Wen was more than five hundred years. Yi Yin and Lai Zhu knew his Way through seeing him; King Wen knew it through hearing of him. From King Wen to Kongzi was more than five hundred years. Taigong Wang and San Yisheng knew his Way through seeing him; Kongzi knew it through hearing of him.

Book of Changes

The gentleman practices these four virtues. Thus it is said: “Qian: origination, success, benefit, and steadfastness.”

The Way of Heaven and Earth endures perpetually and never ceases.

It encompasses the transformations of Heaven and Earth without overstepping them; it brings the myriad things to completion in all their particulars without omitting any; and it comprehends the Way of day and night and knows it. Thus the numinous has no fixed location, and change has no fixed form.

translation_en:
…form.
Taking Heaven as three and Earth as two, they establish the numbers.

Book of Documents
The emperor thereupon composed a song, saying: “Attend to Heaven’s mandate; heed the times and the first signs of change.” Then he sang: “When the arms and legs rejoice, the head rises to action, and the hundred offices flourish!” Gao Yao bowed with his hands joined and touched his forehead to the ground, proclaiming: “Be mindful! In leading undertakings and initiating affairs, be careful of your rules. Be reverent! Repeatedly examine your accomplishments; be reverent!” Then he continued the song: “When the head is enlightened, the arms and legs are worthy, and all affairs prosper!”
Reverently honor the Way of Heaven, and preserve Heaven’s mandate forever.
When the moon follows the stars, wind and rain ensue.
Reverently uphold the great model, and employ the three classes of officeholders and the outstanding men of those three classes. Those in the city of Shang should bring harmony to that city; those throughout the realm should serve as great models, displaying their virtue.

Book of Odes
Gather, gather the plantain; let us pick it.
Gather, gather the plantain; let us collect it.
Gather, gather the plantain; let us pluck it.
Gather, gather the plantain; let us strip off its seeds.
Gather, gather the plantain; let us hold it in our lifted skirts.
Gather, gather the plantain; let us carry it in our skirts tucked into our belts.
It is because he possesses these qualities that he can act accordingly.

寬而靜、柔而正者，宜歌《頌》；廣大而靜、疏達而信者，宜歌《大雅》；恭儉而好禮者，宜歌《小雅》；正直而靜、廉而謙者，宜歌《風》。
translation_en:
This King Wen was circumspect and reverent. He illustriously served the Lord on High and thereby secured abundant blessings. His virtue did not deviate, and thus he received the allegiance of the states in every quarter.
May he enjoy long life and peace, thereby protecting us, his descendants.

In summer, the Marquis of Qi and the Earl of Zheng went to Ji. (Fifth year of Duke Huan.)
In spring, men of Qi, Chen, and Cao attacked Song. (Fourteenth year of Duke Zhuang.)
Qu Wan of Chu came to make a covenant at the army’s camp. (Fourth year of Duke Xi.) Men of Qi came to return the lands of Yun, Huan, and Guiyin. (Tenth year of Duke Ding.)
In winter, the duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, the Viscount of Lesser Zhu, and Guang, heir apparent of Qi, in attacking Zheng. In the twelfth month, on the jihai day [?], they jointly concluded a covenant at Xi. (Ninth year of Duke Xiang.)

Record of Rites
The Son of Heaven then, on the first auspicious day, prays to the Lord on High for grain.
The weimao cap follows the practice of Zhou; the zhangfu cap follows the practice of Yin; the wuzhui cap follows the practice of the Xia rulers. Zhou had the bian cap, Yin the xu cap, and Xia the shou cap. The kings of all three dynasties shared the use of the leather cap and plain white pleated skirt.
Those who are generous and calm, gentle and upright, should sing the Hymns. Those who are magnanimous and calm, open-minded and trustworthy, should sing the Greater Odes. Those who are respectful and restrained, and delight in ritual propriety, should sing the Lesser Odes. Those who are upright and calm, incorruptible and modest, should sing the Airs.

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
問孔子作春秋大一統以尊周其於僭竊
偽邦貶黜嚴甚孟軻氏序羣聖之統歷
數千年而僅得數聖人焉帝王正統道
統之傳若是乎其重以與人也朱子作
綱目進蜀漢而黜曹魏韓子著原道論
謂軻以後不得其傳其於孔孟之意似
合矣而宋蘇軾黃榦所論乃有不同者
何歟漢唐而下能一天下之君與其所
謂闡明道學之士果足以紹是統否歟
===
洪惟我
太祖高皇帝驅逐胡元再造華夏功業之盛前
所未有至其論帝王授受之要觀心之
義皆於典謨所載得其精微我
皇上以天縱之聖應運中興
明倫有典
敬一有箴制禮作樂燦然明備又於勝國則
罷其廟祀於先聖先師則崇祀于
文華東室

洪惟我

罷其廟祀於先聖先師則崇祀于
文華東室
punctuated:
問：孔子作《春秋》，大一統以尊周，其於僭竊偽邦，貶黜嚴甚。孟軻氏序羣聖之統，歷數千年而僅得數聖人焉。帝王正統、道統之傳，若是乎其重以與人也？朱子作《綱目》，進蜀漢而黜曹魏；韓子著《原道論》，謂軻以後不得其傳。其於孔孟之意似合矣，而宋蘇軾、黃榦所論乃有不同者，何歟？漢唐而下，能一天下之君與其所謂闡明道學之士，果足以紹是統否歟？
洪惟我太祖高皇帝驅逐胡元，再造華夏，功業之盛，前所未有。至其論帝王授受之要、觀心之義，皆於《典》《謨》所載得其精微。我皇上以天縱之聖，應運中興，明倫有典，敬一有箴，制禮作樂，燦然明備。又於勝國則罷其廟祀，於先聖先師則崇祀于文華東室。
translation_en:
Question: Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals, exalting unified rule in order to honor the Zhou. He was exceedingly severe in condemning and rejecting usurpers and illegitimate states. Meng Ke traced the succession of the sages, yet over several thousand years he could identify only a few sages. Is the transmission of the legitimate imperial succession and the succession of the Way so weighty a matter when entrusted to others? Master Zhu composed the Outline and Details, elevating Shu Han and rejecting Cao Wei; Master Han composed On the Origin of the Way, stating that after Meng Ke no one received its transmission. These positions appear to accord with the intentions of Confucius and Mencius. Yet the arguments of Su Shi and Huang Gan of the Song differ from them. Why is this? From the Han and Tang onward, were rulers capable of unifying All under Heaven, and those scholars said to have elucidated the Learning of the Way, truly worthy of continuing these successions?
We reverently consider how our Taizu, the Exalted Emperor, expelled the alien Yuan and restored Huaxia. The magnificence of his achievements was unprecedented. In his discussions of the essentials of transmitting and receiving imperial authority and the meaning of examining the mind, he grasped the subtle profundities of what is recorded in the Canons and Counsels of the Book of Documents. Our Emperor, with his Heaven-endowed sagacity, has responded to the destined moment and brought about a restoration. For elucidating human relationships there is a canon; for reverent concentration on the One there is an admonition. He has established rites and instituted music, brilliantly articulated and complete. Moreover, he has abolished temple sacrifices to the preceding dynasty, while providing exalted sacrifices to the former sage and former teacher in the eastern chamber of the Hall of Literary Brilliance…

text:

聖見迥出千古盖帝王正統道統之傳至
聖祖而始續至我
皇上而益光矣爾多士生於茲時涵泳
德化豈不可謂大幸歟願相與鋪張揚厲焉
毋畧
問平心宣化象德昭功樂之用大矣自周
衰樂廢代變新聲而英莖之制日以遠
焉然典籍所載間有存者其微言遺旨
===
可得而聞歟說者謂古樂之復必先考
定鍾律而黃鍾又律呂之原也其詳可
得而言歟漢志三統三正之說似以林
鍾太簇之律與黃鍾並矣其果然歟先
儒損益相生之論變律半聲之制果皆
合於造化自然之數而於樂有所發明
歟古人作樂止於五聲十二律後世乃
益之以六十律衍之以三百六十律八
十四調何古人之樂明白簡徑而後世

宸謨聖見，迥出千古。盖帝王正統、道統之傳，至聖祖而始續，至我皇上而益光矣。爾多士生於茲時，涵泳德化，豈不可謂大幸歟？願相與鋪張揚厲焉，毋畧。
問：平心宣化，象德昭功，樂之用大矣。自周衰樂廢，代變新聲，而英莖之制日以遠焉。然典籍所載，間有存者，其微言遺旨，可得而聞歟？說者謂古樂之復，必先考定鍾律，而黃鍾又律呂之原也，其詳可得而言歟？漢志三統三正之說，似以林鍾、太簇之律與黃鍾並矣，其果然歟？先儒損益相生之論、變律半聲之制，果皆合於造化自然之數，而於樂有所發明歟？古人作樂，止於五聲十二律，後世乃益之以六十律，衍之以三百六十律、八十四調，何古人之樂明白簡徑，而後世
translation_en:
… His imperial plans and sagely insights surpass those of all preceding ages. Indeed, the transmission of the legitimate imperial succession and the succession of the Way was first resumed under the Sagely Progenitor and has become still more glorious under our present Emperor. You assembled scholars, born in this age and steeped in his morally transforming influence, surely may be called most fortunate! We ask you together to expound and celebrate these achievements fully. Omit nothing.
Question: Music calms the heart, spreads transforming influence, represents virtue, and makes achievements manifest: great indeed are its uses. Since the decline of the Zhou and the abandonment of its music, successive ages have introduced new sounds, while the forms of the ancient Ying and Jing music have grown ever more remote. Yet scattered accounts survive in the classical writings. Can their subtle teachings and surviving purport be explained to us? Some say that restoring ancient music requires first examining and establishing the pitch standards of the bells, and that Huangzhong, the Yellow Bell, is itself the source of the twelve pitch standards. Can you explain this in detail? The account of the Three Concordances and the Three Calendar Beginnings in the treatises of the History of the Han seems to place the pitches Linzhong and Taicu on an equal footing with Huangzhong. Is this really so? Do earlier Confucian scholars’ theories of generating pitches from one another by diminution and augmentation, and their systems of altered pitches and half-tones, truly accord with the natural numerical patterns of creation and shed light on music? The ancients made music using only five notes and twelve pitch standards. Later generations increased these to sixty pitch standards and expanded them to three hundred and sixty pitch standards and eighty-four modes. Why was the music of the ancients clear and straightforward, whereas that of later generations …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
繁瑣若是歟至於術家制尺較黍之類
其言不一而足不知亦可用之今日否
歟茲欲審聲以和律定律以正音用復
古樂之盛爾諸士必有定見也盍相與
講明之
問穆叔有言太上立德其次立功其次立
言士徼此三者無以垂不朽然嘗稽之
古昔禹皐陶伊傅周召之徒以德稱而
未嘗無功亦未嘗無言孔孟有德無位
===
始以言爲訓而昔人謂孔子賢于堯舜
孟子功不在禹下是又未可以立言槩
之也然則立德立功立言之分何所始
乎豈春秋之時已有不能兼者而穆叔
言之乎嗣後立言之士代不乏人類湮
沒而名不稱宋蘇軾謂孟子之後五百
餘年而得韓愈愈之後三百餘年而得
歐陽子盖將推韓歐以附孔孟也然而
君子不與焉則士之勤一世以用心于

punctuated:
繁瑣若是歟？至於術家制尺較黍之類，其言不一而足，不知亦可用之今日否歟？茲欲審聲以和律，定律以正音，用復古樂之盛。爾諸士必有定見也，盍相與講明之？
問：穆叔有言：「太上立德，其次立功，其次立言。」士徼此三者，無以垂不朽。然嘗稽之古昔，禹、皐陶、伊、傅、周、召之徒，以德稱，而未嘗無功，亦未嘗無言。孔孟有德無位，始以言爲訓，而昔人謂孔子賢于堯舜，孟子功不在禹下，是又未可以立言槩之也。然則立德、立功、立言之分，何所始乎？豈春秋之時，已有不能兼者，而穆叔言之乎？嗣後立言之士，代不乏人，類湮沒而名不稱。宋蘇軾謂孟子之後五百餘年而得韓愈，愈之後三百餘年而得歐陽子，盖將推韓歐以附孔孟也。然而君子不與焉，則士之勤一世以用心于
translation_en:
…so intricate and cumbersome? As for such practices as specialists’ construction of measuring rules and comparison of millet grains, their explanations are too numerous to enumerate. Could these also be put to use today? We now wish to examine sounds so as to harmonize the pitch standards, and to establish the pitch standards so as to correct musical tones, thereby restoring the flourishing music of antiquity. You scholars surely have considered views. Why not discuss and elucidate these matters together?
Question: Mu Shu said: “Highest is establishing virtue; next is establishing merit; next is establishing words.” A scholar seeks these three, without which he has no means of securing an enduring legacy [?]. Yet, examining antiquity, we find that men such as Yu, Gao Yao, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, Zhou Gong, and Shao Gong were celebrated for virtue, but were never without achievements or words either. Kongzi and Mengzi possessed virtue but lacked official position, and thus turned to words for instruction. Yet earlier thinkers said that Kongzi was worthier than Yao and Shun, and that Mengzi’s achievements were not inferior to Yu’s. Thus, “establishing words” alone cannot adequately characterize them. Where, then, did the distinction between establishing virtue, establishing merit, and establishing words originate? Could it be that already in the Spring and Autumn period there were men unable to combine all three, prompting Mu Shu’s statement? Thereafter, every age had men who sought to establish words, yet most sank into obscurity, their names uncelebrated. Su Shi of the Song said that more than five hundred years after Mengzi there appeared Han Yu, and more than three hundred years after Han Yu there appeared Master Ouyang. Presumably he intended to exalt Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu by placing them alongside Kongzi and Mengzi. Yet gentlemen do not assent to this judgment. Then, as for scholars who labor throughout their lives, devoting their minds to …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
文字者果可以垂不朽否也修之言曰
聖賢之異于衆人不朽而存者修之于
身施之于事見之于言所以能不朽而
存也施于事矣不見于言可也修于身
矣不施于事不見于言亦可也夫修固
喜爲文辭者而其言如此然則言固不
足恃乎諸士挾策而來蓋將以言進者
試爲我折衷之毋曰是亦空言也
問黃河爲患所從來久矣其决不常故其
===
策亦靡定即如漢世文武哀成之間相
去未百年而或塞或不塞何其異歟其
時言不塞者或稱之或謂其未便何歟
今徐房之决或言新安可開而諸决口
必可塞或言河乃天變非人力所爲不
若舍故道而別圖之其說孰當歟萬世
言治河者莫如神禹其事有可施於今
者否歟
明興河之諸道皆已非古二百年間往往數

punctuated:
文字者，果可以垂不朽否也？修之言曰：「聖賢之異于衆人，不朽而存者，修之于身，施之于事，見之于言，所以能不朽而存也。施于事矣，不見于言，可也；修于身矣，不施于事，不見于言，亦可也。」夫修固喜爲文辭者，而其言如此，然則言固不足恃乎？諸士挾策而來，蓋將以言進者，試爲我折衷之，毋曰是亦空言也。
問：黃河爲患，所從來久矣。其决不常，故其策亦靡定。即如漢世文武哀成之間，相去未百年，而或塞或不塞，何其異歟？其時言不塞者，或稱之，或謂其未便，何歟？今徐房之决，或言新安可開，而諸决口必可塞；或言河乃天變，非人力所爲，不若舍故道而別圖之。其說孰當歟？萬世言治河者，莫如神禹，其事有可施於今者否歟？明興，河之諸道皆已非古，二百年間，往往數
translation_en:
…those who devote the labors of a lifetime to writing: can they truly secure an enduring legacy? Ouyang Xiu said: “What distinguishes sages and worthies from ordinary people, allowing them to endure without perishing, is what they cultivate in themselves, put into practice in affairs, and express in words. This is how they achieve an enduring legacy. What has been put into practice in affairs need not appear in words; what has been cultivated in oneself need not be put into practice in affairs or appear in words.” Xiu certainly delighted in literary composition, yet he spoke thus. Are words, then, indeed insufficient to rely upon? You gentlemen have come bearing your writings, presumably seeking advancement through words. Attempt to weigh these views and reach a sound judgment for me; do not say that this, too, is empty talk.
Question: The Yellow River has long been a source of calamity. Its breaches are unpredictable, and consequently the strategies for dealing with them have also lacked consistency. Take, for example, the reigns of Emperors Wen, Wu, Ai, and Cheng of the Han: they were less than a hundred years apart [?], yet sometimes breaches were closed and sometimes they were left open. Why did their approaches differ so greatly? Of those who advocated leaving breaches open at the time, some approved of this course, while others considered it impracticable. Why? Regarding the present breaches at Xu and Fang [?], some say that a channel can be opened at Xin’an and that all the breaches can certainly be closed. Others say that the river’s behavior is a change wrought by Heaven, beyond human power to control, and that it would be better to abandon the old course and devise another plan. Which view is correct? Among all those throughout the ages who have undertaken river management, none equals the divine Yu. Are any of his measures applicable today? When the Ming arose, the river’s various courses were already different from those of antiquity. Over the ensuing two hundred years, time and again, repeatedly…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
决能知諸道所從又知决之之故則可
與言治河矣今聞徐房之上流有所謂
孫繼口趙皮寨諸河議者以為必先治
此而或又言當急治安東其說孰是歟
夫一時而舉諸役恐非所以惜財而體
國者且罷民不可以重勞灾地不可以
處衆宜如何而可今所以進諸士將實
求可行之道幸毋以陳言對
問大學論平天下以理財與用人並言則
===
理財之道固為治者所不可不講也况
在司農告匱之時耶然嘗觀於今日國
無不耕之民野無失時之農則所謂生
之為之者既已衆且疾矣獨食之者或
未寡用之者或未舒故論者謂冗官當
革冗兵當汰力役當罷工作當止而有
司又謂
國家之制率以一官任一事去其人則事遂
廢是官本未嘗冗而難革也

===
理財之道固爲治者所不可不講也況
在司農告匱之時耶然嘗觀於今日國
無不耕之民野無失時之農則所謂生
之爲之者既已衆且疾矣獨食之者或
未寡用之者或未舒故論者謂冗官當
革冗兵當汰力役當罷工作當止而有
司又謂
國家之制率以一官任一事去其人則事遂
廢是官本未嘗冗而難革也
punctuated:
决。能知諸道所從，又知决之之故，則可與言治河矣。今聞徐房之上流，有所謂孫繼口、趙皮寨諸河，議者以為必先治此，而或又言當急治安東，其說孰是歟？夫一時而舉諸役，恐非所以惜財而體國者。且罷民不可以重勞，灾地不可以處衆，宜如何而可？今所以進諸士，將實求可行之道，幸毋以陳言對。
問：大學論平天下，以理財與用人並言，則理財之道固為治者所不可不講也，况在司農告匱之時耶？然嘗觀於今日，國無不耕之民，野無失時之農，則所謂生之、為之者，既已衆且疾矣。獨食之者或未寡，用之者或未舒。故論者謂冗官當革，冗兵當汰，力役當罷，工作當止。而有司又謂：「國家之制，率以一官任一事，去其人則事遂廢，是官本未嘗冗而難革也。」
translation_en:
…breached its banks. Only someone who knows the courses of the various channels, and also the causes of their breaches, can be consulted on controlling the river. We now hear that upstream of Xu and Fang are the waterways known as Sunjikou and Zhaopizhai. Those discussing the matter maintain that these must be dealt with first, while others say that Andong must urgently be dealt with. Which view is correct? To undertake all these works at once would, we fear, scarcely be a way to conserve resources and show due regard for the state. Moreover, an exhausted population cannot be burdened with further labor, and a disaster-stricken area cannot accommodate large numbers of people. What should be done? Our purpose in bringing you candidates forward now is earnestly to seek practicable methods. Please do not answer with stale commonplaces.
Question: In discussing bringing peace to all under Heaven, the Great Learning treats the management of wealth alongside the employment of men. Thus the principles of managing wealth are certainly something those who govern must examine—especially when the officials responsible for state finances report that the treasury is depleted. Yet, observing conditions today, there are no people in the realm who do not cultivate the land, and no farmers in the fields who miss the proper agricultural seasons. Thus those whom the text calls producers are already numerous, and those who work at production are already swift. It is only that those who consume may not yet be few, and those who spend may not yet be restrained. Hence commentators say that redundant officials should be dismissed, surplus soldiers discharged, corvée labor suspended, and construction and manufacture halted. The responsible authorities, however, say: “Under the institutions of the state, each official is generally entrusted with a particular duty. Remove the man, and the duty is consequently neglected. Thus these officials were never actually redundant and are difficult to dismiss.”

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
國家承平日久尺伍消耗過半去之則勢益
以弱是兵本未嘗冗而難汰也王公設
險以守其國今城堡之築皆守國所不
容已者是力役欲罷而不能也先王以
弧矢威天下如戎器之除皆威天下所
不容無者是工作欲止而不能也然則
將遂付之無可奈何而已乎諸士子明
於先王之道當世之務必有以處此矣
願聞其說

punctuated: 國家承平日久，尺伍消耗過半，去之則勢益以弱，是兵本未嘗冗而難汰也。王公設險以守其國，今城堡之築，皆守國所不容已者，是力役欲罷而不能也。先王以弧矢威天下，如戎器之除，皆威天下所不容無者，是工作欲止而不能也。然則將遂付之無可奈何而已乎？諸士子明於先王之道、當世之務，必有以處此矣。願聞其說。
translation_en: The state has long enjoyed peace, and the ranks of its soldiers [?] have dwindled by more than half. To discharge them would further weaken its strength. Thus the troops were never actually superfluous, and it is difficult to reduce their numbers. Kings and dukes establish defenses at strategic points to safeguard their states. The fortresses being built today are all indispensable to defending the state; thus, even if one wishes to end corvée labor, one cannot. The former kings used bows and arrows to overawe all under Heaven. Such work as refurbishing military equipment [?] is indispensable to overawing all under Heaven; thus, even if one wishes to halt manufacturing and construction, one cannot. Are we then simply to leave matters at that, accepting that nothing can be done? You examination candidates understand the Way of the former kings and the affairs of the present age, and surely have a means of dealing with this. I would like to hear your views.

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

大哉，堯之為君也！巍巍乎！唯天為大，唯堯則之。蕩蕩乎！民無能名焉。

馮葉

同考試官左給事中謝批：發明堯則天處，詞不費而意足。

同考試官都給事中姜批：聖人賛堯大處，只上二句已盡；到民無能名，不過足上意耳。此作發明得旨，錄之。

同考試官檢討朱批：無能名即是則天處，此作得之。

同考試官檢討孫批：發明堯配天意，只數語便盡，可取。

同考試官編修瞿批：堯之則天與其無能名處，纔着言語便不是。此作能知之，故錄。

考試官侍講學士敖批：講無能名甚明白。

考試官大學士徐批：能體貼朱傳成文。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Great indeed was Yao as a ruler! How lofty! Heaven alone is great, and Yao alone modeled himself upon it. How vast! The people could find no words to describe him.”

Feng Ye

Comment by Associate Examiner Xie, Left Supervising Secretary: This elucidates how Yao modeled himself upon Heaven; its wording is economical, yet its meaning is fully expressed.

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Chief Supervising Secretary: The Sage’s praise of Yao’s greatness is fully expressed in the first two sentences. The passage about the people’s inability to describe him merely completes the preceding meaning. This composition elucidates the passage’s purport correctly; select it for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhu, Examining Editor: The inability to describe him is precisely where his modeling himself upon Heaven lies. This composition grasps that.

Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, Examining Editor: It fully elucidates the meaning of Yao’s matching Heaven in just a few words. It merits selection.

Comment by Associate Examiner Qu, Junior Compiler: The moment one puts into words Yao’s modeling himself upon Heaven and his indescribability, one misses the mark. This composition understands this; hence its inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Ao, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: Its explanation of the inability to describe him is very clear.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary: It succeeds in composing an essay through a sensitive understanding of Zhu Xi’s commentary.

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
聖人贊前聖君德之大與天為一焉盖大而不
可名者天也堯之德能與之一此其所以為大
歟想吾夫子贊堯之意盖曰君天下者繼天以
為治則必憲天以為德使其德與天有間未足
以言大也吾甞稽古帝王大矣哉堯之為君乎
巍巍乎天之高大物莫過焉而唯堯也俊德之
克明有以格于上下盖其首出庶物者於天之
高獨能準焉而不可踰也帝德之廣運有以被
於四表盖其覆冒天下者於天之大獨能準焉
===
而不可量也故其德之蕩蕩不特後之人莫能
名也當堯之時為堯之民覲德於聖作之際亦
惟有胥戴焉已爾如欲從而名之則其廣也猶
之天然非有局於方體也而何以能為之形容
耶仰德於君臨之下亦惟有相忘焉已爾如欲
即而名之則其遠也猶之天然非有滯於形器
也而又何以能為之擬議耶故曰大哉堯之為
君也知天則知堯矣善觀堯者觀之於天斯可
矣雖然天之生人其所賦予非有異於堯而與

translation_en:
The sage praised the greatness of the former sage ruler’s virtue as being one with Heaven. For Heaven is great beyond the power of words to describe; Yao’s virtue could become one with it. Is this not what made him great? I imagine that our Master’s intention in praising Yao was this: one who rules all under Heaven succeeds Heaven in governing and must therefore take Heaven as the model for his virtue. If his virtue falls short of Heaven, it cannot yet be called great. I have examined the emperors and kings of antiquity: how great was Yao as a ruler! Majestic indeed is Heaven’s loftiness and vastness; nothing surpasses it. Yao alone, by making his illustrious virtue manifest, could reach above and below. Thus, in standing foremost among all things, he alone could match Heaven’s loftiness and could not be surpassed. His imperial virtue, far-reaching in its breadth, extended to the four outermost regions. Thus, in sheltering all under Heaven, he alone could match Heaven’s vastness and could not be measured.

Such was the boundless expanse of his virtue that it was not only later generations who could find no words to describe it. In Yao’s own time, his people, beholding his virtue as the sage arose, could do no more than join together in revering him. If they wished then to describe it, its breadth was like Heaven itself, confined to no fixed shape or form: how could they portray it? Looking up to his virtue under his rule, they could do no more than forget themselves and their ruler in mutual ease. If they wished to approach and describe it, its far-reaching extent was like Heaven itself, restricted by no material form: how, then, could they compare or discuss it? Hence the saying: “Great indeed was Yao as a ruler!” To know Heaven is to know Yao. Those who would contemplate Yao rightly need only contemplate him in Heaven. Nevertheless, when Heaven brings human beings into existence, what it endows them with is no different from what it bestowed upon Yao; yet to join with …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
天合德獨堯能之何也天命之性堯與人同而
允執厥中堯之盡其性者則與人異是故能盡
其性堯之所以合天也不能盡其性衆人之所
以與天不相似也中庸論至誠叅贊義盖如此
學者尚合而觀之
誠者非自成己而已也所以成物也成己
仁也成物知也性之德也合外内之道也
故時措之宜也
莊一兀
===
同考試官署郎中楊 批發明時措處迥異他

同考試官編修胡 批醇正典實一洗時
習之陋
同考試官編修亢 批體認親切而詞復精
當非深於理者不能也
同考試官編修張 批說性之所有爲用知
性矣

…to unite one’s virtue with Heaven—why was Yao alone able to do this? In the nature conferred by Heaven, Yao was the same as other people; but in truly holding fast to the Mean, and thereby fully realizing his nature, Yao differed from others. Thus, fully realizing his nature was how Yao united with Heaven; failing to realize their nature fully is why ordinary people do not resemble Heaven. This is presumably the meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean’s discussion of utmost sincerity and participation in and assistance with Heaven and Earth’s transforming and nourishing work. Students should consider these teachings together.

“Sincerity does not merely complete oneself; it is also the means of completing things. Completing oneself is benevolence; completing things is wisdom. These are virtues of our nature, the Way that unites the external and the internal. Hence, whenever they are put into practice, they are fitting.”

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
考試官大學士徐批典雅不類時作
中庸論誠之及物一性之所有而為用焉盖性
者萬物之一原也君子能誠於已則夫所以成
物者寧外是乎宜中庸言之以明人道也盖謂
君子所性根於心而其道貴於誠夫苟誠矣則
不惟誠之立於我者有以自成而道之行於彼
者自然及物以成已言之妄復無妄渾然全體
之不息非仁而何以成物言之物各付物燦然
妙用之顯行非知而何曰仁與知本諸吾性之
===
固有而為吾心之實德仁非在内也知非在外
也不貳之貞裕吾内者所以致用于外也不測
之化利吾外者所以致養乎内也由是天德妙
道合同而化無適而無莫者與時偕行以盡利
也誠精神應流而不息不習無不利者隨時變
易以盡能也凡所以範圍曲成之道而致彌綸
輔贊之功亦舉此而措之爾大哉誠乎其冒天
下之道者乎君子思誠之功至矣盡矣抑考之
經曰物有本末於此又曰不誠無物然則誠也

中庸論誠之及物，一性之所有而為用焉。盖性者，萬物之一原也。君子能誠於已，則夫所以成物者，寧外是乎？宜中庸言之以明人道也。盖謂君子所性根於心，而其道貴於誠。夫苟誠矣，則不惟誠之立於我者有以自成，而道之行於彼者自然及物。以成已言之，妄復無妄，渾然全體之不息，非仁而何？以成物言之，物各付物，燦然妙用之顯行，非知而何？曰仁與知，本諸吾性之固有，而為吾心之實德。仁非在内也，知非在外也。不貳之貞，裕吾内者，所以致用于外也；不測之化，利吾外者，所以致養乎内也。由是天德妙道，合同而化，無適而無莫者，與時偕行以盡利也；誠精神應，流而不息，不習無不利者，隨時變易以盡能也。凡所以範圍曲成之道，而致彌綸輔贊之功，亦舉此而措之爾。大哉誠乎！其冒天下之道者乎！君子思誠之功，至矣，盡矣！抑考之經，曰：「物有本末。」於此又曰：「不誠無物。」然則誠也

Examiner, Grand Secretary Xu, comments: “Classical and elegant; unlike contemporary compositions.”

The Doctrine of the Mean discusses how sincerity extends to things: it brings into operation all that is inherent in our nature. For nature is the single source of the myriad things. If the noble man can be sincere within himself, could the means by which he brings things to fulfillment lie outside this? It is fitting that the Doctrine of the Mean speaks of this to illuminate the human Way. Its meaning is that the nature of the noble man is rooted in his heart, and that sincerity is paramount in his Way. If he is indeed sincere, then not only does sincerity established within him enable him to fulfill himself, but the Way enacted toward others naturally extends to things. In terms of fulfilling oneself, falsity returns to freedom from falsity, and the undivided whole continues without cease: what is this if not benevolence? In terms of fulfilling things, each thing is accorded what belongs to it, and wondrous functioning manifests itself in brilliant clarity: what is this if not wisdom? Benevolence and wisdom are rooted in what our nature inherently possesses and constitute the genuine virtues of our heart. Benevolence is not confined to the inner realm, nor wisdom to the outer. Unwavering constancy, which enriches us inwardly, is the means of bringing our capacities into use outwardly; unfathomable transformation, which benefits us outwardly, is the means of nourishing us inwardly.

Through this, heavenly virtue and the wondrous Way unite and bring about transformation. Having neither fixed preferences nor fixed aversions, one advances together with the times to realize benefit fully. Sincerity is concentrated and responds numinously [?], flowing without cease; needing no practice yet finding nothing unfavorable, one changes with the times to exercise one’s capacities fully. All the ways of encompassing things and bringing each to fulfillment, and all the achievements of ordering the whole and assisting its workings, consist simply in taking this sincerity and putting it into practice. Great indeed is sincerity! Does it not embrace all the ways of the world? The noble man’s work of seeking sincerity reaches the utmost and leaves nothing undone!

Yet, examining the classics, we find it said: “Things have roots and branches.” Here it is also said: “Without sincerity, there are no things.” Thus sincerity…

…is that which brings others and oneself to fulfillment [?] and encompasses both root and branch. Thus, to treat the root as external and the branches as internal is certainly unacceptable; to attend to the root while neglecting the branches is likewise unacceptable. Hence, for the sage to regard all under Heaven as one family and the Central States as one person is also a matter within his own duties. Yet only the union of benevolence and wisdom is called sagehood; the union of virtue and nature is called sincerity; and the union of understanding and sincerity is called teaching. Thus it is said: “Without understanding goodness, one cannot make oneself sincere.” This, too, is something that those who seek sincerity must know.
From Yao and Shun to Tang, there were more than five hundred years. Yu and Gao Yao knew them through seeing them; Tang knew them through hearing of them. From Tang to King Wen, there were more than five hundred years. Yi Yin and Lai Zhu knew Tang through seeing him; King Wen knew him through hearing of him. From King Wen to Kongzi, there were more than five hundred years. Taigong Wang and San Yisheng knew King Wen through seeing him; Kongzi knew him through hearing of him.

The great worthy recounted in sequence how the Way was transmitted, thereby expressing his intention to assume responsibility for it himself. From Yao and Shun down to Kongzi, although knowing through seeing differed from knowing through hearing, the Way transmitted was one and the same. How fitting that Mengzi should recount this succession to convey his intention to assume that responsibility! Now, the Way has never disappeared from the world; hence the succession of those who transmit it has never been broken. Among the sages and worthies of antiquity, some lived at the same time and personally imparted and received instruction within a single hall: these knew through seeing. Others lived in different ages, yet their minds accorded with those who had lived several hundred years before: these knew through hearing.

Thus, from Yao and Shun’s inauguration of the transmission of this Way, more than five hundred years passed before Tang. Yu and Gao Yao knew through seeing; Tang knew through hearing. The Way embodied in Yao and Shun was thereby carried forward. Another five hundred years and more passed before King Wen. Yi Yin and Lai Zhu knew through seeing; King Wen knew through hearing. The Way embodied in Tang was thereby carried forward. From King Wen to Kongzi, again more than five hundred years passed. 道之在文王者，又於是乎屬焉。其見而知也，有以俟後聖於將來，而不間於世之相去之遠；其聞而知也，有以承先聖於旣往，而不阻於生之相值之難。盖道之所以傳而不絕者如此，而繼孔子者，容獨無其人乎？吁！孟子之意，殆自任於數聖人之後矣。抑觀文王以前，其傳道者皆在於上，至孔子獨在乎下。夫聖賢之生，達而在上則道行，窮而在下則道明。雖於性分無所加損，而其民則有幸不幸焉。孟子此章，固其自任之重，夫亦深有所慨也歟！

易

君子行此四德者，故曰：「乾，元亨利貞。」

莊士元

同考試官署郎中楊，批〔結歸重君德，知乾義之大者。〕

同考試官編修胡，批〔易義本難，諸作多浮泛牽綴，錄此以式。〕

同考試官編修亢，批〔得文言本㫖，錄之。〕
translation_en:
…the Way embodied in King Wen was thus once again entrusted to a successor. Those who understood it through seeing could await future sages, undivided from them by the long interval between their ages; those who understood it through hearing could carry on the legacy of earlier sages, unhindered by the difficulty of being born in time to encounter them. Such is how the Way has been transmitted without interruption. Could there alone have been no one to succeed Confucius? Ah! Mencius surely meant to take this responsibility upon himself as successor to these several sages. Yet consider: before King Wen, those who transmitted the Way all occupied high positions; only with Confucius was its transmitter in a low position. When sages and worthies attain office and occupy high positions, the Way is put into practice; when they lack opportunity and remain below, the Way is elucidated. Although this neither adds to nor detracts from their inherent moral endowment, their people are accordingly fortunate or unfortunate. This chapter of Mencius certainly shows the weight of the responsibility he assumed; does it not also express profound regret?

Book of Changes

“The gentleman practices these four virtues; hence it is said: ‘Qian: origination, flourishing, benefit, and steadfastness.’”

Zhuang Shiyuan

Associate Examiner Yang, Acting Bureau Director, comments: “The conclusion places particular emphasis on the ruler’s virtue: the author understands the greatness of Qian’s meaning.”

Associate Examiner Hu, a Compiler, comments: “Expounding the meaning of the Changes is inherently difficult. Most submissions are superficial and loosely patched together. This one is selected to serve as a model.”

Associate Examiner Kang, a Compiler, comments: “It grasps the original purport of the Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan). Selected for inclusion.”

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
同考試官編修張批講健以行德詞不費
而意自明
考試官侍講學士敖批簡潔
考試官大學士徐批說理明白
文言原君子之所以行德而舉經文以實之焉
夫四德在人非至健無以行之也觀聖人繫乾
之辭其義不可見乎文言以四德發乾之蘊至
此蓋曰四德命于天而具于人唯君子為能全
之者何也盖君子以自強不息之心造純一不
已之極發強剛毅契天運而有常剛健中正配
天行而無間夫是以德性用而物欲不行仁禮
成德而以之長人以之嘉會一其不息之心運
之也陽明勝而陰柔不雜義知成性而以之利
物以之幹事一其不已之純出之也非君子之
至健則四德之命於天者何以能兼體而不累
耶故聖人之繫易也不徒曰元亨利貞而必屬
之於乾者非無義也良以君子之健即乾也四
德之行即乾之元亨利貞也惟乾之純陽至健

《文言》原君子之所以行德，而舉經文以實之焉。夫四德在人，非至健無以行之也。觀聖人繫《乾》之辭，其義不可見乎？《文言》以四德發《乾》之蘊，至此蓋曰：四德命于天而具于人，唯君子為能全之者，何也？盖君子以自強不息之心，造純一不已之極。發強剛毅，契天運而有常；剛健中正，配天行而無間。夫是以德性用而物欲不行，仁、禮成德，而以之長人、以之嘉會，一其不息之心運之也；陽明勝而陰柔不雜，義、知成性，而以之利物、以之幹事，一其不已之純出之也。非君子之至健，則四德之命於天者，何以能兼體而不累耶？故聖人之繫《易》也，不徒曰「元、亨、利、貞」，而必屬之於《乾》者，非無義也。良以君子之健，即《乾》也；四德之行，即《乾》之「元、亨、利、貞」也。惟《乾》之純陽至健…
translation_en:
Associate Examiner and Historiographer of the Hanlin Academy (Bianxiu) Zhang comments: In explaining how vigor puts the virtues into practice, the words are not wasted and the meaning is naturally clear.
Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting (Shijiang xueshi) Ao comments: Concise and neat.
Examiner and Grand Secretary (Daxueshi) Xu comments: The explanation of principle is clear.

The Commentary on the Words of the Text (Wenyan) traces the reason why the noble man practices these virtues, and cites the text of the Classic to substantiate it. Now, although the four virtues reside in man, without the utmost vigor there is no way to put them into practice. Looking at the words that the Sage appended to the Qian hexagram, can its meaning not be seen? The Commentary on the Words of the Text uses the four virtues to bring out the profound meaning of Qian, and up to this point it says in effect: Why is it that of the four virtues ordained by Heaven and endowed in man, only the noble man is able to bring them to completion? It is because the noble man, with a mind of unceasing self-strengthening, reaches the ultimate of pure unity and unremittingness. Vigorous, strong, firm, and resolute, he tallies with the movement of Heaven and has constancy; firm, vigorous, central, and correct, he matches the action of Heaven without interruption. Therefore, his moral nature functions and material desires do not operate; benevolence and propriety perfect his virtue, and his using them to be a leader of men and to bring together excellence is entirely the operation of his unceasing mind. Bright yang prevails and soft yin does not adulterate it; righteousness and wisdom perfect his nature, and his using them to benefit things and to manage affairs is entirely the manifestation of his unremitting purity. Were it not for the utmost vigor of the noble man, how could the four virtues ordained by Heaven be simultaneously embodied without encumbrance? Therefore, when the Sage appended words to the Changes, he did not merely say "originating, penetrating, advantageous, and correct," but necessarily attached them to Qian—this is not without meaning. It is truly because the vigor of the noble man is none other than Qian, and the practice of the four virtues is none other than the "originating, penetrating, advantageous, and correct" of Qian. Only because Qian is pure yang and utmost vigor…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
也而元亨利貞之德所由統焉否則畫有陰陽
斯德有純雜矣而豈能以悉備若此哉惟聖人
觀象於乾也而元亨利貞之辭所由繫焉否則
或偏示其辭或互見其義矣又何以專屬之若
此哉吁聖人繫易之義深矣大抵乾君象也元
亨利貞君德也君德莫大於剛健故夫子翼易
於乾義獨詳焉盖必有配天不息之德而後可
以運御天時乘之化故於彖象互發之意有在
也宋儒之言曰有天德便可語王道殆知易者
===
哉
範圍天地之化而不過曲成萬物而不遺
通乎晝夜之道而知故神无方而易无體
吳可行
同考試官署郎中楊 批陰陽變化至根處即
是神易原非二物此作能說出可錄
同考試官編修胡 批神易通於造化此徹上
徹下之理然非聖人用易之功不可見也是作融
會傳義而詞不煩殆究心于易者

也，而元亨利貞之德所由統焉。否則畫有陰陽，斯德有純雜矣，而豈能以悉備若此哉？惟聖人觀象於乾也，而元亨利貞之辭所由繫焉。否則或偏示其辭，或互見其義矣，又何以專屬之若此哉？吁！聖人繫易之義深矣！大抵乾，君象也；元亨利貞，君德也。君德莫大於剛健，故夫子翼易，於乾義獨詳焉。盖必有配天不息之德，而後可以運御天時乘之化，故於彖象互發之意有在也。宋儒之言曰：「有天德便可語王道。」殆知易者哉！

範圍天地之化而不過，曲成萬物而不遺，通乎晝夜之道而知，故神无方而易无體。

吳可行

同考試官署郎中楊批：陰陽變化至根處，即是神易，原非二物。此作能說出，可錄。

同考試官編修胡批：神易通於造化，此徹上徹下之理，然非聖人用易之功不可見也。是作融會傳義而詞不煩，殆究心于易者。
translation_en:
…and through this the virtues of origination, flourishing, benefit, and firmness are united. Otherwise, if the lines contained both yin and yang, these virtues would be either pure or mixed: how could they all be fully present in this way? It was precisely because the sage contemplated the image of Qian that he attached to it the words “origination, flourishing, benefit, and firmness.” Otherwise, the wording might express only one aspect, or its meaning might appear across different hexagrams. How, then, could these words belong exclusively to Qian in this way? Ah, profound indeed is the meaning of the sage’s attachment of statements to the Changes! In general, Qian is the image of the ruler; origination, flourishing, benefit, and firmness are the ruler’s virtues. No virtue of a ruler is greater than firmness and vigor. Thus, when the Master composed the Wings to the Changes, he treated the meaning of Qian with particular fullness. Only through possessing unceasing virtue matching Heaven can one effect the transformations of governing in accord with Heaven and mounting its forces at the proper times. Hence there is a purpose in the mutually illuminating explanations of the Commentary on the Judgments and the Commentary on the Images. A Confucian scholar of the Song said: “Only with Heaven’s virtue can one speak of the Kingly Way.” Surely he understood the Changes!

“He encompasses the transformations of Heaven and Earth without exceeding them, brings the myriad things to completion in all their particularity without omitting any, and comprehends the Way of day and night and thereby knows. Thus the numinous has no fixed location, and change has no fixed form.”

Wu Kexing

Associate Examiner Yang, Acting Bureau Director, comments: “At their very root, the transformations of yin and yang are precisely the numinous and change; these were never two separate things. This composition succeeds in expressing this and merits inclusion.”

Associate Examiner Hu, Compiler, comments: “The numinous and change pervade the workings of creation. This principle extends throughout the highest and lowest realms, yet it cannot be perceived apart from the sage’s achievement in applying the Changes. This composition integrates the meanings of the commentaries without verbosity. Its author has surely devoted himself to studying the Changes.”

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
同考試官編修亢批潔淨明暢
同考試官編修張批神易之妙在易道上
說則易與天地準不虛矣此作得之
考試官侍講學士敖批精當
考試官大學士徐批簡明
大傳詳聖人以易至命之事有以見神易之妙
焉盖以易至命聖人之極功也神易之妙豈不
於是可見乎大傳賛易之意如此今夫易與天
地準者也聖人既以之窮理盡性矣其至命之
===
事何如哉彼天地之化命之流行也聖人以易
而範圍之化之運也無窮而其裁成也有道何
過之有萬物之生命之賦予也聖人以易而曲
成之物之類也雖衆而其兼體也則同何遺之
有至若晝夜之道命之循環而不已者也聖人
以易通而知之盖其心與晝夜相為終始而於
動靜無端之幾有黙契焉者又何不知之有夫
聖人之以易至命如此而易道之妙不可見乎
盖易之道一陰陽也自其根陰根陽而合一不

大傳詳聖人以易至命之事，有以見神易之妙焉。盖以易至命，聖人之極功也。神易之妙，豈不於是可見乎？大傳賛易之意如此。今夫易與天地準者也，聖人既以之窮理盡性矣，其至命之事何如哉？彼天地之化，命之流行也。聖人以易而範圍之，化之運也無窮，而其裁成也有道，何過之有？萬物之生，命之賦予也。聖人以易而曲成之，物之類也雖衆，而其兼體也則同，何遺之有？至若晝夜之道，命之循環而不已者也。聖人以易通而知之，盖其心與晝夜相為終始，而於動靜無端之幾有黙契焉者，又何不知之有？夫聖人之以易至命如此，而易道之妙不可見乎？盖易之道，一陰陽也。自其根陰根陽而合一不
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Kang, a Compiler, comments: “Pure and uncluttered, clear and fluent.”
Associate Examiner Zhang, a Compiler, comments: “When the subtleties of the numinous and of change are explained in terms of the Way of the Changes, the assertion that the Changes accords with Heaven and Earth is substantiated. This composition grasps that point.”
Examiner Ao, an Academician Expositor, comments: “Precise and apt.”
Examiner Xu, a Grand Secretary, comments: “Concise and clear.”
The Great Commentary describes in detail how the sage uses the Changes to reach an understanding of Heaven’s mandate, thereby revealing the subtleties of the numinous and of change. For reaching Heaven’s mandate through the Changes is the sage’s highest achievement. How could the subtleties of the numinous and of change fail to become evident here? Such is the intent of the Great Commentary in praising the Changes. Now, the Changes accords with Heaven and Earth. Having already used it to fathom principle and fully realize inherent nature, how does the sage proceed to reach Heaven’s mandate?
The transformations of Heaven and Earth are the flowing operation of the mandate. Through the Changes, the sage encompasses and regulates them. The movement of transformation is inexhaustible, yet his shaping and completing of it follows the Way: how could there be any excess? The coming into being of the myriad things is the bestowal of the mandate. Through the Changes, the sage brings each to fulfillment according to its particular circumstances. Though the kinds of things are numerous, he embodies them all alike: how could anything be omitted? As for the course of day and night, it is the unceasing cycle of the mandate. Through the Changes, the sage comprehends and knows it. His mind shares in the endings and beginnings of day and night, tacitly attuned to the incipient workings of movement and stillness, which have no beginning. What, then, could he fail to know?
Such is the sage’s attainment of Heaven’s mandate through the Changes. Does this not reveal the subtlety of the Way of the Changes? The Way of the Changes is simply yin and yang. Consider how it is rooted in yin and rooted in yang, uniting as one and not …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
測者謂之神凡天地之化萬物之理晝夜之道
舉於是乎出焉本無方也使其有方則物而已
爾何以周聖人無方之用耶故觀於至命而所
謂神者可見矣自其陽變陰化而變動不居者

測者謂之神。凡天地之化、萬物之理、晝夜之道，舉於是乎出焉，本無方也。使其有方，則物而已爾，何以周聖人無方之用耶？故觀於至命，而所謂神者可見矣。自其陽變陰化而變動不居者，謂之易。凡天地之化、萬物之理、晝夜之道，皆相為流通焉，本無體也。使其有體，則器而已爾，又何以資聖人無體之用耶？故觀於至命，而所謂易者可見矣。大哉，易也！斯其至乎！雖然，聖人有心易焉，洗心退藏，而神易之妙一以貫之。是故窮理、盡性、至命，一事也；易與聖人，一道也。不然，則索之卦爻，適以為鑿，烏足以語聖人之極功哉？故曰：「神而明之，存乎其人。」

書

帝庸作歌曰：「勅天之命，惟時惟幾。」乃歌曰：「股肱喜哉，元首起哉，百工熙哉！」臯陶拜手稽首，颺言曰：「念哉！率作興事，慎乃憲。欽哉！屢省乃成，欽哉！」乃賡載歌曰：「元首明哉，股肱良哉，庶事康哉！」
translation_en:
…what is unfathomable is called the numinous. The transformations of Heaven and Earth, the principles of the myriad things, and the course of day and night all issue from this; fundamentally, it has no fixed direction. If it had a fixed direction, it would merely be a thing. How could it encompass the sage’s functioning without fixed direction? Thus, by considering the attainment of an understanding of destiny, we can perceive what is called the numinous. Insofar as yang changes and yin transforms, changing and moving without rest, it is called Change. The transformations of Heaven and Earth, the principles of the myriad things, and the course of day and night all circulate through one another within it; fundamentally, it has no fixed form. If it had a fixed form, it would merely be an implement. How, then, could it sustain the sage’s functioning without fixed form? Thus, by considering the attainment of an understanding of destiny, we can perceive what is called Change. Great indeed are the Changes! Surely this is their highest reach! Nevertheless, the sage holds the Changes within his heart [?]: he cleanses his heart and withdraws into concealment, and a single principle runs through the subtleties of the numinous and of Change. Thus, fathoming principle, fully realizing one’s nature, and attaining an understanding of destiny are one undertaking; the Changes and the sage follow one Way. Otherwise, seeking it in the hexagrams and their lines would merely produce forced interpretations. How could that suffice to speak of the sage’s highest achievement? Hence it is said: “To apprehend it numinously and illuminate it depends upon the person.”

Book of Documents

The emperor thereupon composed a song, saying: “Be heedful of Heaven’s mandate; attend to the times and the first signs of change.” Then he sang: “When the arms and legs rejoice, the head rises to action, and the hundred officers flourish!” Gao Yao bowed with his hands together and touched his head to the ground, then declared aloud: “Keep this in mind! In leading undertakings and initiating affairs, be careful of your rules. Be reverent! Repeatedly examine your accomplishments. Be reverent!” Then he continued the song: “When the head is enlightened, the arms and legs are worthy, and all affairs proceed well!”

觀聖世君臣作歌之義而保治之心見矣盖天
===
下之治致之固難而保之尤難也有虞君臣作
歌以責難如此此其所以不可及歟昔帝舜當
至治之時懷惕厲之心用是以作歌曰天命靡
常至可畏也其可以不勅哉殆必謹畏之恒存
幾微之畢察而無有弗戒焉斯則帝之不自恃
而有望於其臣也乃歌曰股肱喜哉元首起哉
百工熙哉盖臣為股肱君所資以賛治者夫既
謹於時幾而奮庸熙載矣則君之治有不興而
百官之功有不廣乎是保治之道在臣君特責

觀聖世君臣作歌之義，而保治之心見矣。盖天下之治，致之固難，而保之尤難也。有虞君臣作歌以責難如此，此其所以不可及歟！昔帝舜當至治之時，懷惕厲之心，用是以作歌曰：「天命靡常，至可畏也，其可以不勅哉！殆必謹畏之恒存，幾微之畢察，而無有弗戒焉。」斯則帝之不自恃而有望於其臣也。乃歌曰：「股肱喜哉，元首起哉，百工熙哉！」盖臣為股肱，君所資以賛治者。夫既謹於時幾，而奮庸熙載矣，則君之治有不興，而百官之功有不廣乎？是保治之道在臣，君特責

Cao Dazhang

Associate Examiner Chen, Director, comments: “The scene of supreme harmony appears vividly before our eyes.”
Associate Examiner Zhang, Left Supervising Secretary, comments: “It captures the intent of the admonitions at the court of Yu. Record it as a model for the many scholars.”
Associate Examiner Dong, Compiler, comments: “The wording is concise, yet the meaning is complete.”
Associate Examiner Quan, Senior Compiler, comments: “Concise and weighty; worthy of selection.”
Examiner Ao, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Rigorous and orderly.”
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: “Refined and meticulous.”

By considering the meaning of the songs composed by ruler and ministers in a sage age, we perceive their concern to preserve good government. For good government throughout the realm is certainly difficult to achieve, but still more difficult to preserve. The ruler and ministers of Yu composed songs in this way to demand of one another the fulfillment of difficult duties. Was this not what made them unsurpassable?

Formerly, Emperor Shun, living in a time of perfect government, maintained a vigilant and cautious heart. Thus he composed a song, saying: “Heaven’s mandate is not constant; it is supremely to be feared. How could we fail to attend to it with care? Surely we must always maintain caution and awe, scrutinize every incipient sign, and leave nothing unguarded against.” This shows that the emperor did not rely upon himself alone, but placed expectations upon his ministers. He then sang: “When the arms and legs rejoice, the head rises, and the hundred offices flourish!”

The ministers are the arms and legs, upon whom the ruler relies to assist in governing. Once they attend carefully to timely action and incipient signs, exert themselves in service, and bring their undertakings to fruition, how could the ruler’s government fail to prosper, or the achievements of the hundred officials fail to expand? Thus the way to preserve good government lies with the ministers; the ruler merely holds them responsible …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
成焉耳帝之所以儆之臣者盖如此皐陶承儆
戒之命懷忠愛之心致敬以颺言曰天位維艱
不可忽也其可以不念哉殆必率作而慎其憲
屢省以考其成而無有弗敬焉斯則臣之有所
感而致望於其君也乃賡載歌曰元首明哉股
肱良哉庶事康哉盖君為元首臣所仰以主治
者夫既勤於綜覈而明庶以功矣則臣之職有
弗良而庶政之績有弗康乎是保治之本在君
臣特效法焉耳皐陶之所以儆之君者盖如此
===
是則于賡歌而見其上下之和焉于交儆而見
其上下之敬焉虞廷明良相遇之盛可以想見
其氣象矣自是而後及于有周鹿鳴諸詩君之
所以貺其臣也天保諸詩臣之所以答其君也
其交相酬和庶幾虞廷之遺響焉噫唐虞之際
于周為盛其信矣哉
嚴惟丕式克用三宅三俊其在商邑用協
于厥邑其在四方用丕式見德
張誼

弗良而庶政之績有弗康乎是保治之本在君

===
是則于賡歌而見其上下之和焉于文敎而見
其上下之敬焉虞廷明良相遇之盛可以想見
其氣象矣自是而後及于有周鹿鳴諸詩君之
所以貺其臣也天保諸詩臣之所以答其君也
其交相酬和庶幾虞廷之遺響焉噫唐虞之際
于周爲盛其信矣哉
嚴惟丕式克用三宅三俊其在商邑用協
于厥邑其在四方用丕式見德
張誼
punctuated:
成焉耳。帝之所以儆之臣者，盖如此。皐陶承儆戒之命，懷忠愛之心，致敬以颺言曰：「天位維艱，不可忽也，其可以不念哉？」殆必率作而慎其憲，屢省以考其成，而無有弗敬焉。斯則臣之有所感而致望於其君也。乃賡載歌曰：「元首明哉，股肱良哉，庶事康哉！」盖君為元首，臣所仰以主治者。夫既勤於綜覈而明庶以功矣，則臣之職有弗良，而庶政之績有弗康乎？是保治之本在君，臣特效法焉耳。皐陶之所以儆之君者，盖如此。是則于賡歌而見其上下之和焉，于交儆而見其上下之敬焉。虞廷明良相遇之盛，可以想見其氣象矣。自是而後，及于有周，《鹿鳴》諸詩，君之所以貺其臣也；《天保》諸詩，臣之所以答其君也。其交相酬和，庶幾虞廷之遺響焉。噫！唐虞之際，于周為盛，其信矣哉！
嚴惟丕式，克用三宅三俊。其在商邑，用協于厥邑；其在四方，用丕式見德。
張誼
translation_en:
…accomplishment from them, that is all. Such was the emperor’s way of admonishing his ministers. Gao Yao received the admonitory command and, cherishing loyalty and affection, reverently raised his voice: “The throne of Heaven is difficult to occupy and must not be treated lightly. How could one fail to keep this in mind?” Surely the ruler must lead the work and carefully observe its rules, repeatedly examining it to assess its accomplishment, leaving nothing unattended to with reverence. Here the minister, moved by what he had heard, expressed his hopes for his ruler. He then continued the song: “When the head is enlightened, the limbs are worthy, and all affairs prosper!” The ruler is the head, to whom ministers look to preside over government. If he diligently oversees and examines their work, discerning the abilities of all through their achievements, how could ministers fail to discharge their duties well, or the conduct of government fail to prosper? Thus the foundation for preserving good government lies with the ruler; ministers merely follow his example. Such was Gao Yao’s way of admonishing his ruler.
In their answering songs, we see the harmony between ruler and ministers; in their mutual admonitions, we see their reverence. We can thus imagine the flourishing court of Shun, where an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers met. Thereafter, in the Zhou dynasty, the poems beginning with “The Deer Cry” (Lu ming) were the means by which the ruler honored his ministers; those beginning with “Heaven Protects” (Tian bao) were the means by which ministers answered their ruler. Their exchanges of song came close to preserving an echo of Shun’s court. Ah! The saying that the achievements of the age of Yao and Shun flourished most fully under Zhou is indeed true!
“Reverently he took this as his great model and was able to employ men for the three offices and the three classes of outstanding men. Those in the capital of Shang brought harmony to that capital; those throughout the four quarters greatly followed his example and manifested virtue.”
Zhang Yi

Associate Examiner Chen, Director, comments: “This succeeds in explaining the substance of Cheng Tang’s understanding of what required his concern. It should be recorded as a model.”
Associate Examiner Zhang, Left Supervising Secretary, comments: “Concise in expression and clear in principle: this is the only composition of its kind I have seen.”
Associate Examiner Dong, Hanlin Editor, comments: “It succeeds in explaining Cheng Tang’s way of employing men to administer the glorious Mandate. Its conclusion returns to governing the mind, showing especially that it has a firm foundation. Accept it.”
Associate Examiner Quan, Hanlin Compiler, comments: “Its elucidation of the meaning of reflection and taking others as models is most pertinent. For this reason, it is selected for inclusion.”
Examiner Ao, Hanlin Academician Expositor, comments: “It grasps the purport.”
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: “Straightforward and substantial.”
When a sage ruler fully realizes the way of employing the worthy, good government throughout the realm is achieved. In governing, nothing takes precedence over employing the worthy. That a sage ruler can fully realize this way and thereby achieve good government reveals the substance of his understanding of what requires his concern. It was fitting that the Duke of Zhou should cite this when instructing King Cheng. His meaning was that, when an enlightened king establishes government, if he wishes fully to discharge his duty of serving Heaven, he must ground it in sincerity in employing the worthy. How did Tang deal with officeholders and men of outstanding talent? When reflection falls short, doubts arise. Tang, however, earnestly cherished a disposition to ponder and examine [?]; his concentrated attention admitted no interruption through names or words [?]. When adherence to models is incomplete, counsels become divided. Tang, however, embodied the benefits of learning from others as teachers and took their plans and counsels as his standard, without the slightest wavering between following and rejecting them. Thus, inspired by his sincerity, his officeholders were able to fulfill their duties, sparing no effort in carrying out the charge of the glorious Mandate. Loyalty…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
信所勸有以著其俊者之才而耿命之陳也無
餘蘊矣吾見賢知有奮庸之美天下登至治之
休以商邑言之未易以協也今則政教施而漸
摩洽有孚惠德有孚惠心翕然習俗之化也情
之難齊者于是乎齊矣不謂純之至乎以四方
言之未易以式也今則章軌立而觀法同會其
有極歸其有極沛然聲教之訖也德之難徧者
于是乎徧矣不謂大之至乎此成湯之知恤而
耿命之不釐也有由然矣抑觀之仲虺之誥曰
===
以義制事以禮制心則知湯之所以克用三宅
三俊者實本於治心以立取人之則也雖然豈
惟湯哉有敬德之禹而後有迪知忱恂之臣有
丕顯丕承之文武而後有克知灼見之臣此周
公之所以告君惓惓而三代有道之長可見矣
詩
維此文王小心翼翼昭事上帝聿懷多福
厥德不回以受方國

信所勸，有以著其俊者之才，而耿命之陳也無餘蘊矣。吾見賢知有奮庸之美，天下登至治之休。以商邑言之，未易以協也。今則政教施而漸摩洽，有孚惠德，有孚惠心，翕然習俗之化也。情之難齊者，於是乎齊矣，不謂純之至乎？以四方言之，未易以式也。今則章軌立而觀法同，會其有極，歸其有極，沛然聲教之訖也。德之難徧者，於是乎徧矣，不謂大之至乎？此成湯之知恤，而耿命之不釐也，有由然矣。抑觀之，《仲虺之誥》曰：「以義制事，以禮制心。」則知湯之所以克用三宅三俊者，實本於治心以立取人之則也。雖然，豈惟湯哉？有敬德之禹，而後有迪知忱恂之臣；有丕顯丕承之文武，而後有克知灼見之臣。此周公之所以告君惓惓，而三代有道之長可見矣。
詩
維此文王，小心翼翼，昭事上帝，聿懷多福。厥德不回，以受方國。
張書紳
translation_en:
…encouraged by trustworthiness, the outstanding men could manifest their talents, leaving nothing unexpressed in their exposition of the illustrious mandate. I see the worthy and wise achieving the distinction of energetic service, and all under Heaven attaining the blessings of consummate order. As for the city of Shang, bringing it into harmony was no easy matter. Now, however, government and instruction were put into effect, and their gradual, formative influence spread everywhere. There was sincerity in beneficent virtue and sincerity in beneficent intentions; customs were transformed in general concord. Human dispositions, so difficult to bring into accord, were thereby harmonized. Could this not be called the utmost purity? As for the four quarters, bringing them to follow a model was no easy matter. Now, however, regulations and standards were established, and all looked to the same example. They assembled around the supreme standard and turned toward it; the influence of instruction reached everywhere in abundance. Virtue, so difficult to spread universally, thereby became universal. Could this not be called the utmost greatness? Thus there was a reason why Cheng Tang understood his responsibilities and why his illustrious mandate was not severed [?].
Moreover, consider the Announcement of Zhonghui, which says: “Regulate affairs by righteousness; regulate the mind by ritual propriety.” From this we know that Tang’s ability to employ men in the three kinds of office and the three categories of outstanding men was fundamentally grounded in governing his own mind, thereby establishing a standard for selecting men. Yet was this true only of Tang? Only after there was a Yu who revered virtue were there ministers possessed of guiding wisdom, sincerity, and trustworthiness. Only after there were Kings Wen and Wu, who greatly manifested and carried forward their inheritance, were there ministers capable of understanding and clear discernment. This is why the Duke of Zhou so earnestly admonished his ruler; here we can see the enduring strength of the Way under the Three Dynasties.
Book of Odes
This King Wen was cautious and reverent. He illustriously served the Lord on High and thereby brought abundant blessings. His virtue did not deviate, and thus he received the states of the four quarters.
Zhang Shushen

translation_en:
Associate Examiner Xie, Left Supervising Secretary, comments: “The discussion of King Wen’s reverent cultivation of virtue and receipt of the Mandate is apt and worth reciting. It affords a glimpse of the writer’s self-cultivation.”

Associate Examiner Jiang, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “King Wen won Heaven and the people through reverence alone. This essay elucidates the point with precision; it profoundly grasps the poet’s intent and should be recorded as a model.”

Associate Examiner Zhu, Hanlin Reviewer, comments: “Heaven’s favor and the people’s allegiance are very easy topics to elaborate upon, so contemporary essays are often prolix and cluttered. This one alone grounds its argument in the learning of the mind-and-heart. Its author evidently possesses cultivated understanding.”

Associate Examiner Sun, Hanlin Reviewer, comments: “The discussion of King Wen’s reverent cultivation of virtue is exceptionally clear and thorough. This is someone with whom one can discuss the learning of the mind-and-heart.”

Associate Examiner Qu, Hanlin Compiler, comments: “The quality of being ‘careful and reverent’ is exceptionally difficult to portray. This essay captures it almost completely. Its author evidently understands King Wen’s mind-and-heart. Record it.”

Examiner Ao, Hanlin Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “Clear and fluent.”

Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: “Skillfully portrays King Wen’s reverent cultivation of virtue.”

A great minister points to the actual circumstances in which an earlier king received the Mandate through abundant virtue: profound indeed is his intention in thereby enlightening a later king. For Heaven to favor him and the people to turn to him is possible only through virtue abundant in the highest degree. Was this not how King Wen received the Mandate and founded Zhou? It was fitting that the Duke of Zhou should recount this to admonish King Cheng. In effect, he said: The Mandate of our Zhou dynasty truly began with King Wen’s virtue. And what was his virtue like? This King Wen, inwardly solemn and reverent …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
蘊天命之顧諟者不以一息而有懈敬畏中存
帝則之默順者不以幾微而有忽齊明以澄其
心既已退藏於密矣視之若猶未也而不顯亦
臨焉緝熙以持其敬既已安於所止矣視之若
猶未也而無射亦保焉其翼翼小心有如此故
以此心而事帝也則為事天之明對越在下秉
精白以承休德者豈有意於徼福哉然天之所
親者敬也其敬不已自足以懷多福而天亦不
能違之矣以此心而治民也則為皇極之建大
===
觀在上履中正而無畔援者豈有意於求媚哉
然民之所懷者德也其德不回自足以受方國
而人亦不能外之矣夫以文王之德始於一敬
而終於天人之相與如此為後王者可不知所
務乎抑祗台德先禹以王夏聖敬日躋湯以王
商然則敬也者非傳心之要王天下之本乎盖
不獨周之世德為然也使其子孫能守而勿失
則周之祚寧有窮乎成王以冲年撫成業其心
易以肆者此周公所以惓惓也卒之基命宥密

punctuated: 蘊，天命之顧諟者，不以一息而有懈；敬畏中存，帝則之默順者，不以幾微而有忽。齊明以澄其心，既已退藏於密矣，視之若猶未也，而不顯亦臨焉；緝熙以持其敬，既已安於所止矣，視之若猶未也，而無射亦保焉。其翼翼小心有如此。故以此心而事帝也，則為事天之明，對越在下，秉精白以承休德者，豈有意於徼福哉？然天之所親者敬也，其敬不已，自足以懷多福，而天亦不能違之矣。以此心而治民也，則為皇極之建，大觀在上，履中正而無畔援者，豈有意於求媚哉？然民之所懷者德也，其德不回，自足以受方國，而人亦不能外之矣。夫以文王之德，始於一敬，而終於天人之相與如此，為後王者可不知所務乎？抑「祗台德先」，禹以王夏；「聖敬日躋」，湯以王商。然則敬也者，非傳心之要、王天下之本乎？盖不獨周之世德為然也。使其子孫能守而勿失，則周之祚寧有窮乎？成王以冲年撫成業，其心易以肆者，此周公所以惓惓也。卒之基命宥密
translation_en:
…held within: in keeping Heaven’s mandate constantly before him, he did not slacken for a single breath. Reverent awe dwelt in his heart: in silently following the Supreme Lord’s standards, he neglected not even the slightest stirrings. Through purification and clarity he made his heart limpid; although he had already withdrawn into its hidden depths, he regarded this as still insufficient, and even where nothing was manifest, he acted as though under watch. Through sustained illumination he maintained his reverence; although already at ease in his proper resting place, he regarded this as still insufficient, and preserved it without weariness. Such was his careful vigilance.

Thus, when he served the Supreme Lord with this heart, he served Heaven with understanding. Responding reverently from below, he maintained purity and sincerity to receive Heaven’s gracious virtue: could he have intended to solicit blessings? Yet what Heaven holds dear is reverence. His unceasing reverence was itself sufficient to attract manifold blessings, and Heaven could not turn away from him. When he governed the people with this heart, he established the sovereign standard. Displaying a great example from above, he followed the mean and what was right, without deviation or grasping ambition: could he have intended to curry favor? Yet what the people cherish is virtue. His undeviating virtue was itself sufficient to win the allegiance of the regional states, and the people could not exclude themselves from his rule.

King Wen’s virtue began in reverence alone and culminated in this mutual accord with Heaven and humanity. Could succeeding kings fail to recognize what they must attend to? Moreover, by ‘reverently putting my virtue first,’ Yu became king over Xia; through ‘sagely reverence daily ascending,’ Tang became king over Shang. Is reverence, then, not the essential means of transmitting the heart’s teaching and the foundation for ruling all under Heaven? Surely this was true not only of the virtue handed down through the generations of Zhou. If his descendants could preserve it without loss, how could Zhou’s dynastic fortune ever come to an end? King Cheng inherited an established dominion while still a child, when his heart could easily grow unrestrained. This was why the Duke of Zhou was so earnestly concerned. In the end, in establishing the mandate with profound stillness …

translation_en:
…became an excellent ruler of Zhou, worthy of comparison with King Wen. From this, the gentleman understands that the Duke of Zhou’s loyal devotion knew no end.

“Long-lived and at peace, to protect us, his descendants.”
Yang Wenzheng

Comment by Associate Examiner Xie, Left Supervising Secretary: This captures the intent of the people of Shang in praising Gaozong, and its language is also classical and elegant. It merits inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Chief Supervising Secretary: This composition elucidates almost fully Gaozong’s achievements and virtue in restoring the dynasty and providing for posterity. It should be included.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhu, Hanlin Academy Examining Editor: His provision for posterity resulted from his long reign. This is where the people of Shang excelled in praising Gaozong, and the language adequately brings it out. It should be included as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, Hanlin Academy Examining Editor: It enters sympathetically into the intent of the people of Shang in praising Gaozong and expresses it in concise, antique language. Indeed, it should not be regarded merely as an examination composition.

Comment by Associate Examiner Qu, Hanlin Academy Compiler: It brings out Gaozong’s provision for posterity. Warm and generous in tone, it rewards recitation; it is no careless composition.

Comment by Examiner Ao, Hanlin Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: The spirit of dynastic restoration comes vividly to life.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary: It captures the intent of the praise of Gaozong.

When the people of Shang praised their worthy king, they invariably spoke of his long reign and the blessings he bequeathed to distant posterity. For a ruler’s long reign is a blessing to all under Heaven. A worthy king enjoyed this, and surely later generations…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
所永賴歟商人之頌高宗若曰我高宗之中興
也表極建而聲威振夫既極一時之盛矣是豈
惟增前人之光哉一德之格天有以凝保定之
命多方之助順有以斂和平之福以總萬幾則
之綱之紀者久而彌見其精明也年所之多歷
有迓續于天者矣以御萬邦則君之宗之者久
而益見其尊安也福履之交綏有獨厚于天者
矣我高宗之壽考且寧如此施之後世不有以
保我後生哉盖其經營之勤固將以貽燕也而
===
化成於悠久則其本固者其廕遠自衍夫宗社
之休興復之勞固將以垂裕也而治隆於熈洽
則其源深者其澤長自篤夫邦家之祜皇圖永
奠而一統之盛猶夫肇域之初也人心永戴而
四海之假猶夫撻武之日也威德之所留豈有
窮哉吁此高宗之功所以當百世祀也抑考高
宗之中興在此詩既稱其不僭不濫不敢怠遑
而監成憲師甘盤相傅說載諸書者又不一而
足盖其所以成外攘之績實本乎內修而所謂
