…upon which later generations may forever rely? The Shang people's praise of Gaozong is as if to say: “In the restoration achieved by our Gaozong, the supreme standard was established, and his fame and might resounded. He had indeed brought the age to the height of prosperity. Could this merely have added lustre to his predecessors? His undivided virtue reached Heaven, thereby securing the mandate that protected and established him; the many regions supported his rightful rule, thereby gathering the blessings of peace and harmony. In overseeing the myriad affairs of government, the guiding principles and ordering rules he applied displayed ever greater clarity and discernment as time passed. Through the many years of his reign, he received from Heaven a continuing succession of blessings. In governing the myriad states, those who acknowledged him as ruler and revered him as their sovereign saw his honour and security increase with time. In the blessings that together brought him peace, Heaven showed him exceptional favour. Since our Gaozong enjoyed such longevity and tranquillity, would their influence upon later ages not protect us, his descendants?

“His diligent labours in ordering the realm were certainly intended to bequeath ease to posterity. As his transforming influence reached fulfilment over a long span of time, its firm roots afforded far-reaching shade, naturally extending the blessings of the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain. His labours of revival and restoration were certainly intended to hand down abundance. As his government flourished in harmony and concord, its deep source sustained a lasting flow of beneficence, naturally enriching the blessings of the state. The imperial enterprise was established forever, and the splendour of unified rule remained as it had been when the realm was first founded. The people's hearts upheld him forever, and the allegiance of all within the four seas remained as it had been in the days of martial might. Could the enduring influence of his majesty and virtue ever be exhausted? Ah! It is for these achievements that Gaozong deserves sacrifices for a hundred generations.”

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
負之以為固舊矣茲而俛首以聽于齊承寡君
之願若恐後者齊何以得此哉良由陘亭之次
桓責之以義耳盖惟義可以服人楚恃其強卑
周而廢職貢非義也于時齊桓申先君之命聲
罪討之徵包茅之不入問王祭之不供齊有詞
矣楚安得不畏而服哉故夫按兵不動以數千
里之強夷帖然而請盟者非中國之力能制之
也義有出於人心之同然耳聖人樂與人為善
者也故特書曰来盟序桓績也不然則後此國
===
佐袁婁之盟耳要之而至豈仗義執言之功哉
齊人曷為歸地乎謝魯過也夫東方之國莫強
於齊鄆讙龜陰之地侵之以為利舊矣茲而藉
手以委于魯聽賢臣之言若弗遑者魯何以得
此哉良由夾谷之會孔子責之以禮耳盖惟禮
可以化人齊逞其詐弱魯以干盟好非禮也于
時仲尼相兩君之好馳詞當之拒兵車之命罷
宴享之設我有禮矣齊安得不感而化哉故夫
歷階一對以數十年之侵疆幡然而效順者非

佐來婁之盟耳要之而至豈仗義執言之功哉
齊人曷為歸地乎謝魯過也夫東方之國莫強
於齊鄆讙龜陰之地侵之以為利舊矣茲而藉
手以委于魯聽賢臣之言若弗違者魯何以得
此哉良由夾谷之會孔子責之以禮耳蓋惟禮
可以化人齊逞其詐弱魯以干盟好非禮也于
時仲尼相兩君之好馳詞當之拒兵車之命罷
宴享之設我有禮矣齊安得不感而化哉故夫
歷階一對以數十年之侵疆幡然而效順者非
punctuated:
負之以為固舊矣。茲而俛首以聽于齊，承寡君之願若恐後者，齊何以得此哉？良由陘亭之次，桓責之以義耳。盖惟義可以服人。楚恃其強，卑周而廢職貢，非義也。于時齊桓申先君之命，聲罪討之，徵包茅之不入，問王祭之不供，齊有詞矣，楚安得不畏而服哉？故夫按兵不動，以數千里之強夷帖然而請盟者，非中國之力能制之也，義有出於人心之同然耳。聖人樂與人為善者也，故特書曰：「来盟。」序桓績也。不然，則後此國佐袁婁之盟耳，要之而至，豈仗義執言之功哉？

齊人曷為歸地乎？謝魯過也。夫東方之國莫強於齊，鄆、讙、龜陰之地，侵之以為利舊矣。茲而藉手以委于魯，聽賢臣之言若弗遑者，魯何以得此哉？良由夾谷之會，孔子責之以禮耳。盖惟禮可以化人。齊逞其詐，弱魯以干盟好，非禮也。于時仲尼相兩君之好，馳詞當之，拒兵車之命，罷宴享之設，我有禮矣，齊安得不感而化哉？故夫歷階一對，以數十年之侵疆幡然而效順者，非
translation_en:
…had long relied on these as secure defenses. Now, however, Chu bowed its head and obeyed Qi, carrying out “my lord’s wish” as though afraid of falling behind. How did Qi achieve this? It was simply because, when encamped at Xingting, Duke Huan called Chu to account on grounds of righteousness. Only righteousness can bring people to submit. Chu relied on its strength, treated Zhou with contempt, and neglected its prescribed tribute: this was unrighteous. Duke Huan of Qi thereupon invoked the mandate received by his former lord, proclaimed Chu’s offenses, and moved against it. He demanded an accounting for its failure to deliver the bundled mao grass and questioned its failure to supply the royal sacrifices. Qi had just grounds for its words; how could Chu fail to submit in fear? Thus, when Qi held its troops motionless and the powerful non-Chinese state, extending over several thousand li, meekly requested a covenant, it was not the military strength of the Central States that could subdue it. Rather, righteousness arose from what all human hearts acknowledge alike. The Sage delighted in helping others do good. Hence he specifically wrote, “came to make a covenant,” recording Duke Huan’s achievement. Otherwise, this would merely have been like Guo Zuo’s later covenant at Yuanlou: he came under compulsion. How could that count as an achievement won by upholding righteousness and speaking on its behalf?

Why did the people of Qi return the territory? To make amends for their offense against Lu. Among the eastern states, none was stronger than Qi. It had long seized the lands of Yun, Huan, and Guiyin for its own advantage. Now, however, it handed them over to Lu, heeding the worthy minister’s words with seemingly breathless haste. How did Lu achieve this? It was simply because, at the meeting at Jiagu, Confucius called Qi to account on grounds of ritual propriety. Only ritual propriety can transform people. Qi gave free rein to its deceit, treating Lu as weak and violating their covenant of friendship: this was contrary to ritual propriety. Zhongni then assisted at the friendly meeting of the two rulers, promptly countering Qi with his words, rejecting the demand concerning war chariots, and having the proposed banquet canceled. With ritual propriety on our side, how could Qi fail to be moved and transformed? Thus, when a single response delivered upon ascending the steps caused Qi abruptly to change course and demonstrate submission by returning territory it had encroached upon for several decades, it was not…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
魯之力能及此也禮有出於人心之同然耳聖
人以天自處者也故亦書曰来歸自序績也不
然則前此齊惠濟西之歸耳請之而得豈過化
存神之妙哉雖然齊之服楚非心服也以力假
仁者也若孔子之化齊則心服也使桓微八國
江黄之助楚肯為齊下乎嗣而圍許敗徐桓盖
不能終抑之矣仲尼試于齊三田歸焉試于魯
三都墮焉使其得邦家綏和動来之效當何如
也女樂歸不稅冕而行天也此固王伯之辨世

punctuated:
魯之力能及此也，禮有出於人心之同然耳。聖人以天自處者也，故亦書曰「来歸」，自序績也。不然，則前此齊惠濟西之歸耳，請之而得，豈過化存神之妙哉！雖然，齊之服楚非心服也，以力假仁者也。若孔子之化齊，則心服也。使桓微八國、江黄之助，楚肯為齊下乎？嗣而圍許、敗徐，桓盖不能終抑之矣。仲尼試于齊，三田歸焉；試于魯，三都墮焉。使其得邦家，綏和動来之效當何如也？女樂歸，不稅冕而行，天也。此固王伯之辨，世道升降之機與！
冬，公會晉侯、宋公、衛侯、曹伯、莒子、邾子、滕子、薛伯、杞伯、小邾子、齊世子光伐鄭。十有二月己亥，同盟于戲。襄公九年。
孫鳴世。
同考試官主事畢批：能言聖人予晉不戰之意。
同考試官檢討林批：得春秋與晉之旨，明暢可錄。
translation_en:
…It was not the power of Lu that could accomplish this; ritual propriety springs from what human hearts universally acknowledge. The sage takes Heaven as his own standard. Thus he also wrote, “came to return,” recording his own achievement. Otherwise, this would merely have been like the earlier return of Jixi by Duke Hui of Qi: something obtained by requesting it. How could that embody the wonder of transforming wherever one passes and exerting a spiritual influence wherever one remains? Yet Qi’s subjugation of Chu did not win submission of the heart: it borrowed the guise of benevolence through force. Confucius’s transformation of Qi, by contrast, won submission of the heart. Had Duke Huan lacked the assistance of the eight states and of Jiang and Huang, would Chu have consented to bow to Qi? Subsequently, Chu besieged Xu 許 and defeated Xu 徐; Duke Huan evidently could not keep it in check to the end. When Zhongni put his abilities to the test in Qi, three tracts of land were returned; when he did so in Lu, the walls of the three cities were demolished. Had he obtained rule over a state, what results might he have achieved in bringing peace and harmony, and in attracting people through his actions? When the female musicians were presented, he departed without taking off his ceremonial cap: this was Heaven’s doing. Surely this is the distinction between true kingship and hegemony, the pivotal point in the rise and decline of the moral order!
“In winter, the duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi 杞, the Viscount of Xiao Zhu, and Guang, heir apparent of Qi 齊, in attacking Zheng. In the twelfth month, on the jihai day, they jointly covenanted at Xi.” Ninth year of Duke Xiang.
Sun Mingshi.
Comment by Associate Examiner Bi, Secretary: “Successfully articulates the sage’s intention in approving Jin for not fighting.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Examining Editor: “Grasps the intent of the Spring and Autumn Annals in approving Jin. Clear and fluent; worthy of inclusion.”

不予之乎且晉悼帥列國之師以伐鄭而為戲
之盟焉固未能即得鄭也春秋遽予之何哉誠
以善用兵者非能戰之貴而能謀之貴非勝敵
之難而不戰以屈人之難晉楚爭鄭為日久矣

===
荀偃以與楚戰豈計之得乎幸而有見于此以
為逞吾之衆以禦楚則我勞而敵未可以力爭
分吾之兵以敝楚則敵勞而我可以坐勝寧還

時之從人徒見反覆之鄭而晉許之盟其成未
可知也而不知所以服鄭者此也以全取勝蓋
無遺策矣人徒見陸梁之楚而晉避其鋒其勢

師養銳不徼乎一勝之捷修德息民不必其一
時之從人徒見反覆之鄭而晉許之盟其成未
可知也而不知所以服鄭者此也以全取勝蓋
無遺筴矣人徒見陸梁之楚而晉避其鋒其勢
若少懦也而不知所以屈楚者此也以靜制動
蓋有成算矣卒之蕭魚之會良霄之執鄭不敢
punctuated:
考試官侍講學士敖批：以謀取勝，於此可見。
考試官大學士徐批：善發揮。
伯主用善勝之謀以敝外，春秋所以予之也。夫善勝敵者以謀也，悼之敝楚進于是矣，春秋得不予之乎？且晉悼帥列國之師以伐鄭，而為戲之盟焉，固未能即得鄭也，春秋遽予之何哉？誠以善用兵者，非能戰之貴，而能謀之貴；非勝敵之難，而不戰以屈人之難。晉楚爭鄭為日久矣，方鄵門之師而鄭人請成也，使悼違知罃而用荀偃以與楚戰，豈計之得乎？幸而有見于此，以為逞吾之衆以禦楚，則我勞而敵未可以力爭；分吾之兵以敝楚，則敵勞而我可以坐勝。寧還師養銳，不徼乎一勝之捷；修德息民，不必其一時之從。人徒見反覆之鄭，而晉許之盟，其成未可知也，而不知所以服鄭者此也。以全取勝，蓋無遺策矣。人徒見陸梁之楚，而晉避其鋒，其勢若少懦也，而不知所以屈楚者此也。以靜制動，蓋有成算矣。卒之蕭魚之會，良霄之執，鄭不敢
translation_en:
Examiner Ao, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Here one can see victory achieved through strategy.”
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: “An effective elaboration.”
The hegemon employed a strategy for securing victory to wear down his external adversaries: this is why the Spring and Autumn Annals approves of him. Those adept at defeating an enemy rely on strategy. Duke Dao’s wearing down of Chu attained this standard; how could the Spring and Autumn Annals fail to approve of him? Duke Dao of Jin led the armies of the various states to attack Zheng and concluded the covenant at Xi. He had certainly not yet secured Zheng’s allegiance. Why, then, did the Spring and Autumn Annals so promptly accord him approval? It is because, in employing armies well, what is prized is skill in planning rather than prowess in battle; the difficult thing is to subdue others without fighting rather than merely to defeat an enemy.
Jin and Chu had long contended over Zheng. When the army was at the gate of Cao and the people of Zheng requested peace, had Duke Dao disregarded Zhi Ying and followed Xun Yan in doing battle with Chu, could that have been sound strategy? Fortunately, he understood this. He reasoned: “If I exert the strength of my host to resist Chu, we will exhaust ourselves, while the enemy cannot yet be overcome by force. If I divide my troops to wear down Chu, the enemy will be exhausted, while we can win without exertion.” He preferred to withdraw his army and husband its vigor, rather than seek the success of a single victory; to cultivate virtue and give the people respite, rather than insist on Zheng’s immediate submission.
Others saw only Zheng’s wavering allegiance and Jin’s willingness to grant it a covenant, whose success remained uncertain. They did not understand that this was precisely the means of bringing Zheng into submission. By securing victory with his strength intact, he had surely left no aspect of strategy unprovided for. Others saw only Chu’s unruly aggression and Jin’s avoidance of its onslaught, which seemed somewhat timid. They did not understand that this was precisely the means of subduing Chu. By using stillness to control movement, he surely had a settled plan. In the end, with the meeting at Xiaoyu and the seizure of Liang Xiao, Zheng did not dare …

translation_en:
…rebel, while Chu could not contend—was this not because he delighted in planning and brought his plans to completion? The gentleman says: “How fitting that Duke Dao of Jin restored his state's hegemony! His minister understood the methods of skillful military deployment and thereby assisted his ruler; his ruler could employ the arts of securing victory and thereby prevail over the enemy. Since Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin, none had achieved such success against Chu as on this occasion. Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals subsequently records the meeting at Xiaoyu to commend him, revealing the Sage's concern for caution in employing military force. Yet Duke Dao's victory over Chu was not due to Ying alone. Wei Jiang, Qi Xi, and the other ministers together assisted him, and his appointments were well chosen. The counselors of rival states had long known that they could not contend with him. Why would they have waited until their strength was exhausted before submitting? Zheng had a Zichan but could not employ him, and Jin and Chu attacked it in turn. With sacrificial animals, jade, and silk held ready at its two borders, could it sustain itself as a state? Alas! Such is the bearing of employing men upon a state. Can we fail to take warning?”
Record of Rites
“The Son of Heaven then, on the first auspicious day, prays to the Lord on High for grain.”
Luo Liang

Associate Examiner Wang, a Hanlin Academy Compiler, comments: “The topic itself is clear, but most writers treat it superficially and vaguely. This essay alone is precise in both language and meaning. I select it.”

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
考試官侍講學士敖批明健
考試官大學士徐批説得先王勤民之意出
王者因時以祈農事勤民之意至矣盖民生所
資以養者穀也先王於元日而預以祈之其知
所重者乎記者之意盖曰天之立君以養民為
職而君之為政以順時為先彼孟春之月農祥
正矣土脉膏矣耕籍之典欲舉於東郊布農之
命将申於田畯於此而祈年之禮其容後乎先
王以為及時而耕者農也而所以使之耕而必
===
穫者則有賴於天之降康生百穀以利民者地
也而所以使之生而必成者則有資乎神之垂
佑于焉值上辛之吉以祗修祀事而一念之精
禋有以孚諸冥漠際發生之候以殷薦明神而
内心之誠敬有以見之禱祠奉帝以祀於郊而
天神於是乎格也推稷以配乎帝而人鬼於是
乎歆也假祝史之薦辭以達有秋之望冀神功
之默相以慰三農之求盖祭非徼福而享獻妥
侑之勤不以為褻志實在民而陶匏藁靿之陳

考試官大學士徐批：説得先王勤民之意出。
王者因時以祈農事，勤民之意至矣。盖民生所資以養者，穀也。先王於元日而預以祈之，其知所重者乎！記者之意盖曰：天之立君，以養民為職；而君之為政，以順時為先。彼孟春之月，農祥正矣，土脉膏矣，耕籍之典欲舉於東郊，布農之命将申於田畯，於此而祈年之禮，其容後乎？先王以為及時而耕者，農也；而所以使之耕而必穫者，則有賴於天之降康。生百穀以利民者，地也；而所以使之生而必成者，則有資乎神之垂佑。于焉值上辛之吉，以祗修祀事，而一念之精禋，有以孚諸冥漠；際發生之候，以殷薦明神，而内心之誠敬，有以見之禱祠。奉帝以祀於郊，而天神於是乎格也；推稷以配乎帝，而人鬼於是乎歆也。假祝史之薦辭，以達有秋之望；冀神功之默相，以慰三農之求。盖祭非徼福，而享獻妥侑之勤，不以為褻；志實在民，而陶匏藁靿之陳，
translation_en:
Examiner Ao, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Clear and vigorous.”
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: “Brings out the former kings’ concern for the people.”
The true king follows the seasons in praying for agricultural success: his concern for the people is utmost. Grain is what sustains the people’s lives. By praying for it beforehand on the auspicious first day, did not the former kings understand what deserved priority? The recorder’s meaning is, it would seem, this: Heaven establishes rulers with the duty of nourishing the people, and rulers, in administering government, give precedence to following the seasons. In the first month of spring, the constellation that signals agricultural work has reached its proper position, and the soil is rich with moisture. The ceremony of plowing the royal field is about to be held in the eastern suburbs, and instructions concerning farming are about to be issued to the field overseers. At such a time, could the rite of praying for a fruitful year be postponed? The former kings considered that farmers plow at the proper time, but ensuring that their plowing yields a harvest depends on Heaven’s bestowing blessings. Earth produces the many grains to benefit the people, but ensuring that what grows reaches maturity depends on the spirits’ protection. Thus, on the auspicious first xin day, the king reverently performs the sacrifices, and the purity of his single-minded devotion reaches the unseen realm. At the season when life begins to emerge, he makes abundant offerings to the luminous spirits, expressing his heartfelt sincerity and reverence in prayers and sacrifices. He honors the Lord on High with sacrifice in the suburbs, and the celestial spirits arrive; he elevates Hou Ji to share in the sacrifice to the Lord on High, and the ancestral spirit accepts the offerings. Through the invocations presented by the invocators and scribes, he conveys his hope for a harvest; he seeks the unseen assistance of divine power to fulfill the wishes of farmers working the three kinds of land. Sacrifice is not a means of begging for blessings, yet the painstaking presentation of offerings and rites to settle and urge the spirits to partake is not regarded as importunate. His purpose truly lies with the people, and the setting out of earthenware and gourd vessels, straw and boot shafts [?] …

translation_en:
…why would they shrink from the trouble? This was one aspect of the former kings’ policies of attending to the foundation of livelihood and benefiting the people. That they undertook it first on the first day of the year shows that they understood the urgency of attending to first things. Moreover, the house of Zhou founded its state through agriculture. Thus the Zhou institutions recorded in the Monthly Ordinances are especially detailed concerning sowing and reaping. Examples include prayers to the celestial powers, sacrifices to mountains, rivers, and the sources of streams, and rain sacrifices to former lords and high ministers. With the ruler directing his attention in this way, there was surely a reason why no farmer left his fields untilled and why abundant harvests repeatedly brought rejoicing year after year! Regrettably, in later ages this concern faded, and there were even those who encroached upon farmers’ working time, ultimately leaving the fields waterlogged and overgrown.

“When employed in winning battles, it is invincible; when employed in ritual and righteousness, it brings obedience and order. Invincible abroad and bringing obedience and order at home: this is called abundant virtue.”
Zhu Shilian

Associate Examiner Wang, a Compiler, comments: “The emphasis of the topic lies in making good use of one’s courage, thereby showing why it is valued. This composition draws out the distinctions clearly and grasps the purport very well.”

Examiner Xu, a Grand Secretary, comments: “Clear and fluent.”

The gentleman achieves results wherever he applies himself; from this we can discern what he has cultivated within. For only after cultivating it deeply can he employ it with ample resources. The gentleman, in his own person, achieves results both at home and abroad; without abundant…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
德其孰能之記聘義者盖以天下之事非有勇
者固不足以任重而非善用其勇者亦不足以
成功君子之以禮自養也而豈徒哉自其有事
而用之戰勝也則謀猷壯而聲威振盖不假於
兵革之強而天下自畏矣孰有抗之者乎自其
無事而用之禮義也則彝倫敘而教本端盖不
出乎揖讓之間而禮俗自刑矣有弗順治者乎
夫戡亂者武也而至於無敵則威加于外者遠
矣附眾者文也而至於順治則化被于內者深
===
矣非君子之盛德孰能與於此乎盖其浩然之
氣得之于天者足以配道義而不餒義理之勇
素豫吾內者足以當大任而不懼夫是以積之
深者用之利而靖內靖外固其優為者矣否則
器有所拘而何以勝天下之重耶蓄之厚者發
之遠而允文允武皆其時出者矣否則才有所
偏而何以成天下之功耶君子用勇之效如此
然則聖王之貴之也豈徒尚其力也哉噫吾于
是而知禮之不可已也夫一勇力也君子用之

氣得之于天者足以配道義而不餒義理之勇
素豫吾內者足以當大任而不懼夫是以積之
深者用之利而靖內靖外固其優爲者矣否則
器有所拘而何以勝天下之重耶蓄之厚者發
之遠而名文名武皆其時出者矣否則才有所
偏而何以成天下之功耶君子用勇之效如此

…virtue, who could accomplish this? The author of The Meaning of Diplomatic Missions (Pin yi) presumably held that, in the affairs of the world, those without courage are certainly unequal to heavy responsibilities, while those unable to employ their courage well are likewise unable to achieve success. Could the gentleman’s cultivation of himself through ritual therefore be purposeless? When affairs demand action and he employs it to prevail in battle, his plans are bold and his prestige resounds. Without relying on the strength of arms, he inspires awe throughout the world. Who could resist him? When no such affairs arise and he employs it in ritual and righteousness, the enduring human relationships are ordered and the foundations of moral instruction are set right. Without going beyond the exchanges of bows and deference, ritual practices and customs take proper form of themselves. Could anyone fail to submit and become well governed?

Quelling disorder is a martial achievement; when it reaches the point where none can withstand him, his authority extends far abroad. Winning the allegiance of the multitude is a civil achievement; when it reaches the point of willing submission and good order, his transforming influence penetrates deeply within. Without the gentleman’s abundant virtue, who could attain this? His vast, flowing vital force, received from Heaven, suffices to accord with the Way and righteousness without flagging; the courage grounded in moral principle, long nurtured within oneself, suffices to shoulder great responsibilities without fear. Thus, what has been deeply accumulated can be effectively employed, and bringing peace both within and without is assuredly well within his capacity. Otherwise, if his capacities were constrained, how could he bear the weight of the world’s responsibilities? What has been amply stored has far-reaching effects when released, and both his civil and his martial excellence emerge as the occasion requires. Otherwise, if his talents were one-sided, how could he accomplish the work of the world?

Such are the effects of the gentleman’s employment of courage. Does the sage king, then, esteem him merely for his physical strength? Ah! From this I understand that ritual must never be abandoned. Courage and physical strength are the same in themselves; the gentleman employs them…

…the intention to teach all under Heaven: this composition alone apprehends it truly and precisely. Its style, moreover, is elegant and ample; without striving for the strange or extravagant, it possesses a bearing that others cannot match. It deserves first place among the candidates.
Examiner Ao, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: There is argument here, and thoughtful insight. Only someone who comprehends the fundamental source of governance and teaching could achieve this.
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: To govern through the three weighty matters, while grounding this in the desire to teach the people to commit fewer errors—this is what constitutes the Kingly Way. You have understood this meaning, and your writing adequately conveys it. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!
The sage possesses the means to govern all under Heaven, but these must be grounded in his desire to teach all under Heaven before his governance can succeed. When the sage possesses all under Heaven, he surely intends to bring it within an ordered framework and unite it as one. Yet the realm is so vast, its people's dispositions so unequal, and their habits so diverse that, if the sage lacked the instruments of government to provide standards for them to observe, everyone would follow whatever suited their dispositions and accommodated their habits, daily falling into error. The sage has compassion for the people of the realm, considering that their nature is originally the same, although their dispositions and habits cannot but differ. He reflects: “If I have yet to show them standards to observe, thereby giving a common direction to their endeavors, but first reproach them for their errors, this would be to neglect the root of the matter and compel them to follow what they cannot.” Thus he establishes the statutes and institutions of a dynasty, providing a thoroughly comprehensive set of instruments for governing them. Yet he proceeds solely from what their natures share, guiding and directing them toward unity, gradually cultivating and perfecting them, nurturing them gently without coercion. This is the sage's intention in teaching…

…the heart with which the sage teaches all under Heaven. All under Heaven are moved by his concern, and they also have institutions and regulations to observe as their standards. Thus, following him is naturally smooth and easy: they lead one another away from error without even knowing it, and only then is the sage’s ordering of the world accomplished. Zisi said: “In ruling all under Heaven, there are three weighty matters. Through these, surely errors will be few!” What are these three weighty matters? Deliberating on ritual, establishing standards, and examining written forms. Ritual originates in the norms governing relations between fathers and sons, rulers and ministers, husbands and wives, elders and juniors, and friends throughout the world. Standards originate in the distinctions among carriages, residences, clothing and ornaments, and implements. Written forms originate in the structures of characters—their forms and sounds, dots and strokes. These are based on the natural principles of Heaven and Earth and rooted in what human beings share in their nature. It should therefore be possible for all the people to participate in their practice. Why, then, do they fail to avoid error?

The people of the world can be made to follow a common way, but they cannot be made to establish order for themselves. The five regions differ in their prevailing influences and dispositions; as their customs are handed down, their habits come to differ in what they find fitting. People’s endowments of vital energy differ in firmness and softness, understanding and obtuseness; constrained by these native qualities, their feelings take different directions. When feelings with these divergent tendencies are put into practice through habits with differing notions of what is fitting, unless the sage has institutions and regulations by which to govern them, people will settle comfortably into their feelings and their intentions will drift ever further; they will find ease in their habits and their customs will become ever more corrupt. Those who indulge their desires, give free rein to evil, lose their moral hearts, and go astray without returning are certainly already numerous. punctuated: 非，欲反情以振習，而拘于其故，厥路無繇。然則斯民之過，未必盡皆其罪也。聖人所以惻然閔之，而思其治之之具者，深有所不能自已矣。故夫民之不知禮之有節也，或失則簡，或失則瀆。簡者闕恩，瀆者踰義，而民親疎貴賤之間，其過多矣。聖人不以為民之過，而曰：「吾禮有未議也。」民之不知度之有等也，或失則侈，或失則儉。侈者偪上，儉者病下，而民尊卑隆殺之間，其過多矣。聖人不以為民之過，而曰：「吾度有未制也。」民之不知文之有體也，或失則俚，或失則訛。俚者亂正，訛者失真，而民象形轉聲之間，其過多矣。聖人不以為民之過，而曰：「吾文有未考也。」聖人視民之有過也，常若在我；而其率民以寡過也，常始于身。故其明物察倫，經禮三百，曲禮三千，而身有其禮矣；制節謹度，周旋中規，折旋中矩，而身有其度矣；仰觀于天，俯察于地，中觀于人，其聲為律，其辭為經，而身有其文矣。此其折衷古今前後聖人之道，體備陰陽造化之理，於辰
translation_en:
…wrong, and wish to turn their dispositions back to what is right and reform their habits, yet are bound by their old ways and have no path to follow. Thus the faults of these people are not necessarily entirely their own blame. The sages therefore feel compassion for them and ponder the means of bringing them into good order, moved by a profound concern they cannot restrain.

When the people do not know that ritual has its proper limits, some err through neglect and others through irreverent excess. Neglect leaves affection unfulfilled; irreverent excess transgresses righteousness. Thus, in their dealings with close and distant kin, and with the noble and the lowly, the people commit many faults. The sage does not regard these as the people's fault, but says: “There are matters of ritual that I have yet to deliberate upon.” When the people do not know that regulations have their gradations, some err through extravagance and others through excessive frugality. Extravagance encroaches upon superiors; excessive frugality brings hardship upon inferiors. Thus, in distinctions between high and low and in degrees of elaboration and reduction, the people commit many faults. The sage does not regard these as the people's fault, but says: “There are regulations that I have yet to establish.” When the people do not know that writing has its proper forms, some err through vulgarity and others through corruption. Vulgarity confounds the correct forms; corruption loses the authentic ones. Thus, in pictographic forms and phonetic transformations, the people commit many faults. The sage does not regard these as the people's fault, but says: “There are forms of writing that I have yet to examine.”

When the sage sees faults among the people, he always regards the responsibility as resting with himself; in leading the people to commit fewer faults, he always begins with his own person. Thus he understands things and discerns human relationships—the three hundred major rules of ritual and the three thousand detailed rules of conduct—and embodies ritual in himself. He establishes proper limits and carefully observes the standards; his circling movements accord with the compass and his angular turns with the square, and he embodies those standards in himself. He looks upward to observe Heaven, downward to examine Earth, and between them to observe humankind; his sounds become pitch standards and his words become canonical models, and he embodies cultural refinement in himself. In this way he harmonizes the Way of sages ancient and modern, earlier and later, and fully embodies the principles of yin and yang and of creative transformation, in chen 辰 [?]…

translation_en:
…what is shared by □ [?] has already been thoroughly comprehended, leaving nothing unexplored. From this, the sage draws upon what he has comprehended to penetrate the source of institutional creation. Examining all under Heaven, he sees the divergent inclinations of people’s feelings and the differing preferences of their customs. He deeply understands the reasons for them all and clearly perceives the principle by which differences may be brought back to a common ground. Thus he deliberates upon rites for them: their natural articulations are what human nature shares. He establishes regulations for them: their natural gradations are what human nature shares. He examines written forms for them: their natural configurations are what human nature shares. Taking this shared ground as his foundation, he first fully realizes it in himself and then extends it to others. Thus those above need not resort to coercion, and those below need not wait to be coerced. All prohibitions, commands, laws, and regulations used as methods of coercing the people, together with punishments inflicted upon skin and body as acts of coercion, have no occasion for use.

He governs together with the people solely by following these three practices. Pitying their inability to understand, he teaches them to understand; pitying their inability to act, he teaches them to act. There is encouragement and guidance without harsh pressure, generosity and forbearance without impatient urging. Through the fixed standards of established institutions, he embodies the benevolence that nurtures people and brings them to maturity. Hence the saying: “This is the sage’s intention in teaching the people to make fewer mistakes.”

Then all under Heaven rely upon his institutions as means of sustaining order and are transformed by the intention with which he teaches them. Everyone says: “Such is the sage’s compassion for what we have yet to attain! Such is his eagerness to bring us to fulfillment without coercing us! Such are his solicitous care and painstaking attention, his earnestness and thorough provision, as he labors for the people and establishes standards for them to observe!” Everyone also says: “Formerly I was led astray by habit and submerged in feelings, entangling myself in error. Now, suddenly enlightened, I feel a deep inward recognition and recover my original …

translation_en:
…their original heart in this way.” All likewise say: “How simple and easy this Way is! Following it accords with our own nature; thus readily can we comply with it.” Hence, in dealings among those close and distant, noble and lowly, all say: “Here are the sage’s rites; we must neither slight them nor treat them irreverently.” In distinguishing higher and lower ranks and greater and lesser degrees of ceremonial observance, all say: “Here are the sage’s standards; we must be neither extravagant nor parsimonious.” Concerning pictographic forms and changes of sound, all say: “Here is the sage’s writing; nothing vulgar or erroneous may intrude.” Those who exceed the standard bend down to meet it; those who fall short rise on tiptoe to reach it. Joyfully inspired within its bounds, all under Heaven converge upon a single course and attain the ultimate perfection of government. Thus it is said: “When instruction takes effect, good government is achieved.”
The Book of Documents says: “Heaven brought forth the people below and established rulers and teachers for them; only the truly discerning and intelligent become sovereigns.” Could those who rule all under Heaven as sovereigns really have no responsibility to act as rulers and teachers [?]? The flourishing rule of the emperors and kings of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties invariably proceeded from this. When Qin arose, it utterly tore apart and discarded the former kings’ instruments of government; it scarcely merits discussion. As for Han and Tang, even at their best, though their laws, ordinances, prohibitions, and regulations were reasonably complete, they could not be spoken of as having achieved perfect government, because fundamentally they lacked the intention to instruct all under Heaven. Alas! Who could attain this without possessing the virtue of a sage, surpassing past and present?
Memorial
A memorial in the voice of Sima Guang of the Song dynasty, presenting the Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government (Zizhi tongjian), in the seventh year of Yuanfeng [1084].
By Zhu Shilian.

Associate Examiner Zhang, a Compiler, comments: “The use of allusions and the crafting of phrases are richly ornamented yet careful and disciplined, fitting the manner in which a subject should address his ruler.”

Associate Examiner Wang, a Compiler, comments: “The exposition is appropriate, and the language is also richly elegant: an excellent example of four-and-six parallel prose.”

Examiner Ao, an Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “Dignified, weighty, and classically correct.”

Examiner Xu, a Grand Secretary, comments: “By using four-and-six parallel prose to convey Sima Guang’s loyal devotion, this may be said to supply what was lacking in his work. Include it.”

Your servant Sima Guang, holding the specified offices, respectfully submits the completed Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government (Zizhi tongjian).

An enlightened king, seeking good government, draws upon written records to find instruction; a subject, offering loyal service, conveys admonition through compilation. The purpose is to provide a mirror for guidance; the aspiration is to assist the grand imperial undertaking. Your servant, in utmost fear and trepidation, bows his head to the ground and knocks his forehead upon it.

I humbly consider that the teachings of the sages’ minds are embodied in the Classics, and the deeds of successive dynasties are fully recorded in the histories. Since the Spring and Autumn period, no age has lacked men of wide learning; since Sima Qian and Ban Gu, every age has had officials who took up the brush to write. Yet thousands of years have passed, and the accounts mingle the words of a hundred schools. Even a Confucian scholar cannot traverse to its limits the surging sea of learning; how could a ruler have leisure to explore all the silken volumes in the forest of letters? I therefore thought that these materials should be condensed into a book, so as to facilitate the study of antiquity. Without properly assessing my own ignorance and limitations, I began a chronological compilation. Favored with recognition [?] …

translation_en:
…received favor under the previous sovereign and was enabled to complete the work I had begun. Then, upon encountering Your Sagely Majesty, I repeatedly received exceptional grace. You permitted the compilation office to continue accompanying me and frequently ordered me to present readings at the Classics Colloquium. You bestowed an auspicious title in advance, an honor surpassing the commendation symbolized by a splendid ceremonial robe; you personally composed the prefatory text, your favor shining forth in the brilliance of your imperial writing.

Deeply moved by gratitude in my own heart, and also enjoying the leisure afforded by an unexacting post, I gathered extensively from earlier accounts and searched widely among miscellaneous narratives. Beginning in the age of the Seven States and ending in the period of the Five Dynasties, the work spans thirteen hundred years and sixteen successive ruling houses. As for the court’s actions and the deliberations of its chief ministers, whenever words bore upon the people’s livelihood, I omitted nothing, however slight; whenever events concerned the ruler’s virtue, I invariably recorded the actions involved. I sought to uncover what was hidden and probe what lay deep, pruning excessive detail and bringing out essentials. Arranged in nearly three hundred juan, the work comprehensively embraces its material without omission. Nineteen years of diligent collation have yielded some modest results from my limited understanding.

In former times, a Tang emperor reflected upon the three mirrors, while Chief Minister Zhang expressed his intentions through the Thousand Autumns. Reverently looking up to these predecessors, I am ashamed that I cannot follow in their footsteps. Respectfully carrying out Your Majesty’s wishes, I am fortunate to have brought this compilation to a rough completion. Having reverently fasted and bathed, I submit it for your consideration, hoping that in a moment of leisure you will graciously inspect it. I respectfully consider that Your Majesty…

translation_en:
…Your Majesty moves with the strength and vigor of Heaven and shines with the cultured brilliance of Fire. Endowed with gifts rarely seen in the world, you exercise your divine discernment independently; devising plans for great achievements, you broadly stretch the strings of the zither of transforming government. This is truly a time for loyal and worthy men to exert their strength, an occasion for outstanding talents to devote themselves to accomplishment. Yet your servant, like a slow and lame horse, is unfit to hasten about in service. I can only rely on the red pigment and lead used in textual work, hoping thereby to assist your undertakings. I reflect earnestly that the way to benefit the people certainly requires adapting to the times; yet among the enduring principles of establishing government, none takes precedence over emulating antiquity. Only by closely examining the tracks of the past can one preserve forever the excellence of the present design. This book embodies precisely that purpose.
Although this modest work of historical recording is insufficient to move your heart, the earnest sincerity with which I offer it is truly like that of the man who wished to offer his sovereign the warmth of the sun on his back. If you graciously discern this intent beyond the written words, you will surely find something of value within these pages. I humbly hope that you will spare a little of your imperial attention and from time to time bestow your discerning gaze upon them: tracing back through Zhou and Han to examine Yao and Shun, and searching deeply for the sources of transformative government; proceeding from historical accounts to investigate the Canons and Counsels, and fully exploring the meaning of the sages and worthies. text:
皇上兼有正統道統之盛盖涵濡
聖化而有得者
帝王之治必得正統而後可以君天下帝
王之學必得道統而後可以師天下何謂
正統其功盖乎宇宙其政本乎綱常者是
也彼土宇之混一不與焉是故正統得而
君道立矣何謂道統其心契乎往聖其德
建乎皇極者是也彼經學之闡明不與焉
是故道統得而師道明矣斯二者惟古帝

punctuated:
皇上兼有正統、道統之盛，盖涵濡聖化而有得者。

帝王之治，必得正統而後可以君天下；帝王之學，必得道統而後可以師天下。何謂正統？其功盖乎宇宙，其政本乎綱常者是也，彼土宇之混一不與焉。是故正統得而君道立矣。何謂道統？其心契乎往聖，其德建乎皇極者是也，彼經學之闡明不與焉。是故道統得而師道明矣。斯二者，惟古帝王兼之，而惟我聖祖則能紹三五之統，我皇上則能增聖祖之光。二百年間，大聖人再出，以隆化理而貽休於無疆。猗歟，盛矣！請敬陳之。昔在《書》曰：「天降下民，作之君，作之師。」則凡有天下者，固皆有君師之責者也。然自三代以降，君道恒不立，師道恒不明者，何歟？正統未得，而其所建立者藐
translation_en:
…His Majesty possesses in full measure both the legitimate succession to rulership and the succession to the Way. The writer has evidently been steeped in the sage influence and gained understanding from it.

In governing, emperors and kings must obtain the legitimate succession before they can rule all under Heaven; in learning, emperors and kings must obtain the succession to the Way before they can teach all under Heaven. What is meant by the legitimate succession? It means that their achievements encompass the cosmos and their government is rooted in the cardinal bonds and constant virtues. Mere territorial unification does not qualify. Thus, when the legitimate succession is attained, the Way of the ruler is established. What is meant by the succession to the Way? It means that their minds accord with the sages of old and their virtue establishes the supreme standard of sovereignty. Mere elucidation of classical learning does not qualify. Thus, when the succession to the Way is attained, the Way of the teacher is made manifest. Only the emperors and kings of antiquity combined these two; and it was our Sagely Ancestor who could continue the succession of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, while our Emperor could enhance the glory of the Sagely Ancestor. Within two hundred years, a great sage has appeared twice, bringing moral transformation and good government to their height and bequeathing blessings without end. Ah, how glorious! Permit me respectfully to set this forth.

Long ago, the Book of Documents said: “Heaven brought forth the people below and provided them with rulers and teachers.” Thus all who possess the realm assuredly bear the responsibilities of both ruler and teacher. Yet since the Three Dynasties, why has the Way of the ruler so often failed to be established, and the Way of the teacher so often failed to be made manifest? Because the legitimate succession was not attained, what they established was paltry…

業乃取諸秦項之手而非有再造區夏之
功其為治乃介乎王霸之間而非有格于
皇天之業而欲以繼帝王之後不亦難哉

乎其卑，道統未得，而其所成就者歐乎其小也。夫正統之說何始乎？其義昉於孔子作《春秋》以尊周，而後世史氏宗之。彼帝曹魏而寇蜀漢者，固已蔽於私；而以漢唐宋之混一土宇，遂謂之得正統，則愚尚有餘論焉。何也？漢唐宋之興，莫正於漢，然其肇業乃取諸秦項之手，而非有再造區夏之功；其為治乃介乎王霸之間，而非有格于皇天之業。而欲以繼帝王之後，不亦難哉？在漢且爾，其餘可知也。故孔子之意，惟朱子《綱目》近之，而蘇軾之論則昧於大義矣。

道統之說何始乎？其端起於孟子之歷叙羣聖，而後世學士宗之。彼其推韓歐以附孔孟者，固已非其倫；而以宋之諸儒闡明經學，遂謂之得道統，則愚亦有餘論焉。何也？諸儒之功，莫盛於周程張朱，然其澤既嗇於所遇之艱，而其道亦未進於作者之聖。而欲以繼帝王之後，豈其然哉？在大儒
translation_en:
…how lowly their foundations were; having failed to obtain the transmission of the Way, their accomplishments were paltry [?]. Where did the doctrine of legitimate succession originate? Its meaning began with Confucius’s composition of the Spring and Autumn Annals to honor the Zhou, and later historians took this as their guiding principle. Those who accorded imperial legitimacy to Cao Wei while treating Shu Han as rebels were certainly blinded by partiality. Yet if the unification of the realm by the Han, Tang, and Song is taken as sufficient grounds for saying that they obtained legitimate succession, I, in my ignorance, still have more to say. Why? Of these three dynasties, none rose more legitimately than the Han. Yet in founding its dominion, it merely took possession from the hands of Qin and Xiang Yu; it did not accomplish the restoration of the Chinese realm. Its government stood midway between the kingly and hegemonic ways; its achievements did not reach august Heaven. Was it not difficult, then, for it to claim succession to the ancient emperors and kings? If this was so even of the Han, the others may readily be judged. Thus only Master Zhu’s Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror approaches Confucius’s intent, whereas Su Shi’s arguments fail to comprehend the great principle.

Where did the doctrine of the transmission of the Way originate? It began with Mencius’s successive account of the sages, and later scholars took this as their guiding principle. Those who elevated Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu to rank alongside Confucius and Mencius certainly placed them in a class to which they did not belong. Yet if the Song Confucians’ elucidation of classical learning is taken as sufficient grounds for saying that they obtained the transmission of the Way, I, in my ignorance, likewise have more to say. Why? Among the Confucians, none made greater contributions than Zhou Dunyi, the Cheng brothers, Zhang Zai, and Zhu Xi. Yet the benefits they bestowed were restricted by the difficult circumstances they encountered, and their attainment of the Way had not advanced to the sagehood of those who established civilization’s institutions. How, then, could they claim succession to the ancient emperors and kings? If even the great Confucian masters…

translation_en:
…even they were thus; what may be said of the others is clear. Thus, only Master Han’s Discourse on the Origin of the Way comes close to Mencius’s intent, whereas Huang Gan’s discussion verges on excessive praise. Did carrying on the succession of the sage emperors and kings, and fully embodying the Way of both ruler and teacher, therefore have to await our sagely founding ancestor’s receiving Heaven’s mandate to inaugurate a new age, and our reigning emperor’s continuing the succession and bringing about a restoration? The Yuan, led by the fiercest of dogs and sheep, entered and ruled the Central Realm. Their rank stench spread throughout the nine regions, and a foul haze filled the space between Heaven and Earth: the upheavals of all time had reached their utmost extreme. Our sagely founding ancestor commanded righteous troops and drove them out. Through this, Heaven and Earth were opened anew, and the sun and moon shone once more. Even the Yellow Emperor’s campaign at Zhuolu and the great Shun’s expedition against the Sanmiao cannot compare with his divine achievements and mighty deeds. These are what is meant by achievements that overshadow the universe.
As for his government, there were proclamations explaining the Five Constant Virtues, instructions admonishing the four classes of people, a Record of Filial Piety and Parental Kindness, prescribed forms of ritual and ceremony, public notices to instruct the people, and recumbent stone tablets to educate scholars. His government through the cardinal relationships and constant virtues was precisely what the ancients called giving due weight to the enduring norms and establishing the proper ways. Thus, the legitimate succession of the sage emperors and kings rested with our sagely founding ancestor. In moments free from the myriad affairs of state, he frequently summoned Confucian officials and discussed learning with them. He once instructed Zeng Lu, Vice Minister of Rites, saying: “The ruler’s single mind is the foundation of orderly government and moral transformation. What is preserved…”

translation_en:
…if what one holds within is not the heart of Yao and Shun, it is impossible to achieve the government of Yao and Shun in administering affairs.” He told Academician Song Lian: “The human heart is empty and numinously perceptive; it moves in and out with the workings of vital energy. To grasp and preserve it is difficult.” In discussing with Xu Cunren the responses manifested in the various signs described in the “Great Plan,” and with Xu Haowen the way of praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate, he inwardly apprehended the profound essence of the classics, attaining an extraordinary understanding of his own. This extended through successive reigns: sage succeeded sage, following the same Way from first to last. Yet although government and moral transformation flourished in harmony [?], established ritual forms largely continued unchanged. Thus no one had proposed abolishing the sacrifices to Shizu of the Yuan. A chieftain who brought disorder upon China was someone whom emperors were bound to punish; yet he was allowed to occupy the same hall alongside them and share the offerings in the ritual vessels. The people’s hearts had long been indignant at this! Our Emperor, deciding from his own imperial heart, rejected and removed him. Hence those who fasten their robes on the left could no longer rank alongside those wearing the caps and robes of civilization, nor could an intercalary remainder intrude upon the legitimate succession of Heaven’s mandate. Such brilliant planning and outstanding discernment were surpassed neither by the court of Shun’s precautions against those who disturbed the Chinese realm nor by the intent behind Yu the Great’s division of the Five Zones. This is the means of preserving the great imperial enterprise forever. As for his conduct of government…

…in governing, he deepened his filial devotion in serving his parents, and the Great Compendium for Clarifying Human Relations was compiled; he instituted the rites for honoring his father, and the regulations for the Great Sacrifice were established. In reverence for Heaven, he established the suburban sacrificial altars; in honoring his ancestors, he exalted their temple titles. Governance through the cardinal bonds and constant virtues was precisely how the sagely founder promoted moral transformation and brought about good order. Thus the legitimate succession of emperors and kings resides in our Sovereign.
His sagely learning is refined and subtle, wondrously attuned to the wisdom of the ages. For example, his Admonition on Reverent Single-mindedness says: “At the suburban sacrifice, be reverent and sincere; in the ancestral temple, attend with solemn filial devotion [?]. translation_en:
…enshrined the Former Sage and Former Teacher for sacrifice in the eastern chamber of the Wenhua Hall, sharing with the sages a mutual communion of spirit and purpose. Is it not also evident from this that Our Emperor has received the transmission of the Way? Possession of the legitimate imperial succession establishes the Way of the ruler; possession of the succession of the Way makes manifest the Way of the teacher. Our Sagely Ancestor arose before, and Our Emperor carries on after him. This is something that even Yao and Shun could not have, and that has scarcely been seen in the several thousand years since Kings Wen and Wu.
Thus I, in my humble judgment, have surveyed the present day: the enduring human relationships are duly ordered; the guiding principles of government are upheld; rites and music are illustrious and complete; punishments and administration are carefully regulated; the assembled officials are both awed and devoted; the myriad people show reverence and affection; all within the seas enjoys peace; and the foreign peoples submit. That the court’s commands carry such imposing authority throughout the realm is because the Way of the ruler has long been established. Learning is pure and unified; discussion is balanced and upright; talented men emerge in succession; customs are greatly transformed; the sounds of strings and recitation are heard everywhere; punishments are almost set aside; the common people are enlightened; and the myriad states are brought into harmony…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:

羅良
===

敷建之德教沛然洋溢於天下者，則師道之素明也。於戲休哉！雖帝王且不能及，而况其下者乎？愚也生際昌時，涵泳聖化，鋪張揚厲之心盖激於中，而頌天地者難為言，繪日月者難為工，惴然懼無以塞明問也。惟執事進而教之。

第二問
羅良

同考試官編修張批：考索精詳，博而有見，非徒撫拾陳言者。佳士！佳士！

同考試官編修汪批：樂律一策，士子類能言之，但多勦述舊聞而無定見。此作深繹其指，而敷衍明白，可與言樂矣。

考試官侍講學士敖批：音樂不傳久矣，此對條析明白，中亦有見，豈嘗究心於此者？

考試官大學士徐批：樂書，後生所厭觀。此作按問目條答無遺，信是積學之士。
translation_en:
…That the moral teaching he has established flows abundantly throughout the realm is due to the long-standing clarity of his Way as teacher. Ah, how splendid! Even the emperors and kings of old could not equal him—how much less could those below them? I, in my ignorance, have been born into a flourishing age and steeped in the sage sovereign’s transforming influence. The impulse to proclaim and extol his achievements wells up within me. Yet one who praises Heaven and Earth finds words inadequate, and one who paints the sun and moon finds artistry inadequate. I tremble with fear that I cannot adequately answer your discerning question. I ask only that you, sir, guide and instruct me.

Second Question
Luo Liang 羅良

Comment by Examiner Xu 徐, Grand Secretary: Books on music are something younger scholars dislike reading. This composition answers every item in the question, point by point, omitting nothing. Its author is indeed a scholar of accumulated learning.

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
至哉音樂之妙其天地自然之數乎其天
地自然之氣乎盖必與陰陽合其德斯足
以察聲氣之元而音可正也與陰陽合其
化斯足以致和平之治而樂可作也不然
徒規規於度數之間辨其清濁高下之倫
較其長短廣狹之制則聲容雖盛節奏雖
協亦何以序氣成物助流政教而媲美古
樂之盛邪噫此作樂者之所以當探其本
也記曰知禮樂之情者能作識禮樂之文
===
者能述作者之謂聖述者之謂明夫樂豈
易言乎執事策諸生以後世諸儒辨析度
數之末愚固知其不安於是也然欲究微
詞奧旨於往籍之中以求至當不一之論
則又豈愚生所敢望哉慨自聖人不作非
惟性靈之聰不足以達天德之妙雖度數
之相沿襲亦彌久而彌失其真矣彼伊耆
氏之土鼓葦籥軒轅氏之截管製律不可
得而考矣所可言者若后夔典樂之訓小

translation_en:
How consummate is the subtlety of music! Does it lie in the natural numbers of Heaven and Earth? Does it lie in their natural vital energy? Only when its potency accords with yin and yang can the origins of sound and vital energy be discerned and musical tones rectified; only when its transformations accord with yin and yang can peaceful and harmonious government be achieved and music created. Otherwise, if one merely confines oneself to measurements and numbers, distinguishing the categories of clear and turbid, high and low sounds, and comparing prescribed lengths and widths, then, however splendid the sounds and ceremonial displays, however coordinated the rhythms, how could these order vital energy and bring things to completion, help spread governance and moral instruction, and rival the magnificence of ancient music? Ah! This is why those who create music must investigate its foundations. The Record of Rites says: “Those who understand the essential nature of rites and music can create them; those who recognize their outward forms can transmit them. Those who create are called sages; those who transmit are called discerning.” Can music, then, be discussed lightly?

You, honored examiners, have questioned us students about later scholars’ analyses of the subsidiary matters of measurements and numbers. I certainly understand that you are not content with these alone. Yet to investigate subtle expressions and profound meanings in ancient writings, seeking judgments of the utmost soundness amid divergent views—is this something that an ignorant student such as I could dare hope to accomplish? Alas, since sages have ceased to arise, not only has our innate acuity proved insufficient to comprehend the subtle workings of Heaven’s potency, but even the measurements and numbers handed down through successive generations have departed ever further from their true forms. Yiqi’s earthen drums and reed flutes, and Xuanyuan’s cutting of pipes to establish pitch standards, can no longer be examined. What can be discussed includes the instructions concerning Hou Kui’s direction of music, and the Lesser …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
胥樂懸之陳固虞夏之道也南風之歌商
頌之篇固韶濩之遺也賓牟賈之問對固
大武之形容也十五國風王侯卿大夫士
庶通用之樂也二雅燕饗朝會之樂也周
魯之頌宗廟郊社之樂也嗣是而降音響
益微自鄶之譏延陵所以悼時也在齊之
歎孔子所以志古也後有作者吾何以觀
之哉燕筑齊竽桑間濮上徒以增悲導欲
而無所補於世教蓋非特魏文侯聞古樂
===
而恐臥晉文公聽新聲而忘食也噫俗尚
如此古樂雖欲不亡得乎自漢以來儒者
論議紛紜各是其說竊嘗考之而得其槩
矣夫律吕之數陰陽奇偶之情也陽六為
律律以統氣類物陰六為吕吕以旅陽宣
氣凡十二管而黃鍾之長獨得九寸大吕
而下律吕相間以次而短至應鍾而極焉
蓋黃鍾陽聲之始故其數九而度量權衡
由是而出十一律由是而損益此則黃鍾

胥樂懸之陳，固虞夏之道也；南風之歌、商頌之篇，固韶濩之遺也；賓牟賈之問對，固大武之形容也。十五國風，王侯卿大夫士庶通用之樂也；二雅，燕饗朝會之樂也；周魯之頌，宗廟郊社之樂也。嗣是而降，音響益微。自鄶之譏，延陵所以悼時也；在齊之歎，孔子所以志古也。後有作者，吾何以觀之哉？燕筑齊竽、桑間濮上，徒以增悲導欲，而無所補於世教。蓋非特魏文侯聞古樂而恐臥、晉文公聽新聲而忘食也。噫！俗尚如此，古樂雖欲不亡，得乎？
自漢以來，儒者論議紛紜，各是其說。竊嘗考之，而得其槩矣。夫律吕之數，陰陽奇偶之情也。陽六為律，律以統氣類物；陰六為吕，吕以旅陽宣氣。凡十二管，而黃鍾之長獨得九寸。大吕而下，律吕相間，以次而短，至應鍾而極焉。蓋黃鍾，陽聲之始，故其數九，而度量權衡由是而出，十一律由是而損益。此則黃鍾
translation_en:
…the arrangements of suspended musical instruments prescribed for the Junior Music Master certainly embody the Way of Yu and Xia. The Song of the South Wind and the Hymns of Shang certainly preserve vestiges of the Shao and Huo music. The questions and answers involving Bin Moujia certainly describe the Great Martial Dance. The Airs of the Fifteen States were music used alike by kings, regional lords, ministers, grand masters, gentlemen, and commoners. The two sets of Elegantiae were music for banquets, ceremonial feasts, and court assemblies. The Hymns of Zhou and Lu were music for ancestral temples and sacrifices at the suburban altars and altars of soil. Thereafter, these musical sounds increasingly faded. The criticism implicit in declining to comment from the Airs of Kuai onward was how the Lord of Yanling lamented his times; Confucius’s exclamation while in Qi was how he expressed his devotion to antiquity. If later composers arose, by what standard could I judge them? The zhu zithers of Yan, the yu mouth organs of Qi, and the music of Sangjian and Pushang merely intensified sorrow and stirred desire, contributing nothing to the moral instruction of the age. It was surely not just Marquis Wen of Wei who feared falling asleep when hearing ancient music, or Duke Wen of Jin who forgot to eat when listening to new melodies. Alas! With popular tastes like these, could ancient music have escaped extinction, even had one wished to preserve it?
Since the Han, Confucian scholars have advanced a welter of arguments, each taking his own explanation to be correct. I have ventured to investigate these and have grasped their broad outlines. The numerical relationships of the pitch standards express the inherent properties of yin and yang, odd and even. The six yang pitches are called lü 律: they govern vital energies and classify things. The six yin pitches are called lü 吕: they marshal yang and disseminate vital energies. There are twelve pitch pipes in all, but only Huangzhong measures nine cun in length. From Dalü downward, the yang and yin pitch pipes alternate, becoming successively shorter until they reach their limit at Yingzhong. Huangzhong is the beginning of the yang tones, and thus its number is nine. Measures of length and capacity, weights, and balances derive from it; the other eleven pitch standards are generated from it through diminution and augmentation. This, then, is Huangzhong …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
萬事根本之說也十一月乾之初九陽氣
始動而鍾於物故黃鍾為天統六月坤之
初六陰氣始動而林於物故林鍾為地統
正月乾之九三萬物奏進人奉而承之故
太簇為人統黃鍾子為天正陽之始也林
鍾未之衝丑為地正陰之始也太簇寅為
人正陰陽得而人物生之候也此則三統
三正之義也然天兼乎地而地無踰天之
理人法乎天而天有始物之功林鍾太簇
===
之律雖與黃鍾相配而不敢以相役則君
有常尊而位定矣故明於三統之義而陰
陽之情得然後損益之分定而律呂之位
可求也何也陽以圓為形其性動故其數
三陰以方為節其性靜故其數二以陽生
陰三分本律而損其一是曰下生以陰生
陽三分本律而增其一是曰上生上生不
得過黃鍾之清濁下生不得及黃鍾之數
實故曰黃鍾律呂之首而生十一律者也

punctuated: 萬事根本之說也。十一月，乾之初九，陽氣始動而鍾於物，故黃鍾為天統；六月，坤之初六，陰氣始動而林於物，故林鍾為地統；正月，乾之九三，萬物奏進，人奉而承之，故太簇為人統。黃鍾子為天正，陽之始也；林鍾未之衝丑為地正，陰之始也；太簇寅為人正，陰陽得而人物生之候也。此則三統三正之義也。然天兼乎地，而地無踰天之理；人法乎天，而天有始物之功。林鍾、太簇之律，雖與黃鍾相配，而不敢以相役，則君有常尊而位定矣。故明於三統之義，而陰陽之情得，然後損益之分定，而律呂之位可求也。何也？陽以圓為形，其性動，故其數三；陰以方為節，其性靜，故其數二。以陽生陰，三分本律而損其一，是曰下生；以陰生陽，三分本律而增其一，是曰上生。上生不得過黃鍾之清濁，下生不得及黃鍾之數實。故曰黃鍾律呂之首，而生十一律者也。
translation_en:
…the explanation of Huangzhong as the root of all things. In the eleventh month, corresponding to the initial nine of Qian, yang qi begins to move and gathers within things; hence Huangzhong constitutes the celestial succession. In the sixth month, corresponding to the initial six of Kun, yin qi begins to move and spreads abundantly among things; hence Linzhong constitutes the terrestrial succession. In the first month, corresponding to the nine in the third place of Qian, all things advance, and human beings reverently receive and sustain them; hence Taicu constitutes the human succession. Huangzhong, associated with zi, marks Heaven’s beginning of the year, the inception of yang. Chou, opposite wei, with which Linzhong is associated, marks Earth’s beginning of the year, the inception of yin. Taicu, associated with yin 寅, marks the human beginning of the year, the season when yin and yang attain harmony and human beings and other things come into being. Such is the meaning of the Three Successions and the Three Beginnings of the Year.

Yet Heaven encompasses Earth, and there is no principle by which Earth can surpass Heaven; human beings model themselves on Heaven, and Heaven has the merit of initiating all things. Although the pitch standards of Linzhong and Taicu are paired with Huangzhong, they do not presume to command it. Thus the ruler possesses enduring supremacy, and his position is fixed. Consequently, once the meaning of the Three Successions is understood and the nature of yin and yang grasped, the respective operations of diminution and augmentation can be determined, and the positions of the yang and yin pitch standards can be ascertained.

Why is this? Yang takes the circle as its form, and its nature is active; therefore its number is three. Yin takes the square as its measure, and its nature is still; therefore its number is two. To generate yin from yang, divide the original pitch pipe’s length into three parts and subtract one: this is called downward generation. To generate yang from yin, divide the original pitch pipe’s length into three parts and add one: this is called upward generation. Upward generation must not pass beyond Huangzhong in pitch, and downward generation must not reach Huangzhong’s full numerical measure. Thus it is said that Huangzhong is the foremost of the yang and yin pitch standards and generates the other eleven.

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
自黃鍾而至應鍾陽皆下生陰皆上生盖
從子至巳陽生而陰退也自蕤賓以至仲
呂陰反下生陽反上生盖從午至亥陰升
而陽退也凡此莫非順陰陽之消長以為
損益而豈能以私意參於其間哉至於變
律之說所以補正律之不足者盖十二律
各自為宮每一律則役六律以生五聲二
變自黃鍾以至林鍾則各足其相役之數
故不用變律而以本律當之自蕤賓以至
===
仲呂未免上役黃鍾太簇故不用正律而
以變律應之此所以相和而不至於相凌
也變聲所以濟五聲之不及者自殷以前
惟五音而已至周則加二變謂之七聲盖
角徵之間近徵收一聲謂之變徵羽宮之
間近宮收一聲謂之變宮邇而不偪遠而
不携此所以克諧而無相奪倫也然變律
止於六者以數至應鍾而窮至此則十二
律七聲循環相役固不俟強加而自足也

律七聲循環相役固不俟强加而自足也
punctuated:
自黃鍾而至應鍾，陽皆下生，陰皆上生，盖從子至巳，陽生而陰退也。自蕤賓以至仲呂，陰反下生，陽反上生，盖從午至亥，陰升而陽退也。凡此莫非順陰陽之消長以為損益，而豈能以私意參於其間哉？
至於變律之說，所以補正律之不足者，盖十二律各自為宮，每一律則役六律，以生五聲二變。自黃鍾以至林鍾，則各足其相役之數，故不用變律，而以本律當之。自蕤賓以至仲呂，未免上役黃鍾、太簇，故不用正律，而以變律應之。此所以相和而不至於相凌也。
變聲所以濟五聲之不及者，自殷以前，惟五音而已，至周則加二變，謂之七聲。盖角徵之間，近徵收一聲，謂之變徵；羽宮之間，近宮收一聲，謂之變宮。邇而不偪，遠而不携，此所以克諧而無相奪倫也。然變律止於六者，以數至應鍾而窮。至此則十二律七聲循環相役，固不俟強加而自足也。
translation_en:
From Huangzhong to Yingzhong, the yang pitch standards all generate downward, and the yin pitch standards all generate upward. This is because, from zi to si, yang grows while yin recedes. From Ruibin to Zhonglü, yin instead generates downward and yang instead generates upward. This is because, from wu to hai, yin rises while yang recedes. All these reductions and augmentations follow the waxing and waning of yin and yang. How could one interpose personal notions among them?
As for the theory of modified pitch standards, these remedy the deficiencies of the regular standards. Each of the twelve pitch standards serves in turn as gong, and each employs six other standards to produce the five notes and the two altered notes. From Huangzhong to Linzhong, each has the full complement required for their mutual employment. Thus modified standards are unnecessary: the original standards suffice. From Ruibin to Zhonglü, however, one cannot avoid drawing upon Huangzhong and Taicu above; hence modified standards are used to answer them instead of the regular standards. This allows them to harmonize without overpowering one another.
Altered notes remedy what the five notes cannot encompass. In Yin times and earlier, there were only the five notes. Under the Zhou, two altered notes were added, making what were called the seven notes. Between jue and zhi, a note close to zhi was incorporated and called altered zhi; between yu and gong, a note close to gong was incorporated and called altered gong. They are close without crowding and distant without becoming disconnected. Thus they achieve harmony without usurping one another’s proper order. Modified pitch standards are limited to six because the numerical sequence reaches its limit at Yingzhong. At this point, the twelve pitch standards and seven notes serve one another in a recurring cycle: they are inherently sufficient, without any need for forced additions.

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
變聲止於二者以音節相去太遠而設若
宮與商商與角徵與羽相去皆一律固不
待變聲而自和也京房不知此義自仲吕
而下再生執始以至南事四十八律其於
三分損益不盡之算或棄或增破壞自然
之數尚得謂之律乎萬寶常用禮運旋宮
之法以五正二變衍之而為八十四調沈
重準易之策當期之日而為三百六十律
牽合傅會日繁雜而無統紀尚得謂之樂乎
===
夫不能審聲故無以正律而得其周徑冪
積之數不能正律故無以定器而辨其高
下清濁之宜何怪乎議者之紛紛而莫一
也他如漢人作準以代竹而其法罔效晉
人制尺以定律而其聲過高梁隋以來或
求之金石而音韻鮮諧或參之秬黍而肥
瘠難定古器散亡音聲微妙樂果何時而
興乎近世儒者乃倡為之說曰黃鍾非九
寸之管而引通鑑外紀呂氏春秋所載舍

積之數不能正律故無以定器而辨其高
下清濁之宜何怪乎議者之紛紛而莫一
也他如漢人作準以代竹而其法罔效晉
人制尺以定律而其聲過高繼隋以來或
求之金石而音韻鮮諧或參之秬黍而肥
瘠難定古器散亡音聲微眇樂果何時而
興乎近世儒者乃倡為之說曰黃鍾非九
寸之管而引通鑑外紀呂氏春秋所載合
punctuated:
變聲止於二者，以音節相去太遠而設。若宮與商、商與角、徵與羽，相去皆一律，固不待變聲而自和也。京房不知此義，自仲吕而下，再生執始，以至南事四十八律。其於三分損益不盡之算，或棄或增，破壞自然之數，尚得謂之律乎？萬寶常用《禮運》旋宮之法，以五正二變衍之而為八十四調。沈重準《易》之策當期之日，而為三百六十律。牽合傅會，日繁雜而無統紀，尚得謂之樂乎？

夫不能審聲，故無以正律，而得其周徑冪積之數；不能正律，故無以定器，而辨其高下清濁之宜。何怪乎議者之紛紛而莫一也？他如漢人作準以代竹，而其法罔效；晉人制尺以定律，而其聲過高。梁隋以來，或求之金石，而音韻鮮諧；或參之秬黍，而肥瘠難定。古器散亡，音聲微妙，樂果何時而興乎？近世儒者乃倡為之說曰：「黃鍾非九寸之管。」而引《通鑑外紀》《呂氏春秋》所載舍
translation_en:
The altered tones are limited to two because they were established to bridge excessively wide intervals between notes. The intervals between gong and shang, shang and jue, and zhi and yu each span only one pitch standard; these therefore harmonize naturally without requiring altered tones. Jing Fang did not understand this principle. Continuing downward from Zhonglü, he generated Zhishi and proceeded as far as Nanshi, producing forty-eight pitch standards. In calculations using subtraction or addition of one-third, he either discarded or augmented the remainders, disrupting the natural numerical relationships. Can these still be called pitch standards? Wan Baochang employed the method of rotating the tonal center found in “The Operation of Ritual,” extending the five principal tones and two altered tones into eighty-four modes. Shen Zhong modeled his system on the Changes, whose divining-stalk numbers correspond to the days of the year, and produced three hundred and sixty pitch standards. Such forced correspondences and strained associations grew ever more complicated, without any governing order. Can this still be called music?

Without discerning sounds, one cannot rectify the pitch standards and obtain the numerical measurements of circumference, diameter, cross-sectional area, and volume. Without rectifying the pitch standards, one cannot establish instruments correctly and distinguish the appropriate high and low, clear and deep tones. Why be surprised that those discussing the matter offer a profusion of conflicting views? Other examples include the Han scholars’ construction of a monochord pitch regulator to replace bamboo pipes, a method that proved ineffective, and the Jin scholars’ establishment of a measuring rule to determine the pitch standards, which made the pitches too high. Since the Liang and Sui dynasties, some have sought the standards in metal bells and stone chimes, yet their tones seldom harmonized; others have checked them against black millet grains, whose thickness or thinness was difficult to standardize. Ancient instruments have been scattered and lost, and the subtleties of musical sound are elusive. When, indeed, will music flourish again? Scholars of recent times have advanced the claim: “Huangzhong is not a pipe nine cun long.” They cite the Supplementary Records to the Comprehensive Mirror and Master Lü’s Spring and Autumn Annals, which record she [?]…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
少之說為徵殊不知黃鍾以八十一分之
管吹三十九分以為聲故謂之含少今遂
以三十九分為黃鍾之律而執含少以為
清管使十一律無從取正是詆毁儒先之
言而增異說之蹊徑何足取信於後哉如
欲見諸施行莫若截竹為筩以擬黃鍾之
管築室布灰以為候氣之法如宋儒蔡元
定之所論近世丘文莊之所議庶幾黃鍾
之律可得而十一律可因之以損益矣雖
===
然此特度數之末耳推原其極則天地有
元聲知元聲則元數可得而求矣何則盈
天壤間陰陽五行之氣而已天地人物皆
由是以生有氣則有聲十二律之聲天地
之聲也上古之時風氣未散聖人取天地
中和自然之氣而為中和之樂故其感召
也百獸且猶率舞而況於人乎嗟乎元數
者即律呂損益生變之義猶可說也至於
元聲即所謂黃鍾律呂之原非聖人莫之

管槃室布灰以為候氣之法如宋儒蔡元
定之所論近世丘文莊之所議庶幾黃鍾
之律可得而十一律可因之以損益矣雖
===
然此特度數之末耳推原其極則天地有
元聲知元聲則元數可得而求矣何則盈
天壤間陰陽五行之氣而已天地人物皆
由是以生有氣則有聲十二律之聲天地
之聲也上古之時風氣未散聖人取天地
中和自然之氣而為中和之樂故其感召
也百獸且猶率舞而況於人乎嗟乎元數
者即律呂損益生變之義猶可說也至於
元聲即所謂黃鍾律呂之原非聖人莫之
punctuated:
少之說為徵，殊不知黃鍾以八十一分之管吹三十九分以為聲，故謂之含少。今遂以三十九分為黃鍾之律，而執含少以為清管，使十一律無從取正，是詆毁儒先之言而增異說之蹊徑，何足取信於後哉？如欲見諸施行，莫若截竹為筩，以擬黃鍾之管，築室布灰，以為候氣之法。如宋儒蔡元定之所論、近世丘文莊之所議，庶幾黃鍾之律可得，而十一律可因之以損益矣。
雖然，此特度數之末耳。推原其極，則天地有元聲，知元聲則元數可得而求矣。何則？盈天壤間陰陽五行之氣而已，天地人物皆由是以生。有氣則有聲，十二律之聲，天地之聲也。上古之時，風氣未散，聖人取天地中和自然之氣而為中和之樂，故其感召也，百獸且猶率舞，而況於人乎？嗟乎！元數者，即律呂損益生變之義，猶可說也。至於元聲，即所謂黃鍾律呂之原，非聖人莫之
translation_en:
…the explanation concerning “little” [?] as evidence. They fail entirely to understand that the Huangzhong pitch uses a pipe eighty-one fen long, sounded at thirty-nine fen to produce its tone [?]; hence it is called “containing little.” Now they consequently take thirty-nine fen as the standard for Huangzhong and insist that “containing little” means a high-pitched pipe, leaving the other eleven pitches without a standard by which to be corrected. This disparages the words of earlier Confucian scholars and opens further paths for heterodox explanations. How could it win the trust of later generations? If one wishes to put this into practice, nothing is better than cutting bamboo into tubes to reproduce the Huangzhong pipe, and building a chamber and laying out ashes to implement the method of observing the seasonal qi. Following the discussions of the Song Confucian scholar Cai Yuanding and the proposals of the more recent Qiu Wenzhuang, one might then recover the Huangzhong standard and derive the other eleven pitches from it through proportional diminution and augmentation.
Nevertheless, these are merely the lesser details of measurement and number. Tracing the matter to its ultimate source, Heaven and Earth possess a primordial sound; once one understands this sound, its primordial numbers can be sought and found. Why is this so? What fills the space between Heaven and Earth is simply the qi of yin and yang and the Five Phases. Heaven, Earth, human beings, and all things arise from it. Where there is qi, there is sound. The sounds of the twelve pitches are the sounds of Heaven and Earth. In high antiquity, before the prevailing qi had dispersed, the sages drew upon the naturally balanced and harmonious qi of Heaven and Earth to make music of balance and harmony. Such was its power to evoke a response that even the hundred beasts joined in dancing—how much more so human beings! Alas! Primordial numbers concern the principles by which the pitch standards generate transformations through diminution and augmentation; these can still be explained. As for primordial sound, it is what is called the source of Huangzhong and all the pitch standards. None but a sage can…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
能也有志於樂者不求諸制度而驗之於
造化不求諸造化而本之於吾身反情和
志比類成行而其德備矣人主和於上卿
大夫和於朝萬民和於野而其治隆矣天
地訢合陰陽相得寒暑節風雨時而造化
無不順矣夫然後稽之以度數文之以雅
頌蕩之以鐘石播之以絲管而樂興焉則
奏於郊廟而神鬼格用於朝廷而上下讓
施於燕饗而賓主和達之于天下而風化
===
美古樂之盛可復見矣否則區區度數之
詳雖使諸儒復生論議合一而依古律度
數劑量以制器吾未見其有益於世有裨
於樂也孔子曰人而不仁如樂何樂云樂
云鍾鼓云乎哉執是以往諸儒之說不待
辨而明而作樂之道得矣請以是為明問
復
第三問
馮葉

志比類成行而其德備矣人主和於上卿
大夫和於朝萬民和於野而其治隆矣天
地訢合陰陽相得寒暑節風雨時而造化
無不順矣夫然後稽之以度數文之以雅
頌蕩之以鍾石播之以絲管而樂興焉則
奏於郊廟而神鬼格用於朝廷而上下讓
施於燕饗而賓主和達之于天下而風化
===
美古樂之盛可復見矣否則區區度數之
詳雖使諸儒復生論議合一而律古律度
數劑量以制器吾未見其有益於世有裨
於樂也孔子曰人而不仁如樂何樂云樂
云鍾鼓云乎哉執是以往諸儒之說不待
辨而明而作樂之道得矣請以是為明問
復
第三問
馮葉
punctuated:
能也。有志於樂者，不求諸制度而驗之於造化，不求諸造化而本之於吾身，反情和志，比類成行，而其德備矣。人主和於上，卿大夫和於朝，萬民和於野，而其治隆矣。天地訢合，陰陽相得，寒暑節，風雨時，而造化無不順矣。夫然後稽之以度數，文之以雅頌，蕩之以鐘石，播之以絲管，而樂興焉。則奏於郊廟而神鬼格，用於朝廷而上下讓，施於燕饗而賓主和，達之于天下而風化美，古樂之盛可復見矣。否則區區度數之詳，雖使諸儒復生，論議合一，而依古律度數劑量以制器，吾未見其有益於世、有裨於樂也。孔子曰：「人而不仁，如樂何？」「樂云樂云，鍾鼓云乎哉？」執是以往，諸儒之說不待辨而明，而作樂之道得矣。請以是為明問復。
第三問
馮葉
translation_en:
…can accomplish it. Those devoted to music should not seek it in institutional prescriptions but test it against the workings of creation; nor should they seek it in creation, but ground it in their own persons. By returning their feelings to their proper state, harmonizing their intentions, and bringing their conduct into accord with what is fitting, they perfect their virtue. When the ruler is harmonious above, the ministers and great officers are harmonious at court, and the myriad people are harmonious in the countryside, governance flourishes. Heaven and earth unite in harmony, yin and yang accord with one another, cold and heat observe their proper bounds, and wind and rain arrive in season: all the workings of creation proceed in due order.
Only then should this harmony be examined through measures and numbers, adorned with the Elegantiae and Hymns, stirred through bells and stone chimes, and spread through strings and pipes; thus music arises. Performed at the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples, it brings spirits to attend; employed at court, it makes superiors and subordinates defer to one another; performed at banquets, it harmonizes hosts and guests; extended throughout the realm, it ennobles customs through moral influence. The flourishing of ancient music may then be seen again.
Otherwise, with nothing but minute particulars of measures and numbers, even if the various scholars returned to life and reached agreement in their discussions, and instruments were made according to ancient pitch standards, measurements, numerical proportions, and calculated quantities, I do not see how this would benefit the world or contribute to music. Confucius said: “If a man lacks benevolence, what can he do with music?” And: “Music, music—is it merely bells and drums?” Proceeding on this basis, the scholars’ doctrines become clear without needing debate, and the way to create music is attained. I respectfully offer this as my reply to your discerning question.
Third Question
Feng Ye

text:
同考試官左給事中謝　批立德立功立言論者
已謂非古後世狥名之士愈熾可慨也子獨能
折衷前聞力洗時習蓋亦知尚德者錄之不
獨以其文巳
同考試官都給事中姜　批聖人作經垂訓何嘗
不本於功德後世始岐為二穆叔之言殆亦有激
於季世然者此作反覆鋪張深為有見宜錄之
以為尚言者戒
同考試官檢討朱　批三不朽之說陳矣後
===
===

文知不徒以言進者

punctuated:
同考試官左給事中謝批：「立德、立功、立言，論者已謂非古。後世狥名之士愈熾，可慨也！子獨能折衷前聞，力洗時習，蓋亦知尚德者。錄之，不獨以其文巳。」

同考試官都給事中姜批：「聖人作經垂訓，何嘗不本於功德？後世始岐為二。穆叔之言，殆亦有激於季世然者。此作反覆鋪張，深為有見，宜錄之，以為尚言者戒。」

同考試官檢討朱批：「三不朽之說陳矣，後世士多狥名，而志于立德者甚不多見。讀子之文，知不徒以言進者。」

同考試官檢討孫批：「古人尚德不尚言，故天下大治。言之尚，蓋叔季也。子於是策反覆千餘言，而歸重尚德，固知子為治世士矣。吁，其尚毋負而言哉！」

同考試官編修瞿批：「敷奏以言，雖唐虞不廢，而靜言庸違，又其所深戒也。古今論者多謂文士無實，蓋文士之茹家此譏，亦有以致之矣。子
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Xie, Left Supervising Secretary, comments: “Establishing virtue, establishing achievements, and establishing words: critics have already argued that this formulation does not accord with antiquity. In later ages, men who pursue fame have grown ever more numerous—a lamentable development! You alone have been able to weigh received teachings and vigorously purge contemporary habits; you evidently understand the importance of esteeming virtue. I accept this essay not solely for its literary merits.”

Associate Examiner Jiang, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “When the sages composed the Classics to transmit instruction, when did they ever fail to ground them in achievement and virtue? Only in later ages were these divided into two separate pursuits. Mu Shu’s statement was probably likewise provoked by the conditions of a declining age. This essay develops its argument at length and from several angles, displaying considerable insight. It deserves acceptance as a warning to those who esteem words.”

Associate Examiner Zhu, Examining Editor, comments: “The doctrine of the three forms of immortality has long been set forth. In later ages, scholars have mostly pursued fame, while those intent on establishing virtue have been very rarely seen. Reading your essay, I know that you are someone who seeks advancement through more than words alone.”

Associate Examiner Sun, Examining Editor, comments: “The ancients esteemed virtue rather than words, and thus all under Heaven was well governed. The esteem accorded to words belongs, surely, to an age of decline. In this policy essay, you discuss the matter from several angles in more than a thousand words, ultimately placing the emphasis on esteeming virtue. I therefore know you to be a scholar suited to a well-governed age. Ah, may you live up to your words!”

Associate Examiner Qu, Compiler, comments: “Reporting one’s accomplishments in words was not dispensed with even under Tang and Yu; yet speaking fine words while acting contrary to them was also something they sternly warned against. Commentators past and present have often said that literary men lack substance. Literary men have evidently done something to bring this criticism upon themselves [the transcription 茹家 is doubtful]. title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
蓋有志者錄之非徒以文也
考試官侍講學士敖批先言篤實立志已見大意
反覆揚抑歸重古之聖賢又可見其願學必
佳士也
考試官大學士徐批此策正欲觀士子所志讀
子之文卓然志於立德可以為
明時薦矣
君子之自立于天下者有文焉有行焉行
也者本也君子之所當先也文也者末也
===
君子之所當後也知所先後則雖言語文
字之工有所不足而大者已立亦足以立
于天下而垂無疆之聞使行之不修而徒
文焉是工則藝焉耳矣而又何稱哉執事
當春闈以文試士之日而舉古之三不朽
者下詢蓋欲諸士之篤其實而不溺于文
藝之末也然士之篤其實者莫先于立志
愚請先陳立志之說而後及執事之所詢
可乎夫志于功名亦志也志于功名而不

translation_en:
…surely a man of resolve; his selection is not based solely on his writing.
Examiner Ao, Academician Expositor, comments: By speaking first of earnestness and firmness of purpose, you have already made your main intention clear. Through repeated praise and criticism, you give chief weight to the sages and worthies of antiquity, further revealing your desire to learn from them. You must surely be a worthy scholar.
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: This policy question was intended precisely to reveal the aspirations of the candidates. Reading your essay, I see that you are firmly resolved to establish virtue. You may be recommended for service in this enlightened age.
A gentleman establishes himself in the world through both writing and conduct. Conduct is the root, which a gentleman ought to put first; writing is the branch, which he ought to put afterward. If he understands what comes first and what comes afterward, then even if his skill in speech and writing is somewhat deficient, the greater thing is already established. This is enough for him to stand in the world and leave an enduring reputation. If, however, he fails to cultivate his conduct and is skilled only in writing, this is merely an art. What further merit can be claimed for it? You, honored examiner, at this spring Metropolitan Examination, when men are being tested through their writing, have graciously put to us a question concerning the three forms of imperishability recognized in antiquity. Surely you wish all the candidates to strengthen their substantive attainments and not become absorbed in the secondary pursuit of literary arts. Yet for a scholar seeking to strengthen those attainments, nothing takes precedence over firmness of purpose. May I, in my ignorance, first present an account of establishing one’s purpose, and afterward address what you have asked? To aspire to achievement and renown is indeed an aspiration; but to aspire to achievement and renown without…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
志于道德則其志也為狥外志于文辭亦
志也志于文辭而不志于道德則其志也
為逐末君子之立志盖真知所重在此所
輕在彼而不以彼易此也盖真舉之欲其
勝行之欲其至而不諉于力之不足也盖
真始而習焉久而安焉不以異物遷也如
顏子之簞瓢陋巷不改其樂始可謂之有
志若入聞仁義之言而心悅出見紛華盛
麗而心眩雖謂之無志可也志立而後其
===
擇審擇審而後其守固守固而後天下之
一德在我矣且立德立功立言之分何所
始乎上古未之有也穆叔之言盖見春秋
之時士有不能兼者而言之也其所稱魯
之先大夫臧文仲身沒而言立亦謂之不
朽姑以傲范宣子世祿之徒則可耳文仲
之不仁不智君子盖深譏之非所以稱于
有道之門也上古之時士多全德禹平水
土臯陶明五刑未嘗無功禹有克艱之謨
