punctuated: 志于道德，則其志也為狥外。志于文辭，亦志也；志于文辭而不志于道德，則其志也為逐末。君子之立志，盖真知所重在此，所輕在彼，而不以彼易此也；盖真舉之欲其勝，行之欲其至，而不諉于力之不足也；盖真始而習焉，久而安焉，不以異物遷也。如顏子之簞瓢陋巷，不改其樂，始可謂之有志。若入聞仁義之言而心悅，出見紛華盛麗而心眩，雖謂之無志可也。志立而後其擇審，擇審而後其守固，守固而後天下之一德在我矣。且立德、立功、立言之分，何所始乎？上古未之有也。穆叔之言，盖見春秋之時士有不能兼者而言之也。其所稱魯之先大夫臧文仲，身沒而言立，亦謂之不朽，姑以傲范宣子世祿之徒則可耳。文仲之不仁不智，君子盖深譏之，非所以稱于有道之門也。上古之時，士多全德。禹平水土，臯陶明五刑，未嘗無功；禹有克艱之謨，
translation_en:
…aspire to moral virtue, then his aspiration is a pursuit of externals. Aspiring to literary expression is also an aspiration; but to aspire to literary expression without aspiring to moral virtue is to pursue secondary things. In establishing his resolve, the gentleman truly knows that what deserves weight lies here and what deserves little weight lies there, and he does not exchange the former for the latter. He truly takes up the burden intending to bear it, and puts his resolve into practice intending to carry it through, without pleading insufficient strength. He truly practices it at first and, with time, becomes at ease in it, without being diverted by external things. Only when one resembles Master Yan, whose basket of rice, gourd of water, and humble alley did not diminish his joy, can one be said to possess resolve. If, upon entering, one hears words of benevolence and righteousness and feels pleased, but upon going out, sees extravagant splendor and magnificence and is dazzled, one may indeed be said to lack resolve. Only after resolve is established does one choose discerningly; only after choosing discerningly does one hold firmly to one's choice; and only after holding firmly does the constant virtue of all under Heaven reside in oneself.

Moreover, where did the distinction between establishing virtue, establishing achievements, and establishing lasting words begin? It did not exist in high antiquity. Mu Shu spoke as he did because he saw that, in the Spring and Autumn period, some men could not accomplish all three. He cited Zang Wenzhong, a former grand master of Lu, whose words endured after his death, and called this too a form of immortality. This was acceptable merely as a means of looking down upon Fan Xuanzi and others who enjoyed hereditary emoluments. Yet gentlemen deeply criticized Wenzhong's lack of benevolence and wisdom; he was no exemplar to praise among those who possessed the Way. In high antiquity, men of service often possessed complete virtue. Yu brought the waters and lands into order, and Gao Yao clarified the Five Punishments: they certainly did not lack achievements. Yu had his counsel on confronting difficulties…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
皐陶有知人安民之謨亦未嘗無言伊尹
爰革夏正傳說嗣美阿衡周公之篤棐召
公之保釐未嘗無功伊有伊訓說有說命
周公作無逸陳豳詩召公作旅獒陳敬德
亦未嘗無言是數聖賢者豈有意于立功
立言哉盖其存之為德行措之為事業著
之為話言一以貫之者也逮乎周末聖如
孔子歷聘不遇始退而述六經賢如孟子
所如不合始退而作七篇若無功可言者
===
然人極賴以立天常賴以存萬世而下猶
得聞仁義道德之說而人類不胥為夷狄
禽獸者孔孟之力也故宰我謂孔子賢于
堯舜韓退之謂孟子功不在禹下是豈可
以後之立言者槩之哉古之君子先篤其
實而文行出于一後之君子不篤其實而
文行出于二此古之人所以不朽而非文
士之所及也孔子嘗曰文王既沒文不在
茲乎而孟子亦以承三聖為己任此固韓

translation_en:
…Gao Yao had his counsels on knowing men and bringing peace to the people; thus he, too, was by no means without enduring words. Yi Yin changed the calendar of Xia; Fu Yue continued the excellence of the A-heng [Yi Yin]. The Duke of Zhou gave steadfast assistance, and the Duke of Shao protected and governed: they were by no means without achievements. Yi Yin had the Instructions of Yi, and Fu Yue the Charge to Yue. The Duke of Zhou composed Against Luxurious Ease and set forth the Odes of Bin; the Duke of Shao composed the Hounds of Lü and expounded reverence for virtue. They, too, were by no means without enduring words. Did these sages and worthies deliberately seek to establish achievements or enduring words? What they preserved within themselves became virtuous conduct; what they put into practice became undertakings; what they expressed became words of instruction. A single principle ran through them all.

By the end of the Zhou, even one as sagely as Kongzi traveled among the courts without finding a ruler who would employ him, and only then withdrew to transmit the Six Classics. Even one as worthy as Mengzi found no agreement wherever he went, and only then withdrew to compose his seven books. They seemed to have no achievements to speak of. Yet the supreme standard of humanity depended on them for its establishment, and Heaven’s enduring norms depended on them for their preservation. That people, even ten thousand generations later, can still hear teachings of benevolence, righteousness, the Way, and virtue, and that humankind has not altogether become barbarians or beasts—this is due to the efforts of Kongzi and Mengzi. Thus Zai Wo declared Kongzi worthier than Yao and Shun, and Han Tuizhi declared that Mengzi’s achievements were no less than Yu’s. How could they be placed in the same category as later men who established enduring words?

The gentlemen of antiquity first made their inner substance firm, so that their writings and conduct issued from a single source. Later gentlemen did not make their inner substance firm, so that their writings and conduct issued from two separate sources. This is why the ancients attained immortality, beyond the reach of mere men of letters. Kongzi once said, “Since King Wen has died, does not this cultural tradition reside here in me?” Mengzi likewise took it as his own responsibility to carry on the legacy of the three sages. This is indeed what Han…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
退之所謂堯舜禹湯文武周公之傳傳之
孔子而孔子傳之孟軻者也蘇子瞻氏謂
孟子之後五百餘年而後得韓愈愈之後
又三百餘年而後得歐陽子盖將推韓歐
以附孔孟韓歐之文果孔孟之所謂文哉
六經之修孔子之文也七篇之垂孟子之
文也然必有為之實者矣美在其中而暢
于四肢者文之本也發于事業而經緯天
地者文之用也播之訓辭而中國之人世
===
守之者文之昭也是謂有德之言文行出
于一者也若韓子之奧衍雄深永叔之醇
深炳鬱雖稱文章大家然踐履則未至也
充養則未完也雖其議論亦多崇正闢邪
左右六經然質之孔孟則未純也故退之
之可稱者文起八代之衰忠犯人主之怒
勇奪三軍之帥唐之文士誠莫之先矣然
平生所為多浮華放浪之習富貴利達之
求視孔孟之進以禮退以義者何如也永

punctuated: 退之所謂堯舜禹湯文武周公之傳，傳之孔子，而孔子傳之孟軻者也。蘇子瞻氏謂孟子之後五百餘年，而後得韓愈；愈之後又三百餘年，而後得歐陽子，盖將推韓歐以附孔孟。韓歐之文，果孔孟之所謂文哉？六經之修，孔子之文也；七篇之垂，孟子之文也。然必有為之實者矣。美在其中而暢于四肢者，文之本也；發于事業而經緯天地者，文之用也；播之訓辭而中國之人世守之者，文之昭也。是謂有德之言，文行出于一者也。若韓子之奧衍雄深、永叔之醇深炳鬱，雖稱文章大家，然踐履則未至也，充養則未完也。雖其議論亦多崇正闢邪、左右六經，然質之孔孟則未純也。故退之之可稱者，文起八代之衰，忠犯人主之怒，勇奪三軍之帥，唐之文士誠莫之先矣。然平生所為，多浮華放浪之習、富貴利達之求，視孔孟之進以禮、退以義者何如也？永
translation_en:
…what Han Tuizhi described as the tradition of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and the Duke of Zhou, transmitted to Kongzi, who in turn transmitted it to Meng Ke. Su Zizhan said that only after more than five hundred years following Mengzi did Han Yu appear, and only after another three hundred years following Han Yu did Master Ouyang appear. He presumably intended to exalt Han and Ouyang by placing them alongside Kongzi and Mengzi. But was the writing of Han and Ouyang truly what Kongzi and Mengzi understood by “writing”?

The editing of the Six Classics was Kongzi’s literary work; the handing down of the seven books was Mengzi’s literary work. Yet these must have had a substantive foundation. Beauty residing within and flowing through the four limbs is the root of literary expression; its manifestation in undertakings that order Heaven and Earth is its function; its dissemination in words of instruction, preserved generation after generation by the people of the Central Kingdom, is its visible expression. These are what are called the words of one possessed of virtue: writing and conduct proceeding from a single source.

As for Master Han’s profundity, amplitude, grandeur, and depth, and Yongshu’s purity, depth, brilliance, and richness, although both are acclaimed as great masters of writing, their practice had not reached perfection, nor was their cultivation complete. Although their arguments often upheld the orthodox, refuted the heterodox, and supported the Six Classics, when measured against Kongzi and Mengzi they were not wholly pure. Thus, what merits praise in Tuizhi is that his writing revived literature from the decline of eight dynasties, his loyalty braved his ruler’s anger, and his courage could wrest the commander from the Three Armies. Truly, no man of letters of the Tang surpassed him. Yet his lifelong conduct often displayed habits of ostentation and unrestrained indulgence, and the pursuit of wealth, rank, advantage, and advancement. How does this compare with Kongzi and Mengzi, who entered service according to ritual propriety and withdrew according to righteousness? Yong…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
叔之可稱者以通經學古為高以救時行
道為賢以犯顏敢諫為忠宋之文士誠莫
之及矣然平生所玩多琴樽文翰之溺視
孔孟之忘食忘憂存心養性者何如也是
韓歐之在唐宋謂之立言之士則可而欲
以附孔孟天下其誰與之哉夫文如韓歐
而君子猶不與焉則士之欲自立于天下
者亦可以志于本矣蓋嘗論士之品有三
有道德之士有功名之士有文辭之士道
===
德之士上也功名之士次也文辭之士又
其次也言誠立矣則雖沉抑下位而文采
表于後世藏之名山傳之通都亦足以稱
于君子之林然未離于技壯夫之所不為
也使能乘時自奮以竒策材力結知明主
內之能謀安宗社澤潤生民外之能式遏
亂畧綏靖疆圉書之旂常而昭明勒之鼎
彛而不磨即言語之工何以稱焉功誠立
矣則雖跅弛之士有負俗之累而名著丹

彝而不磨即言語之工何以稱焉功誠立

punctuated:
叔之可稱者，以通經學古為高，以救時行道為賢，以犯顏敢諫為忠，宋之文士誠莫之及矣。然平生所玩，多琴樽文翰之溺，視孔孟之忘食忘憂、存心養性者何如也？是韓歐之在唐宋，謂之立言之士則可，而欲以附孔孟，天下其誰與之哉？夫文如韓歐，而君子猶不與焉，則士之欲自立于天下者，亦可以志于本矣。
蓋嘗論士之品有三：有道德之士，有功名之士，有文辭之士。道德之士上也，功名之士次也，文辭之士又其次也。言誠立矣，則雖沉抑下位，而文采表于後世，藏之名山，傳之通都，亦足以稱于君子之林。然未離于技，壯夫之所不為也。使能乘時自奮，以竒策材力結知明主，內之能謀安宗社、澤潤生民，外之能式遏亂畧、綏靖疆圉，書之旂常而昭明，勒之鼎彛而不磨，即言語之工何以稱焉？功誠立矣，則雖跅弛之士，有負俗之累，而名著丹
translation_en:
…What merits praise in Yongshu is that he esteemed mastery of the Classics and study of antiquity as lofty, regarded saving his age and putting the Way into practice as worthy, and considered braving the ruler’s displeasure and daring to remonstrate as loyal. Among the literary men of the Song, truly none could match him. Yet his lifelong diversions often involved an excessive attachment to the zither, wine cups, and literary pursuits. How does this compare with Kongzi and Mengzi, who forgot food and cares, preserved their minds, and nourished their nature? Thus, of Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu in the Tang and Song, one may call them men who established enduring words; but if one wished to rank them alongside Kongzi and Mengzi, who in the world would agree? If even literary achievement such as Han’s and Ouyang’s does not win the gentleman’s full approval, then scholars who wish to establish themselves in the world may well direct their aspirations toward the root.
I have maintained that scholars fall into three grades: men of the Way and virtue, men of achievement and renown, and men of literary expression. Men of the Way and virtue rank highest; men of achievement and renown come next; and men of literary expression follow them. If a man has truly established enduring words, then even though he languishes in a low position, his literary brilliance may shine forth to later generations. His writings may be stored in famous mountains and circulated in great cities, sufficient to earn him recognition among gentlemen. Yet this still does not transcend a specialized skill, something a mature man disdains to pursue. Suppose instead that he can seize the opportunity of his times and exert himself, winning an enlightened ruler’s recognition through extraordinary plans, ability, and strength; at home, he can devise ways to secure the dynasty and bestow benefits upon the people; abroad, he can check disorder and aggression and pacify the frontiers. His deeds would be recorded upon banners in splendor and engraved upon ritual vessels never to be effaced. How could mere skill in words compare with this? If a man has truly established achievements, then even though he is unrestrained in conduct and bears the stigma of flouting convention, his name is recorded in the vermilion…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
書盟藏天府亦且為一代宗臣然血氣用
事仲尼之門所羞稱也使能斂其馳騖之
氣而遜志典學以性情則得其理以彝倫
則得其敘以出處進退辭受取予則得其
正雖身在側微而天下推之後世頌之即
事功之粗又何以稱焉善乎永叔之言曰
聖賢之不朽而存特異于衆人者修之于
身施之于事見之于言所以能不朽而存
也施于事矣不見于言可也修于身矣不
===
施于事不見于言亦可也嗚呼人能修于
身則其不朽而存者豈不賢于能言之士
哉吾獨怪夫天下之人不知以立言之心
立德也如班固藝文志所稱唐四庫書目
所載能言之士代不下數十家方其有意
于立言也自以為戴盆不可以望天絕賓
客之知忘室家之業覃思載籍以成其一
家之言雖迫于困辱而不倦不沮此其心
亦勤矣然視六經語孟之言皆若贅疣雖

吾獨怪夫天下之人，不知以立言之心立德也。如班固《藝文志》所稱、唐《四庫書目》所載，能言之士，代不下數十家。方其有意于立言也，自以為戴盆不可以望天，絕賓客之知，忘室家之業，覃思載籍，以成其一家之言。雖迫于困辱，而不倦不沮，此其心亦勤矣。然視六經、《語》《孟》之言，皆若贅疣，雖
translation_en:
…in vermilion records, with their covenants preserved in the imperial treasury, they may indeed become eminent ministers of their age. Yet to act on impetuous passions is something that the school of Zhongni [Confucius] would be ashamed to praise. If they could restrain their restless drive, humble their aspirations, and devote themselves to learning, they would grasp the principles governing human nature and feelings, the proper ordering of enduring human relationships, and the right course in serving or withdrawing, advancing or retiring, declining or accepting, taking or giving. Though they occupied humble and obscure positions, all under Heaven would esteem them and later generations would praise them. How could the comparatively coarse achievements of practical service measure up to this? Well said are the words of Yongshu [Ouyang Xiu]: “What makes sages and worthies endure imperishably, distinct from ordinary people, is what they cultivate in themselves, put into practice in affairs, and express in words. This is how they endure imperishably. If they put it into practice in affairs, it is acceptable not to express it in words. If they cultivate it in themselves, it is also acceptable neither to put it into practice in affairs nor to express it in words. Alas! If people can cultivate themselves, does not what endures imperishably in them surpass that of men skilled in words?”

What especially puzzles me is that people do not know to apply their dedication to establishing lasting words to establishing virtue. Among those mentioned in Ban Gu’s Treatise on Literature and those listed in the Tang Catalogue of the Four Repositories, every age had at least several dozen writers skilled in words. When they set their minds on establishing lasting words, they believed that one cannot gaze at the sky while carrying a basin on one’s head. They broke off associations with visitors and friends, neglected their household affairs, and pondered the written records deeply, seeking to formulate a distinctive body of thought. Though beset by hardship and humiliation, they neither tired nor lost heart. Their dedication was indeed strenuous. Yet, compared with the words of the Six Classics, the Analects, and the Mencius, their writings all seem like superfluous growths. Although…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
足以悅一時之耳目而隨即泯沒使能以
立言之心而立德則何德不立乃為彼而
不為此亦惑矣夫易勉者德也難必者功
也難工者辭也禹皐之賢不加于孔孟而
功在天下聲施萬世遇也孔孟之賢不減
于禹皐而不獲一試卒老于行不遇也故
曰事與時並名與功偕是難必者功也自
人人觀之則人人各有短長如隨陸無武
絳灌無文房杜不見于文章韓柳無稱于
===
事業是也自一人觀之則一人亦有短長
如退之文之名家也而劣于詩杜甫詩之
名家也而劣于文是也是難工者辭也若
立德則理吾性情敦吾彝倫慎吾素履有
不思思則必得有不行行則必至是易勉
者德也夫文難工也而爭致力焉德易勉
也而顧舍之不修豈不惑甚矣哉若此者
盖皆志之不立其待聖賢也常太高其自
待也常太卑故皆以傑然之材而又勤一

punctuated: 足以悅一時之耳目，而隨即泯沒。使能以立言之心而立德，則何德不立？乃為彼而不為此，亦惑矣。夫易勉者德也，難必者功也，難工者辭也。禹皐之賢不加于孔孟，而功在天下，聲施萬世，遇也；孔孟之賢不減于禹皐，而不獲一試，卒老于行，不遇也。故曰：「事與時並，名與功偕。」是難必者功也。自人人觀之，則人人各有短長，如隨陸無武，絳灌無文，房杜不見于文章，韓柳無稱于事業，是也。自一人觀之，則一人亦有短長，如退之文之名家也，而劣于詩；杜甫詩之名家也，而劣于文，是也。是難工者辭也。若立德，則理吾性情，敦吾彝倫，慎吾素履，有不思，思則必得；有不行，行則必至。是易勉者德也。夫文難工也，而爭致力焉；德易勉也，而顧舍之不修，豈不惑甚矣哉？若此者，盖皆志之不立，其待聖賢也常太高，其自待也常太卑，故皆以傑然之材，而又勤一
translation_en:
…they may delight the eyes and ears for a time, yet soon vanish into oblivion. If these men could apply their determination to establish lasting words to establishing virtue, what virtue could they not establish? To pursue the former rather than the latter is indeed misguided. Virtue readily rewards effort; achievement is difficult to ensure; literary expression is difficult to perfect. Yu and Gao Yao were no worthier than Confucius and Mencius, yet their achievements benefited the realm and their renown extended through ten thousand generations: they met with opportunity. Confucius and Mencius were no less worthy than Yu and Gao Yao, yet they never obtained even one chance to put their teachings into practice and finally grew old in their travels: they met with no opportunity. Hence the saying: “Deeds depend upon their times; fame accompanies achievement.” This is why achievement is difficult to ensure.

Looking at different individuals, each has strengths and weaknesses. Sui He and Lu Jia lacked military accomplishments; Jiang and Guan lacked literary accomplishments; Fang Xuanling and Du Ruhui were not distinguished in literary composition; Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan were not renowned for practical achievements. Looking at a single individual, too, one finds both strengths and weaknesses. Tuizhi [Han Yu] was a master of prose, yet inferior in poetry; Du Fu was a master of poetry, yet inferior in prose. This is why literary expression is difficult to perfect.

As for establishing virtue, it requires ordering my nature and feelings, strengthening my observance of the enduring human relationships, and taking care in my everyday conduct. One may fail to reflect, but if one reflects, one will surely gain understanding; one may fail to act, but if one acts, one will surely reach the goal. This is why virtue readily rewards effort. Literary composition is difficult to perfect, yet men compete in devoting their energies to it; virtue readily rewards effort, yet they abandon it and neglect its cultivation. Is this not profoundly misguided? Such men have, in every case, failed to establish a firm resolve. They habitually set the sages and worthies too high and their expectations of themselves too low. Thus, despite their exceptional talents, and despite laboring diligently for an entire…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
世以用心其所成就卒局于文藝之末不
能越藝苑而有進也愚也生逢
盛世獲與計偕雖不敢侈然自附于古人然
進而廣業退而修身無不可者古之聖賢
猶汲汲皇皇日有不暇愚也獨何暇工其
無實之文哉執事幸與其進
第四問
曹大章
同考試官郎中陳批漕河最今日急務此
===
作獨能詳析經處殆有心計者
同考試官左給事中張批治河之策士子類能
言之率汗漫無從子能歷陳往事及今日先後緩急
之序如指諸掌經濟之學不可以觀其深耶
同考試官編修董批誠如策所陳四役兼
舉者雖不得已而用財然此業一定亦當世大計
也策事者貴圖其全子則慮之悉矣取之
同考試官修撰全批今人皆以河決歸之
天數若欲棄而不治此策獨能詳叙原委而區

同考試官修撰全批：今人皆以河決歸之天數，若欲棄而不治。此策獨能詳叙原委而區

…a lifetime of effort, yet their achievements ultimately remain confined to the lesser pursuits of literary composition, unable to advance beyond the literary sphere. I, in my humble capacity, was born into a flourishing age and have been privileged to join those sent to the capital for the examination. Although I dare not presumptuously rank myself with the ancients, nothing prevents me from broadening my undertakings when advancing into office or cultivating myself when withdrawing. Even the sages and worthies of antiquity exerted themselves with anxious diligence, finding each day too short. How, then, could I alone have leisure to perfect writing devoid of substance? May you, honored sir, look favorably upon my progress.
Fourth Policy Question
Cao Dazhang
Associate Examiner Chen, Director, comments: The grain-transport canal is the most urgent concern today. This essay alone analyzes its management and treatment in detail; its author evidently possesses a calculating mind.
Associate Examiner Zhang, Left Supervising Secretary, comments: Candidates can generally discuss policies for river control, but their discussions are mostly diffuse and offer no clear course to follow. You can set forth past events in sequence and explain the order in which present measures should be undertaken, distinguishing the urgent from those that can wait, as clearly as pointing to something in your palm. Does this not reveal the depth of your learning in statecraft?

…its plans for remedial measures all suit the needs of the time. This must be someone who has long possessed a grasp of statecraft.
Examiner Ao, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: Taking the regulation of the upper reaches as the strategy for managing the Yellow River today: surely the proper approach lies here.
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: Everyone knows that the calamity of the Yellow River’s breaches demands urgent attention, yet no strategy for dealing with it has emerged. This essay offers detailed historical evidence and appropriate measures; hence its selection.
You, honored examiners, concerned about the Yellow River’s breach between Xu and Fang, have put a policy question to us students. Your concern for a great undertaking of our age shows the utmost solicitude. Though I am unworthy to submit a point-by-point reply, allow me nevertheless to offer an outline.
The Yellow River and the sea are among the greatest bodies of water under Heaven. The sea is greater still, and all rivers flow into it. Yet the sea causes no calamity, because the force of flowing water diminishes at its destination, where it finds room to be received. The Yellow River, however, rises at Xingxiu, crosses Kunlun, and reaches Jishi over a distance of several thousand li; from Jishi it travels several thousand li more to Bian and to the Huai. Its course is long and steep, its current swift and fierce, and it has yet to find room to be received. Gathering the various streams of Shan, Shaan, He, and Bian, it swells after prolonged rains and floods. That it should surge violently and burst sideways through its banks is therefore its normal tendency.
Since the Han dynasty, enlightened rulers have labored diligently and consulted widely above, while ministers charged with deliberation and action have exhausted their ingenuity and strength below. Yet the river has never ceased to breach its banks, nor has there ever been a settled strategy for managing it. In the time of the Han emperors Wen and Wu, the priority was to close breaches, as in the closures at Suanzao and Xuanfang. In the time of Emperors Ai and Cheng, …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
則議不塞如賈讓所謂徙民當水衝者不
與河爭地李尋解光所謂因其自决以觀
水勢聽河欲居之者是也後之言治河者
大槩不出此二端然河者數變而不可逆
者也使塞之于此而復决于彼是不知河
之變而逆其性者也故丘文莊獨稱賈讓
者蓋見河之不易塞也然地不可以數徙
水不可以徐觀即河所欲居林莽荒曠之
墟待其自定可也即貫城郭歷郡縣國家
===
所繫者大其亦可待否也故文莊又以賈
讓諸人皆隨時制宜之策今日未必便者
蓋見河之不易議也而在今日尤有難者
河自汴而南則鳳陽淮泗之間
祖陵及王墳在焉王氣所鍾天下之根本也東
則會通河在焉漕江南數百萬之粟集百
貨以充京師天下之咽喉也皆國家之所
甚繫者也河不東則漕不通而河之勢非
會通所能當也故方欲引而東又防其有

punctuated:
則議不塞，如賈讓所謂徙民當水衝者，不與河爭地，李尋、解光所謂因其自决以觀水勢，聽河欲居之者是也。後之言治河者，大槩不出此二端。然河者，數變而不可逆者也。使塞之于此而復决于彼，是不知河之變而逆其性者也。故丘文莊獨稱賈讓者，蓋見河之不易塞也。然地不可以數徙，水不可以徐觀。即河所欲居，林莽荒曠之墟，待其自定可也；即貫城郭，歷郡縣，國家所繫者大，其亦可待否也？故文莊又以賈讓諸人皆隨時制宜之策，今日未必便者，蓋見河之不易議也。
而在今日，尤有難者。河自汴而南，則鳳陽淮泗之間，祖陵及王墳在焉，王氣所鍾，天下之根本也。東則會通河在焉，漕江南數百萬之粟，集百貨以充京師，天下之咽喉也，皆國家之所甚繫者也。河不東則漕不通，而河之勢非會通所能當也。故方欲引而東，又防其有
translation_en:
…then the proposal was not to close the breaches. Examples are Jia Rang’s proposal to relocate people living in the path of the water’s onrush and not contend with the Yellow River for land, and Li Xun and Xie Guang’s proposal to let the river breach its banks, observe the force and direction of the water, and allow it to occupy whatever course it sought. Later discussions of river management have generally remained within these two approaches. Yet the river frequently changes and cannot be forced against its natural tendencies. To close a breach here only for another to open there is to misunderstand the river’s changes and oppose its nature. Thus Qiu Wenzhuang singled out Jia Rang for praise because he recognized how difficult it was to close the river’s breaches. Yet places of habitation cannot repeatedly be relocated, nor can one take one’s time observing the water. If the place the river seeks to occupy is a wild, uninhabited expanse of woodland and brush, one may wait for it to settle of its own accord. But if it passes through walled cities and traverses prefectures and counties, where the interests of the state are deeply involved, can one still wait? Thus Wenzhuang also held that the proposals of Jia Rang and the others were all measures adapted to the circumstances of their times and might not be suitable today. He recognized how difficult it was to determine a policy for the river.
Today, moreover, there are particular difficulties. Where the river runs south from Bian, the imperial ancestral mausoleum and princely tombs lie in the region of Fengyang, Huai, and Si. This is where the vital force of kingship gathers, the very foundation of the realm. To the east lies the Huitong Canal, which transports several million measures of grain from Jiangnan and gathers goods of every kind to supply the capital: it is the throat of the realm. Both are of the utmost consequence to the state. Unless the river flows east, grain transport cannot get through; yet the force of the river is more than the Huitong Canal can withstand. Thus, just as one seeks to divert it eastward, one must also guard against the risk of its…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
決會通之患及其障而南又防其爲
陵寢之患自古治河兩難未有如今日之甚者
使漢人復生亦未知何以措其智也今徐
房之間河既橫決或者徒見天變方甚以
爲其道必不可復不若任其所決而別徙
道以屬之于邳獨不知河之入徐束之以
徐呂之洪而當兩涯之險此天之設竒以
濟漕而制河者也尚不能制而至于決況
去崇山之險無兩洪之束而循漫流以通
===
道勢之必不可者也故議者專意于新安
以爲新安淤而徐房決今開淤以容水而
塞其決以制橫流則故道宜復然亦不知
徐房者受上流之輸而建瓴于新安者也
今不急治其上流而欲開數十里之淤以
當橫潰無涯之水則塞者必復決而開者
必復淤此亦勢之所不可也故禹之治河

汭至于大伾厮爲二渠過洚水至于大陸

punctuated: 決會通之患；及其障而南，又防其爲陵寢之患。自古治河兩難，未有如今日之甚者。使漢人復生，亦未知何以措其智也。今徐房之間，河既橫決，或者徒見天變方甚，以爲其道必不可復，不若任其所決，而別徙道以屬之于邳。獨不知河之入徐，束之以徐呂之洪，而當兩涯之險，此天之設竒以濟漕而制河者也。尚不能制而至于決，況去崇山之險，無兩洪之束，而循漫流以通道，勢之必不可者也。故議者專意于新安，以爲新安淤而徐房決，今開淤以容水，而塞其決以制橫流，則故道宜復。然亦不知徐房者，受上流之輸，而建瓴于新安者也。今不急治其上流，而欲開數十里之淤，以當橫潰無涯之水，則塞者必復決，而開者必復淤，此亦勢之所不可也。故禹之治河，自積石，鑿龍門，闢伊闕，下砥柱，抵孟津、洛汭，至于大伾，厮爲二渠，過洚水，至于大陸，
translation_en:
…the danger of its breaching the Huitong Canal; yet when it is embanked and directed southward, precautions must again be taken against its threatening the imperial tombs. Since ancient times, the dilemma of controlling the Yellow River has never been as acute as it is today. Even if the men of the Han dynasty returned to life, they would not know how to apply their ingenuity.

Now that the river has breached its banks and surged across the country between Xu and Fang, some people, seeing only that the anomalies of Heaven are particularly severe, believe that its former course cannot possibly be restored. They think it better to let the river follow its breach and divert its course elsewhere to connect with Pi. They fail to understand that, where the river enters Xu, it is confined by the Xu and Lü rapids and hemmed in by steep banks on both sides. These are extraordinary features provided by Heaven to facilitate grain transport and restrain the river. If even these cannot restrain it and it still breaks through, how could one possibly abandon the steep mountain barriers and the confinement of the two rapids, and establish a navigable route by following its spreading waters? The physical conditions make this impossible.

Thus those discussing the matter concentrate their attention on Xin’an. They reason that silting at Xin’an caused the breaches between Xu and Fang: if the silt is now cleared to accommodate the water, and the breaches closed to restrain its uncontrolled flow, the former course should be restored. Yet they too fail to understand that the stretch between Xu and Fang receives the discharge from upstream and sends it plunging down toward Xin’an, like water poured from a tilted vessel. Unless its upper course is urgently brought under control, clearing several tens of li of silt in an attempt to accommodate waters pouring unchecked across the land will only mean that the closed breaches break open again and the cleared channels silt up again. This too is precluded by the physical conditions.

Thus, when Yu controlled the river, he began at Jishi, cut through Longmen, opened Yique, proceeded down past Dizhu, reached Mengjin and Luorui, and arrived at Dapi. There he divided it into two channels, passed the Jiang River, and reached Dalu…

地則厮之而為二大陸以下地益平土益

上流而分其支者也導而分之則河雖欲

明興九河之迹既遠然其始自汴而出者河
猶有六其二入淮其四合漕以入于淮出

播爲九河。方大伾以下，河始出險而就平地，則厮之而為二；大陸以下，地益平，土益疏，水益善潰，則播之而為九。此所以導其上流而分其支者也。導而分之，則河雖欲決而不可得也。
明興，九河之迹既遠，然其始自汴而出者，河猶有六：其二入淮，其四合漕以入于淮。出滎澤者，至壽入淮；出祥符者，至懷遠入淮；出長垣者，至陽穀入漕；出曹州者，至魚臺入漕；出儀封者，至徐之小浮橋入漕；出沛之南者，飛雲橋入漕；出徐沛之中、鏡山之北者，溜溝入漕。是其始猶有禹分之遺意也。及其後，或塞或微，或并為二，或合為一，而河之道愈寡，其力愈專，則其决固宜也。
愚甞觀明興以來，河凡數决矣。洪武間决魚臺，其後魚臺塞，而正統間决沙灣、大洪之口；沙灣塞，而弘治間决金龍口，又决張秋。當是時，
translation_en:
…and spread into nine channels. Below Dapi, where the Yellow River first emerged from confined terrain onto level ground, Yu divided it into two channels. Below Dalu, where the land became still flatter, the soil looser, and the water more prone to bursting its banks, he spread it into nine. This was how he guided its upper course and divided its branches. Once guided and divided, the river could not breach its banks even if it wished to.
When the Ming arose, the traces of the nine channels were already remote. Yet initially the river still had six channels emerging from Bian: two entered the Huai, while four joined the grain-transport canal and thereby entered the Huai. The channel emerging at Xingze entered the Huai at Shou; that emerging at Xiangfu entered the Huai at Huaiyuan; that emerging at Changyuan entered the canal at Yanggu; that emerging at Caozhou entered the canal at Yutai; that emerging at Yifeng entered the canal at the Little Pontoon Bridge in Xu; that emerging south of Pei entered the canal at Feiyun Bridge; and that emerging between Xu and Pei, north of Jingshan, entered the canal at Liugou. [The text states six channels but lists seven.] Thus, at the outset, something of Yu’s intention in dividing the river still survived. Later, some channels became blocked and others dwindled; some merged into two, others combined into one. As the river’s courses grew fewer, its force became more concentrated, so it was only to be expected that it would breach its banks.
I have observed that since the founding of the Ming the river has breached its banks several times. During the Hongwu reign it breached at Yutai. After the Yutai breach was closed, it breached during the Zhengtong reign at Shawan and the Dahong opening. After Shawan was closed, it breached during the Hongzhi reign at Jinlongkou, and then again at Zhangqiu. At that time…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
沙灣之功成乃作九堰八閘開渠二十里
而猶不免于决及張秋之功成乃浚賈魯
河孫家渡諸口其法尤備然其後又决曹
單及正德間曹單塞又决豐沛及嘉靖初
豐沛塞又復决魚臺及魚臺决乃濬趙皮
寨而數年復决夏邑遂徙而入渦奔亳泗
而趙皮寨又塞復數年諸河之入漕者皆
不來清濟間流幾絶而入渦者溢于泗震
驚
===
陵寢於是諸臣皆惶恐待罪開孫繼口而渦河
塞漕復得通及孫繼口入徐又有今日之
决始孫繼口之役諸臣之受切責懼無以
報命也故盡截野雞岡之水以入新口又
捲埽築壩橫亘而逼之不容入渦所以為
漕計而護
陵寢者非不甚重然河之正派皆歸孫繼而以
全力入徐矣是河之所以暴决者以其專
而不分故也愚嘗問長老皆言今諸河巳

而不分故也愚嘗聞長老皆言今諸河巳
punctuated: 沙灣之功成，乃作九堰八閘，開渠二十里，而猶不免于决。及張秋之功成，乃浚賈魯河、孫家渡諸口，其法尤備，然其後又决曹單。及正德間，曹單塞，又决豐沛。及嘉靖初，豐沛塞，又復决魚臺。及魚臺决，乃濬趙皮寨，而數年復决夏邑，遂徙而入渦，奔亳泗，而趙皮寨又塞。復數年，諸河之入漕者皆不來，清濟間流幾絶，而入渦者溢于泗，震驚陵寢。於是諸臣皆惶恐待罪，開孫繼口，而渦河塞，漕復得通。及孫繼口入徐，又有今日之决。始孫繼口之役，諸臣之受切責，懼無以報命也，故盡截野雞岡之水，以入新口，又捲埽築壩，橫亘而逼之，不容入渦。所以為漕計而護陵寢者，非不甚重，然河之正派皆歸孫繼，而以全力入徐矣。是河之所以暴决者，以其專而不分故也。愚嘗問長老，皆言今諸河巳
translation_en:
…When the works at Shawan were completed, nine weirs and eight sluices were constructed and a channel twenty li long was excavated, yet breaches still could not be avoided. When the works at Zhangqiu were completed, the Jialu River and the various outlets at Sunjiadu were dredged. These measures were especially comprehensive, yet afterward the river again breached its banks in Cao and Shan. During the Zhengde reign, the breaches at Cao and Shan were closed, but the river then broke through at Feng and Pei. Early in the Jiajing reign, the breaches at Feng and Pei were closed, but the river again broke through at Yutai. After the Yutai breach, Zhaopizhai was dredged; a few years later, however, the river again broke through at Xiayi. It then shifted course into the Guo River, rushing toward Bo and Si, while Zhaopizhai silted shut again. After several more years, none of the streams that had fed the grain-transport canal reached it any longer, and the flow between Qing and Ji had almost ceased. Meanwhile, the waters entering the Guo overflowed at Si, causing alarm for the imperial mausoleums. The officials were all terrified and awaited punishment. They opened Sunjikou and blocked the Guo River route, restoring passage along the grain-transport canal. But once the waters from Sunjikou entered Xu, the present breach occurred.

At the outset of the Sunjikou works, the officials had been severely reprimanded and feared they could not fulfill their orders. They therefore intercepted all the water at Yejigang and directed it into the new outlet. They also bound brushwood into rolls and built a dam across the channel to force the water onward, preventing it from entering the Guo. Their concern for grain transport and the protection of the imperial mausoleums was certainly very great. Yet the river’s main stream was thereby directed entirely through Sunjikou, entering Xu with its full force. Thus the river’s violent breaches occur because its flow is concentrated rather than divided. I have asked the elders, and they all say that the various river channels have now already…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
塞惟孫家渡與孫繼口而孫家渡廣不能
數丈不足以分孫繼獨趙皮寨廣加數倍
河之正派也今誠急濬趙皮寨導河之四
以入淮而其六之由孫繼以入徐者開别
支以殺其勢又於孫家渡諸口按河脉而
時疏之彼其力既分則可以漸制既不至
為
陵寢患而漕亦宜通故言當先治上流者此一
計也然禹導九河自碣石北放于海及隋
===
鑿汴始南通于淮則淮者非受河之正也
故余闕宋學士皆謂以河之大不宜以一
淮為之委者明淮不足以當河也今聞淮
之安東其淤畧與新安等矣夫以全淮注
河而又不能即達于海則河益激而淮益
不能容其與新安之淤相乘而積亦其所
必至者故當并治下流者又一計也夫治
上流以救其源治下流以疏其委然後徐
房之决可塞而新安可開此四役者宜同

爲
陵寢患而漕亦宜通故言當先治上流者此一
計也然禹導九河自碣石北放于海及隋
===
鑿汴始南通于淮則淮者非受河之正也
故余闕宋學士皆謂以河之大不宜以一
淮爲之委者明淮不足以當河也今聞淮
之安東其淤塞與新安等矣夫以全淮注
河而又不能即達于海則河益激而淮益
不能容其與新安之淤相乘而積亦其所
必至者故當并治下流者又一計也夫治
上流以救其源治下流以疏其委然後徐
房之决可塞而新安可開此四役者宜同
punctuated:
塞，惟孫家渡與孫繼口，而孫家渡廣不能數丈，不足以分孫繼。獨趙皮寨廣加數倍，河之正派也。今誠急濬趙皮寨，導河之四以入淮，而其六之由孫繼以入徐者，開别支以殺其勢；又於孫家渡諸口，按河脉而時疏之。彼其力既分，則可以漸制，既不至為陵寢患，而漕亦宜通。故言當先治上流者，此一計也。
然禹導九河，自碣石北放于海，及隋鑿汴，始南通于淮，則淮者非受河之正也。故余闕、宋學士皆謂以河之大，不宜以一淮為之委者，明淮不足以當河也。今聞淮之安東，其淤畧與新安等矣。夫以全淮注河，而又不能即達于海，則河益激，而淮益不能容，其與新安之淤相乘而積，亦其所必至者。故當并治下流者，又一計也。
夫治上流以救其源，治下流以疏其委，然後徐房之决可塞，而新安可開。此四役者宜同
translation_en:
…have been blocked, leaving only Sunjiadu and Sunjikou. Yet Sunjiadu is not even several zhang wide and cannot sufficiently divert the flow from Sunjikou. Zhaopizhai alone is several times wider and is the Yellow River’s main channel. If Zhaopizhai were urgently dredged to conduct four-tenths of the river into the Huai, while additional branches were opened to reduce the force of the six-tenths entering Xu through Sunjikou, and if the various outlets at Sunjiadu were also dredged periodically in accordance with the river’s channels, its force, once divided, could gradually be brought under control. It would then no longer threaten the imperial tombs, and grain transport by water should also proceed unobstructed. Thus, attending first to the upper reaches is one measure.
Now Yu channelled the Nine Rivers into the sea north of Jieshi. Only when the Sui excavated the Bian did the river connect southward with the Huai; the Huai was therefore not the natural recipient of the Yellow River’s main flow. Thus Yu Que and Academician Song both maintained that a river as large as the Yellow River should not have the Huai alone as its outlet: they understood that the Huai could not accommodate it. I now hear that the silting of the Huai at Andong is roughly equal to that at Xin’an. If the entire Huai pours into the Yellow River but cannot then reach the sea directly, the Yellow River becomes still more turbulent, while the Huai becomes still less able to contain the water. Its silting and that at Xin’an will inevitably aggravate one another and accumulate. Thus, attending to the lower reaches as well is another measure.
By regulating the upper reaches to remedy the trouble at its source, and regulating the lower reaches to clear its outlet, the breaches at Xu and Fang can then be closed and Xin’an opened. These four undertakings should be carried out at the same …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
時而並舉不可闕一者也然察執事之意
顧以同時舉天下之四大役非所以惜財
而體國者嗟乎愚之為此議者正恐財之
妄費也夫興天下之役而成天下之功此
自古用財之道也不得謂之費惟顧惜而
功不成則其所用乃所謂費也昔秦皇將
伐楚問王翦曰非六十萬人不可問李信
曰二十萬人然李信以二十萬人而不勝
則二十萬人皆費也王翦之勝則六十萬
===
人而不為費治河亦若是也去年
天子閔被水之地蠲郡縣以萬計遣大臣往賑
又十萬計夫今河不治則他日宜蠲宜賑
者又不知其幾也今以蠲與賑者倍其數
即河可成民得其業是愈于蠲與賑者甚
遠也宋人防河與防虜等夫虜之可憂未
必如中原之可憂惜財之說非所以施于
遇變不得已之時者也然執事又以罷民
不可以重勞灾地不可以處眾斯固慮之

妄費也夫興天下之役而成天下之功此
自古用財之道也不得謂之費惟顧惜而
功不成則其所用乃所謂費也昔秦皇將

曰二十萬人然李信以二十萬人而不勝
則二十萬人皆費也王翦之勝則六十萬
===
人而不為費治河亦若是也去年
天子閔被水之地蠲郡縣以萬計遣大臣往賑
又十萬計夫今河不治則他日宜蠲宜賑
者又不知其幾也今以蠲與賑者倍其數
即河可成民得其業是愈于蠲與賑者甚
遠也宋人防河與防虜等夫虜之可憂未
必如中原之可憂惜財之說非所以施于
遇變不得已之時者也然執事又以罷民
不可以重勞灾地不可以處衆斯固慮之
punctuated:
時而並舉，不可闕一者也。然察執事之意，顧以同時舉天下之四大役，非所以惜財而體國者。嗟乎！愚之為此議者，正恐財之妄費也。夫興天下之役，而成天下之功，此自古用財之道也，不得謂之費。惟顧惜而功不成，則其所用乃所謂費也。昔秦皇將伐楚，問王翦，曰：「非六十萬人不可。」問李信，曰：「二十萬人。」然李信以二十萬人而不勝，則二十萬人皆費也；王翦之勝，則六十萬人而不為費。治河亦若是也。
去年天子閔被水之地，蠲郡縣以萬計，遣大臣往賑，又十萬計。夫今河不治，則他日宜蠲宜賑者，又不知其幾也。今以蠲與賑者倍其數，即河可成，民得其業，是愈于蠲與賑者甚遠也。宋人防河與防虜等。夫虜之可憂，未必如中原之可憂。惜財之說，非所以施于遇變不得已之時者也。然執事又以罷民不可以重勞，灾地不可以處眾，斯固慮之
translation_en:
…undertaken together at the same time; not one can be omitted. Yet, as I understand your view, you consider that undertaking four great public works in the realm simultaneously is no way to conserve resources and show due concern for the state. Alas! My very reason for advancing this proposal is fear that resources will be wasted. To undertake public works in the realm and accomplish benefits for the realm—this has been the proper way to use resources since antiquity, and cannot be called waste. Only when concern for conserving resources prevents the work from succeeding does what has been spent become waste. In former times, when the emperor of Qin was preparing to attack Chu, he consulted Wang Jian, who replied, “No fewer than six hundred thousand men will do.” He consulted Li Xin, who replied, “Two hundred thousand men.” Yet Li Xin failed to win with two hundred thousand men, so all two hundred thousand were wasted; Wang Jian won, so even six hundred thousand men were no waste. Managing the Yellow River is just the same.
Last year, the Son of Heaven took pity on the flooded regions and remitted taxes in the prefectures and counties amounting to tens of thousands. He dispatched high officials to provide relief, amounting to another hundred thousand. If the river is not brought under control now, there is no knowing how much will have to be remitted and distributed in relief hereafter. If we now double the sums spent on remissions and relief, the river works can be completed and the people can regain their livelihoods. This is far better than tax remissions and relief. The people of the Song treated defense against the river as equal in importance to defense against foreign foes. Yet the danger posed by foreign foes is not necessarily as grave as the danger within the Central Plain. Arguments for conserving resources are inappropriate in an emergency when action is unavoidable. But you further hold that an exhausted populace must not be burdened with further labor, and that a disaster-stricken region cannot accommodate large numbers of people. This indeed reflects your consideration of…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
深也而愚以為是則在夫撫之得失而不
可以議役之興沮也何者興四大役法當
用數萬人不可謂不勞以數萬人之眾而
合處千里荒蕪之間不可以不備此所謂
深慮也然令數萬人急者得錢饑者得食
如逐貨于市趨稼于田仰給而有藉則所
以收離散之民而為救荒之策者也其何
勞之得怨令千里之間畫地而居分功而
作如身之使臂臂之使指輻凑而得所歸
===
則所以寓部伍之法而兼制變之術者也
其何眾之能為是誠在夫官之得人而撫
之有道也不可以是而議夫役也雖然知
天下利病之情而張弛運量措之几席廟
堂之事也察海內遠近之形而疆理擘畫
視諸掌上經營者之責也愚且賤何以辱
明問謹對
第五問
姜寶
alt_text:
深也而愚以爲是則在夫撫之得失而不
可以議役之興沮也何者興四大役法當
用數萬人不可謂不勞以數萬人之衆而
合處千里荒蕪之閒不可以不備此所謂
深慮也然令數萬人急者得錢饑者得食
如逐貨于市趨稼于田仰給而有藉則所
以收離散之民而爲救荒之策者也其何
勞之得然令千里之閒畫地而居分功而
作如身之使臂臂之使指輻湊而得所歸
===
則所以寓部伍之法而兼制變之術者也
其何衆之能爲是誠在夫官之得人而撫
之有道也不可以是而議夫役也雖然知
天下利病之情而張弛遲量措之几席廟
堂之事也察海内遠近之形而疆理擘畫
視議掌上經營者之責也愚且賤何以辱
明問謹對
第五問
姜寶
punctuated:
深也。而愚以為，是則在夫撫之得失，而不可以議役之興沮也。何者？興四大役，法當用數萬人，不可謂不勞；以數萬人之眾，而合處千里荒蕪之間，不可以不備，此所謂深慮也。然令數萬人急者得錢，饑者得食，如逐貨于市，趨稼于田，仰給而有藉，則所以收離散之民，而為救荒之策者也。其何勞之得怨？令千里之間，畫地而居，分功而作，如身之使臂，臂之使指，輻凑而得所歸，則所以寓部伍之法，而兼制變之術者也。其何眾之能為？是誠在夫官之得人，而撫之有道也，不可以是而議夫役也。雖然，知天下利病之情，而張弛運量，措之几席，廟堂之事也；察海內遠近之形，而疆理擘畫，視諸掌上，經營者之責也。愚且賤，何以辱明問？謹對。

第五問
姜寶
translation_en:
…is far-sighted. Yet I believe that this depends on whether the people are properly cared for, and cannot serve as grounds for deciding whether to undertake or obstruct the works. Why? Undertaking the four great works will necessarily require tens of thousands of people; one cannot say that this entails no toil. Bringing tens of thousands together amid a thousand li of desolate land also requires precautions. This is what is meant by far-sighted concern. Yet if, among these tens of thousands, those in urgent need receive money and the hungry receive food, they will come as people pursue goods in the marketplace or hasten to cultivate the fields. With provisions on which to rely, this would be a means of gathering the scattered population and a policy for relieving famine. What cause would they then have to resent their toil? If, throughout those thousand li, areas are demarcated for their lodging and tasks apportioned for their work, they will function as the body directs the arms and the arms direct the fingers, converging like spokes upon a hub, each finding where he belongs. This would incorporate a system of organized units while also providing a means of controlling disturbances. What trouble could their numbers then cause? This truly depends on finding the right officials and caring for the people in the proper way. These concerns cannot be grounds for opposing the works.

Nevertheless, understanding the benefits and harms affecting the realm, determining when to tighten or relax measures, and weighing and planning affairs at the council table are matters for the central government. Examining conditions throughout the empire, near and far, demarcating and planning with everything as clear as if held in the palm of one’s hand—these are the responsibilities of those directing the undertaking. Ignorant and lowly as I am, how could I merit your discerning inquiry? Respectfully submitted in reply.

Fifth Question
Jiang Bao

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
同考試官主事畢批酌當事情而歸究於
用人雖舉而措之可也
同考試官檢討林批商確理財切中時弊
末復歸重用人誠探本之論子其明當世之
務者耶
考試官侍講學士敖批區處四事甚切時政足見
有用之學
考試官大學士徐批此作只就問目平平說去
事皆可行自勝於逞華衒博者
===
蓋聞守簿書而襲故常者有司之職也避
嫌遠怨苟焉以自保者具臣之心也毅然
以天下國家為已任開誠心布公道集衆
思廣忠益於難處之中而必求善處之術
者大臣之事也嗟乎大臣之事舉而財用
自無不理矣竊甞詢諸司農
國家之賦自漕運外其以銀輸者歲不過一
百八十七萬有竒而各邊主客兵之餽餉
歲為銀三百五十四萬有竒以一歲之入

考試官侍講學士敖批：區處四事，甚切時政，足見有用之學。
考試官大學士徐批：此作只就問目平平說去，事皆可行，自勝於逞華衒博者。
蓋聞守簿書而襲故常者，有司之職也；避嫌遠怨，苟焉以自保者，具臣之心也；毅然以天下國家為已任，開誠心，布公道，集衆思，廣忠益，於難處之中而必求善處之術者，大臣之事也。嗟乎！大臣之事舉，而財用自無不理矣。竊甞詢諸司農，國家之賦，自漕運外，其以銀輸者，歲不過一百八十七萬有竒，而各邊主客兵之餽餉，歲為銀三百五十四萬有竒。以一歲之入
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Bi, Secretary, comments: “The proposals are judiciously suited to the circumstances, and the discussion ultimately returns to the employment of capable men. They could indeed be put into practice.”
Associate Examiner Lin, Examining Editor, comments: “The careful discussion of financial administration strikes directly at present abuses. At the end, it again places the emphasis on employing capable men: this is truly an argument that probes the root. Are you perhaps one who understands the affairs of the present age?”
Examiner Ao, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “The handling of the four matters is highly pertinent to current government affairs and amply demonstrates learning of practical use.”
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: “This composition simply follows the questions and discusses them straightforwardly. Its proposals are all practicable, and it naturally surpasses writings that flaunt literary ornament and parade erudition.”
I have heard that keeping registers and documents and following established routines are the duties of the responsible officials; avoiding suspicion and keeping resentment at a distance, merely to preserve oneself, is the disposition of a minister who does no more than fill his post. Resolutely taking responsibility for the realm and the state, displaying sincerity, upholding impartial principles, gathering the thoughts of many and welcoming loyal counsel, and insisting on finding sound ways to deal with difficult circumstances—these are the tasks of a great minister. Ah! Once the tasks of great ministers are carried out, public finances will naturally be brought into order. I have privately inquired of the revenue authorities: apart from the grain transported by water, the state's tax revenues paid in silver amount annually to no more than 1,870,000 taels and some additional amount, whereas provisions and pay for the regular garrison troops and visiting troops along the various frontiers amount annually to 3,540,000 taels and some additional amount. title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
較一歲之出恒不足十四至於
上供之所須京官之折俸邊吏額外之請乞四
方水旱之賑貸不與焉邇年所以僅給者
以有輸粟之令逋負之徵百司贖金之積
銀庫往年之羡餘也顧所謂羡餘者今既
無復存而彼三者又不可以繼茲非國用
大詘之時乎論者誦書生之舊聞懷杞人
之過慮於是謂冗官當革冗兵當汰力役
當罷工作當止冀以少紓度支而有司又
===
輒有異議焉然揣時度勢論者之言固本
諸經義而有司之言亦不失為審慎之謀
然則付之無可奈何者非也知其不可而
冒為之者亦非也其必有善處之術乎所
謂善處者斟酌劑量費於此或取償於彼
費於今或取償於後是也愚請試陳之而
執事擇焉蓋今之官固未易革然其不職
者眾矣用舍獨不可公乎誠使屏斥貪殘
停抑庸懦而改以任夫賢能則祿之在額

停抑庸懦而改以任夫賢能則祿之在額
punctuated: 較一歲之出，恒不足十四。至於上供之所須、京官之折俸、邊吏額外之請乞、四方水旱之賑貸，不與焉。邇年所以僅給者，以有輸粟之令、逋負之徵、百司贖金之積、銀庫往年之羡餘也。顧所謂羡餘者，今既無復存，而彼三者又不可以繼，茲非國用大詘之時乎？論者誦書生之舊聞，懷杞人之過慮，於是謂冗官當革，冗兵當汰，力役當罷，工作當止，冀以少紓度支，而有司又輒有異議焉。然揣時度勢，論者之言固本諸經義，而有司之言亦不失為審慎之謀。然則付之無可奈何者，非也；知其不可而冒為之者，亦非也。其必有善處之術乎？所謂善處者，斟酌劑量，費於此或取償於彼，費於今或取償於後，是也。愚請試陳之，而執事擇焉。蓋今之官固未易革，然其不職者眾矣，用舍獨不可公乎？誠使屏斥貪殘，停抑庸懦，而改以任夫賢能，則祿之在額
translation_en:
…compared with a year's expenditure, regularly falls short by four tenths. This does not include the supplies required for the imperial household, commuted salaries for officials in the capital, requests from frontier officials for funds beyond their quotas, or relief grants and loans for floods and droughts throughout the realm. In recent years, expenses have barely been met through orders for grain contributions, the collection of arrears, accumulated payments for the commutation of punishments in the various offices, and surpluses from previous years in the silver treasury. Yet those so-called surpluses are now entirely exhausted, and the other three sources cannot be sustained. Is this not a time of grave constraint in state finances?

Those who discuss the matter repeat the familiar learning of scholars and harbor the excessive anxieties of the man of Qi who feared that the sky would fall. They therefore say that redundant offices should be abolished, surplus troops discharged, corvée service suspended, and construction work halted, hoping thereby to ease fiscal pressures somewhat. Yet the responsible authorities invariably raise objections. When one assesses the times and weighs the circumstances, however, the proposals of these commentators are indeed grounded in the principles of the Classics, while the authorities' arguments also qualify as prudent counsels. Thus it is wrong to abandon the matter as hopeless; it is equally wrong to proceed recklessly with measures one knows to be impracticable. Surely there must be a sound way to handle it? By sound management I mean weighing and balancing expenditures: what is spent here may be offset there, and what is spent now may be offset later. Allow me, in my ignorance, to set out some proposals for your consideration and selection.

The offices now established admittedly cannot readily be abolished, but many of their holders fail in their duties. Can appointments and dismissals not at least be impartial? If the greedy and cruel were truly expelled, the mediocre and cowardly held back, and worthy and capable men appointed in their place, then the salaries attached to the established…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
員者雖不能遽省而
朝廷每有任使不必別有遣命不必別有建
設其所省自多矣況得人於藩臬郡縣則
足以牧民而常賦不至日虧得人於帥閫
衛所則足以牧軍而屯政不至日廢乎今
之兵固未易汰然其無實者多矣簡練獨
不可嚴乎誠使黜去老羸削奪占冒而專
以養乎勇銳則食之在見伍者雖不能遽
省而
===
朝廷遇有邊警不必為之調遣不必為之召
募其所省自多矣況兵精於內郡則足以
鎮弭盜賊而無出師攻討之費兵精於諸
塞則足以攘却虜寇而無終歲備禦之費
乎是所謂費於此取償於彼者也城堡之
築以為守國所不容已是矣嘗觀諸往時
方其建議而上請莫不謂於
朝廷有金城湯池之固然爵賞之命方行而
虜騎則已肆然而南入于時財之妄費者

punctuated: 員者雖不能遽省，而朝廷每有任使，不必別有遣命，不必別有建設，其所省自多矣。況得人於藩臬郡縣，則足以牧民，而常賦不至日虧；得人於帥閫衛所，則足以牧軍，而屯政不至日廢乎？今之兵固未易汰，然其無實者多矣，簡練獨不可嚴乎？誠使黜去老羸，削奪占冒，而專以養乎勇銳，則食之在見伍者雖不能遽省，而朝廷遇有邊警，不必為之調遣，不必為之召募，其所省自多矣。況兵精於內郡，則足以鎮弭盜賊，而無出師攻討之費；兵精於諸塞，則足以攘却虜寇，而無終歲備禦之費乎？是所謂費於此、取償於彼者也。城堡之築，以為守國所不容已，是矣。嘗觀諸往時，方其建議而上請，莫不謂於朝廷有金城湯池之固。然爵賞之命方行，而虜騎則已肆然而南入。于時財之妄費者
translation_en: …although the salaries of officials within the authorized establishment cannot immediately be reduced, whenever the court has duties to assign, it need not issue separate commissions or establish additional offices. The savings would naturally be considerable. Moreover, if suitable men serve in the Provincial Administration and Surveillance Commissions and in the prefectures and counties, would they not be able to govern the people, so that regular tax revenues cease to diminish day by day? If suitable men serve in military commands, guards, and battalions, would they not be able to govern the troops, so that the administration of military agricultural colonies ceases to deteriorate day by day? It is admittedly difficult to reduce the present military establishment immediately, yet many on its rolls provide no actual service. Surely selection and training could be made rigorous? If the old and weak were indeed discharged, and the practices of appropriating soldiers for private service and fraudulently claiming places on the rolls were eliminated, with support devoted exclusively to the brave and vigorous, then, although expenditure on provisions for those currently in the ranks could not immediately be reduced, the court would not need to transfer troops or recruit additional men whenever an alarm arose on the frontier. The savings would naturally be considerable. Moreover, if the troops in the interior prefectures were effective, would they not be able to suppress bandits, avoiding the expense of dispatching armies on punitive campaigns? If the troops at the frontier strongholds were effective, would they not be able to repel barbarian raiders, avoiding the expense of defensive preparations throughout the year? This is what is meant by spending here and recouping the cost elsewhere. As for building fortified towns and forts, it is correct to say that this is indispensable to defending the realm. Yet when I consider past occasions, whenever proposals were made and submitted for approval, all claimed that they would provide the court with defenses as secure as metal walls and moats of boiling water. But scarcely had orders conferring ranks and rewards been issued when barbarian cavalry were already advancing south unchecked. By then, the funds recklessly squandered…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
既不可復還而恩之冒受者亦不聞追奪
此豈不可痛惜乎今而後中外之吏能毋
為蔽欺則一歲之勞可以得百歲之逸而
旋仆旋修之費省矣戎器之除以為威天
下所不容無是矣嘗觀諸往時方其工成
而奏報莫不謂於
朝廷有堅甲利兵之實及綜核之命一下而
奸弊則遂紛然而畢露于時吏之侵盜者
雖不免於刑而器之濫惡者已無濟於用
===
此豈不可痛惜乎今而後小大之務能不
為虛偽則一事之舉可以得一事之益而
數壞數置之費省矣是所謂費於今取償
於後者也然此特就明問所及言之耳若
其他固有非愚所能盡知亦有非愚所敢
遽論者使推此義而為之豈獨無少補乎
顧無其才者既不能為無其志者又不肯
為無其節者又惕於利害而不力於為愚
故謂毅然以天下國家為己任開誠心布

translation_en: …could no longer be recovered, while those who had fraudulently received imperial favors were never heard to have been stripped of them. Is this not deeply regrettable? If henceforth officials at court and in the provinces can refrain from concealment and deception, one year’s labor can secure a hundred years of ease, and the expense of rebuilding structures that collapse almost as soon as they are repaired will be saved. It is indeed true that the preparation of military equipment is indispensable for inspiring awe throughout the realm. Yet when I consider past practice, whenever manufacture was completed and a report submitted, all claimed before the court that stout armor and sharp weapons had actually been supplied. Once an order for thorough inspection came down, however, fraudulent abuses were exposed in profusion. Although the officials who had embezzled funds did not escape punishment, the shoddy equipment was already unfit for use. Is this not deeply regrettable? If henceforth affairs great and small can be conducted without deception, each undertaking can yield its proper benefit, and the expense of repeated breakage and replacement will be saved. This is what is meant by spending now and obtaining recompense later. These remarks, however, address only the matters raised in your illuminating question. As for other matters, there are certainly some that I, in my ignorance, cannot fully understand, and others on which I dare not hastily pronounce. If this principle were extended and put into practice, could it fail to bring at least some benefit? Yet those lacking the ability cannot act; those lacking the resolve will not act; and those lacking integrity are apprehensive about personal advantage and harm, and so fail to exert themselves. I therefore hold that one must resolutely take responsibility for the realm and the state, open one’s heart in sincerity, and spread…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
公道集衆思廣忠益於難處之中而必求
善處之術乃大臣之事而非有司及具臣
者所能與也然則為執事計請毋汲汲於
理財亦勉諸此而已大學論平天下雖以
用人理財並言而用人實居其先於戲執
事誠以大學之訓為必可師當不以愚之
言為狂也已

言爲狂也已
punctuated: 公道，集衆思，廣忠益，於難處之中而必求善處之術，乃大臣之事，而非有司及具臣者所能與也。然則為執事計，請毋汲汲於理財，亦勉諸此而已。《大學》論平天下，雖以用人理財並言，而用人實居其先。於戲！執事誠以《大學》之訓為必可師，當不以愚之言為狂也已。
translation_en: …impartiality, gather the thoughts of many, and draw widely on loyal counsel; amid difficult circumstances, insist on finding sound ways to deal with them: these are the duties of great ministers, beyond what officials charged with particular responsibilities or ministers who merely fill their posts can undertake. Thus, in offering advice to you, I ask that you not be so anxiously preoccupied with managing finances, but instead exert yourself in these matters. When the Great Learning discusses bringing peace to all under Heaven, it speaks of employing men and managing finances together, yet employing men actually comes first. Ah! If you truly regard the teachings of the Great Learning as a model that must be followed, surely you will not dismiss my humble words as wild presumption.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

On the guiyou day of the second month in the spring of the guichou year of Jiajing [1553], the business of the Metropolitan Examination was completed. The names, rankings, and compositions of the successful candidates were arranged into a record. When the record was complete, your servant Jie, Grand Secretary, had already supplied a preface for its opening leaves. Your servant Xian ventures to append a few words at the end to address the assembled scholars.

Your servant has heard that the birth of worthy and talented men is bound up with the cycles of cosmic forces. In former times, when Shun ruled All under Heaven, he selected from the multitude and obtained five ministers. By the Zhou, their number was several times greater. This was not because the talents of the Zhou could surpass those of Shun’s time. Rather, with sages occupying the throne, their Way enduring and their transforming influence fully realized, the spiritual essence of the luminous heavens and lofty mountains had by then become concentrated in a greater number of people.

Our Emperor has grandly received Heaven’s Mandate…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
君師天下自
臨御以迄于今開科取士凡十
一舉矣若今百辟卿士暨于
有位孰非
聖化所造而進之者乎臣以爲今
之所進又非昔比矣
國家樹人如種植然種木者求
===
用於十年之後栽培已至况
今歷年既多又從而長茂之
者乎宜乎人才若是其衆多
也然人有恒言天畀人以才
豈使自有餘而已是故古之
賢士奮庸戒勉必曰時亮天
工示不敢私也雖上之人操

translation_en:
…as ruler and teacher of all under Heaven. From Your Majesty’s accession to the present, examinations have been held to select scholars on eleven occasions in all. Among the many ministers, high officials, and all others holding office today, who has not been formed by Your Majesty’s sagely transforming influence and advanced through it? Your servant believes that those now advanced surpass even those of former times.
The state’s cultivation of men is like planting and tending trees. Those who plant trees seek to use them ten years later and devote the utmost care to their cultivation. How much more so now, when so many years have passed and further care has made them grow tall and flourish! It is fitting that talented men should be so numerous. Yet people have a common saying: “When Heaven endows people with talent, can it intend merely that they themselves should have an abundance?” Thus, when worthy scholars of antiquity exerted themselves in service, remaining vigilant and diligent, they would invariably say, “We assist in Heaven’s work,” showing that they dared not treat their talents as their private possession. title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
其柄以進天下之士亦曰與
之共天職爾由是觀之用人
者非私於其人為人用者非
私於其用而舉人者亦非私
於其舉皆所以奉天命也是
故唐虞三代相與弼成駿明
之業豈非達於此乎夫古之
===

闡明之以經萬世將使天下
後世之人自得之以盡其才
而適於用也後世明經之士
不此之務顧規規於佔畢詞
章之習文則似矣而生於其
心者微也及見諸事功視古

translation_en:
…that authority to advance the scholars of the realm, they too say only that they share with them the duties entrusted by Heaven. Viewed in this light, those who employ men do not act out of personal partiality toward them; those employed do not regard their service as a matter of private advantage; and those who recommend men likewise do not make their recommendations out of private interest. All these actions serve to fulfill Heaven’s mandate. Thus, under Tang and Yu and throughout the Three Dynasties, men assisted one another in bringing great and illustrious achievements to completion. Was this not because they understood this principle?

Such was the reason the ancients valued their talents. The sages elucidated this principle to guide all ages, intending that people throughout the realm in later generations should grasp it for themselves, fully develop their talents, and become fit for service. Scholars of later ages versed in the Classics do not devote themselves to this. Instead, they confine themselves narrowly to rote recitation and literary composition. Their writings may resemble those of the ancients, yet little arises from their own hearts. When this finds expression in practical achievements, compared with the ancients…

translation_en: …they fall far short of the men of antiquity. Is this because the institutions differ? Is this not a delusion? The former kings’ system for selecting men sought only to obtain talented men and employ them. What scholars should expect of themselves, however, does not depend on this; moreover, the talents with which people are born do not differ between antiquity and the present. You assembled scholars now have the good fortune to live under a sage sovereign who cultivates men through reverent single-mindedness, an endeavor that has flourished through long accumulation. Can there be none among you who rise above their peers like the renowned worthies of old? If there are none among you, on whom can the realm and the state rely? Nevertheless, would your servant dare assert that there truly are no such men? If even one or two should emerge from among you, they would not merely attest to this illustrious dynasty’s era of flourishing prosperity and its civilizing influence: the boundless blessings of the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain would also forever find support in them. translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the thirty-second year of Jiajing, it was again time to hold the Metropolitan Examination for the scholars of the realm. Your servants De, Minister of Rites, and Rulin, Right Vice Minister, reported this to the throne. At that time, your servant Sheng, Left Vice Minister, had been dispatched to perform sacrifices at Chengtian and had not yet returned, while your servant Rulin had responsibility for the wedding ceremonies of two princes. Accordingly, on the yisi day of the first month, an imperial decree appointed your servant Wende, Left Vice Minister of Personnel, to oversee the examination. On the guichou day of the second month, an imperial decree ordered me, together with your servant Xian, Academician, to take charge of evaluating the examination essays.

I reverently reflect that His Majesty selects the worthy and gathers men of talent to plan the good governance of the realm with them. Once every three years he holds an examination, encouraging learning and promoting disciplined cultivation, and accords this particular importance above other affairs of government. For this examination, I came from attendance at His Majesty’s side, and your servant Wende from the Ministry of Personnel, to receive…

punctuated: 以前，其詞簡而質；弘治以前，其詞雅而暢；至正德間，其詞蔚以昌矣。然厭棄師說而流於詭僻、騖於怪竒者，亦間有之。乃今閱多士所為文，率能發抒所自得，而實未嘗違背經傳，及逸而出於繩墨。盖我皇上繼天立極，道隆君師。《敬一》之箴、《五箴》之註，士相與講誦服習，已非一時，乆道化成，理固然也。臣自甲子迄於辛未，屢為之
translation_en: …before [the Xuande reign], their language was concise and plain; before the Hongzhi reign, it was elegant and fluent; by the Zhengde reign, it had become rich and flourishing. Yet occasionally there were also those who rejected their teachers’ explanations and drifted into eccentricity, pursuing the bizarre and unusual. Now, however, when I read the essays these candidates have written, I find that they generally express insights they have attained for themselves, without contravening the classics and their commentaries or straying beyond established standards. For our Emperor has succeeded Heaven and established the supreme standard, exalting the Way in his roles as ruler and teacher. The scholars have long discussed, recited, practiced, and studied his Admonition on Single-minded Reverence (Jingyi) and his Commentary on the Five Admonitions (Wuzhen). That sustained adherence to the Way should bring about transformation is naturally to be expected. From the jiazi year through the xinwei year, your servant repeatedly, on this account…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
撫卷嘉歎以為人才之盛如
此凡亮工熙載之用皆將於
是乎取之而不窮竊深自慶
焉既而思曰多士之爛然在
臣目者文也其亮工熙載卓
然著於用世者行與業也自
進士之科立士豈無聲實相
===
副如唐宋璟張九齡裴度陸
贄宋李沆王旦韓琦范仲淹
司馬光歐陽修諸人者乎抑
豈無靜言庸違文有可觀而
人無足稱者乎使多士能為
文能以行業著於用世臣則
可自慶矣不然是臣欲藉以

translation_en:
…I perused the papers with admiration and delight, reflecting that, with talent flourishing so abundantly, all those needed to assist in public affairs and advance the work of government could be drawn from this source without exhaustion. Privately, I felt deep satisfaction.

Then I reflected: “What shines so brilliantly before your servant’s eyes in these many scholars is their writing. What will distinguish them in service to the world, assisting in public affairs and advancing the work of government, is their conduct and accomplishments. Since the establishment of the examination for metropolitan graduates (jinshi), have there not been scholars whose reputations matched their actual worth—men such as Song Jing, Zhang Jiuling, Pei Du, and Lu Zhi of the Tang, and Li Hang, Wang Dan, Han Qi, Fan Zhongyan, Sima Guang, and Ouyang Xiu of the Song? Yet have there not also been those whose words are fair but whose deeds run contrary, whose writing offers something to admire but whose persons offer nothing worthy of praise? If these many scholars can write well and can also distinguish themselves through their conduct and accomplishments in service to the world, then your servant may indeed feel satisfaction. Otherwise, though your servant wishes to rely upon them to…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
報
主不可得也於是又竊有深懼焉
謹因錄成恭述
德意而併及臣將
命之心以示多士書有之萬邦黎
獻共惟帝臣夫
聖人在上固黎獻所願出而有爲
===
之時也矧夫豫教素養於學
校而又設科以求之若是其
重者耶多士有感於曠世之
遭
作人之澤則夫交相戒勗以期
光贊
聖治而因以釋主司之懼者殆弗

之時也矧夫豫教素養於學
校而又設科以求之若是其
重者耶多士有感於曠世之
遭
作人之澤則夫奕相戒勗以期
光贊
聖治而因以釋主司之懼者殆弗
punctuated:
報主不可得也，於是又竊有深懼焉。
謹因錄成，恭述德意，而併及臣將命之心，以示多士。《書》有之：「萬邦黎獻，共惟帝臣。」夫聖人在上，固黎獻所願出而有爲之時也，矧夫豫教素養於學校，而又設科以求之，若是其重者耶？多士有感於曠世之遭、作人之澤，則夫交相戒勗，以期光贊聖治，而因以釋主司之懼者，殆弗
translation_en:
…to repay my sovereign would be beyond my reach. At this thought, I privately feel profound apprehension once more.
Now that this record is complete, I respectfully recount His Majesty’s gracious intentions, together with the thoughts with which I, his servant, have carried out his command, to make them known to the assembled scholars. The Book of Documents says: “The many worthy men of the myriad states are all servants of the emperor.” With a sage upon the throne, this is indeed the time when worthy men wish to come forward and accomplish something. How much more so when they have been educated beforehand and steadily nurtured in the schools, and examinations have also been established to seek them out—such is the importance attached to them! If the assembled scholars are moved by this opportunity rarely encountered in an age, and by the grace shown in nurturing talent, then surely they cannot fail to admonish and encourage one another, hoping to contribute lustre to His Majesty’s sagely governance and thereby relieve the apprehensions of the official presiding over the examination…

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Thirty-second Year of Jiajing (1553)

Examination Administrators

Ouyang De, holding the prestige rank Zishan dafu, was Minister of Rites and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Chongyi; he was from Taihe County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the guiwei year (1523).

Cheng Wende, holding the prestige rank Jiayi dafu, was Left Vice Minister of Personnel. His courtesy name was Shunfu; he was from Yongkang County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jichou year (1529).

Examiners

Xu Jie, holding the prestige rank Guanglu dafu and the merit title Pillar of State, was Junior Guardian, concurrently Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Rites, and Grand Secretary of the Eastern Hall. His courtesy name was Zisheng; he was from Huating County in the directly administered metropolitan region, and became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year (1523).

Ao Xian was Expositor-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Fengxun dafu. His courtesy name was Chunzhi; he was from Gao'an County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).

Associate Examiners

Quan Yuanli was Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Rulin lang. His courtesy name was Rude; he was from Yin County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).

Dong Fen was Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Wenlin lang. His courtesy name was Yongjun; he was from Wucheng County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).

Qu Jingchun was Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Wenlin lang. His courtesy name was Shidao; he was from Changshu County in the directly administered metropolitan region, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiachen year (1544).

Zhang Chun was Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Chengshi lang. His courtesy name was Renbo; he was from Xinyu County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Kang Siqian was Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Wenlin lang. His courtesy name was Ziyi; he was from Linfen County, Shanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Wang Tangsun was Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Wenlin lang. His courtesy name was Zhenzong; he was from Yin County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Zhang Juzheng was Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Chengshi lang. His courtesy name was Shuda; he was from Jingzhou Guard, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Hu Jie was Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Wenlin lang. His courtesy name was Ziwen; he was from Fengcheng County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Sun Shifang was Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Congshi lang. His courtesy name was Kecheng; he was from the jurisdiction of the Wanquan Regional Military Commission and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

Lin Lian was Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy and held the prestige rank Zhengshi lang. His courtesy name was Zhenheng; he was from Min County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year (1547).

文林郎雲南道監察御史徐南金〔體乾，江西豐城縣人，辛丑進士〕。

提調官：

收掌試卷官：
辦中書舍人事大理寺左寺左寺副張子和〔節之，直隸滄州人，官生〕。

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
大哉堯之爲君也巍巍乎唯天爲大唯堯
則之蕩蕩乎民無能名焉
誠者非自成己而已也所以成物也成己
仁也成物知也性之德也合外內之道

How great was Yao as a ruler! How lofty! Heaven alone is great, and Yao alone took it as his model. So vast was his achievement that the people could find no words to name it.

The emperor thereupon composed a song, saying: “Be attentive to Heaven’s mandate; attend to the proper time and to the first stirrings of events.” He then sang: “When the arms and legs rejoice, the head rises to action, and the hundred officials flourish.” Gao Yao bowed with his hands joined and his forehead to the ground, and proclaimed: “Be mindful! In leading undertakings and initiating affairs, be careful of your rules. Be reverent! Reverently take this as your great model: be able to employ worthy men in the three offices and in the three ranks of service. Those in the city of Shang should bring harmony to that city; those throughout the four quarters should serve as great models, displaying their virtue.

Book of Odes
Lush grows the plantain; let us gather it. Lush grows the plantain; let us take it home. Lush grows the plantain; let us pick it up. Lush grows the plantain; let us strip off its seeds. Lush grows the plantain; let us hold it in our lifted skirts. Lush grows the plantain; let us tuck up our skirts to carry it.
Because he possesses these qualities, he can thus carry on the legacy of his forebears.

問：孔子作《春秋》，大一統以尊周，其於僭竊僞邦，貶黜嚴甚。孟軻氏序羣聖之統，歷數千年而僅得數聖人焉。帝王正統、道統之傳，若是乎其重以與人也？朱子作《綱目》，進蜀漢而黜曹魏；韓子著《原道論》，謂軻以後不得其傳。其於孔孟之意似合矣，而宋蘇軾、黃幹所論乃有不同者，何歟？漢唐而下，能一天下之君，與其所謂闡明道學之士，果足以紹是統否歟？
洪惟我太祖高皇帝驅逐胡元，再造華夏，功業之盛，前所未有。至其論帝王授受之要、觀心之義，皆於《典》《謨》所載得其精微。我皇上以天縱之聖，應運中興，明倫有典，敬一有箴，制禮作樂，燦然明備。又於勝國則罷其廟祀，於先聖先師則崇祀于文華東室，
translation_en:
Question: Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals, exalting unity under a single legitimate rule in order to honor the Zhou. His condemnation and rejection of usurpers and illegitimate states were exceedingly severe. When Meng Ke (Mencius) set out the succession of sages, he identified only a few sages over several thousand years. Was the transmission of the legitimate imperial succession and the succession of the Way something so weighty that it could be entrusted to others only with such care? Master Zhu composed the Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror, elevating Shu Han and rejecting Cao Wei; Master Han wrote the Discourse on the Origin of the Way, declaring that after Meng Ke no one received its transmission. These positions seem consistent with the intentions of Confucius and Mencius. Yet the Song scholars Su Shi and Huang Gan expressed differing views. Why was this? From the Han and Tang onward, were rulers capable of unifying all under Heaven, and those scholars said to have elucidated the Learning of the Way, truly worthy to continue these successions?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao expelled the Mongol Yuan and restored the Chinese realm. The greatness of his achievements was unprecedented. In his discussions of the essentials of transmitting and receiving imperial rule and the meaning of examining the mind, he grasped the subtle essence of what is recorded in the Canons and Counsels of the Book of Documents. Our reigning Emperor, with his Heaven-endowed sagacity, has responded to the destined age and brought about a restoration. For elucidating human relationships there is his Canon; for reverent single-mindedness there is his Admonition. He has instituted rites and established music, splendidly articulated and complete. Furthermore, he has discontinued temple sacrifices to the preceding dynasty, while honoring the former sages and teachers with sacrifices in the eastern chamber of Wenhua Hall…

皇上而益光矣爾多士生於茲時涵泳
德化豈不可謂大幸歟願相與鋪張揚厲焉
毋畧
問平心宣化象德昭功樂之用大矣自周
衰樂廢代變新聲而英莖之制日以遠
焉然典籍所載間有存者其微言遺旨
===
可得而聞歟說者謂古樂之復必先考
定鍾律而黃鍾又律呂之原也其詳可
得而言歟漢志三統三正之說似以林
鍾太簇之律與黃鍾並矣其果然歟先
儒損益相生之論變律半聲之制果皆
合於造化自然之數而於樂有所發明
歟古人作樂止於五聲十二律後世乃
益之以六十律衍之以三百六十律八
十四調何古人之樂明白簡徑而後世
punctuated:
宸謨聖見，迥出千古。盖帝王正統、道統之傳，至聖祖而始續，至我皇上而益光矣。爾多士生於茲時，涵泳德化，豈不可謂大幸歟？願相與鋪張揚厲焉，毋畧。
問：平心宣化，象德昭功，樂之用大矣。自周衰樂廢，代變新聲，而英莖之制日以逺焉。然典籍所載，間有存者，其微言遺旨，可得而聞歟？說者謂古樂之復，必先考定鍾律，而黃鍾又律吕之原也，其詳可得而言歟？漢志三統三正之說，似以林鍾、太簇之律與黃鍾並矣，其果然歟？先儒損益相生之論、變律半聲之制，果皆合於造化自然之數，而於樂有所發明歟？古人作樂，止於五聲十二律，後世乃益之以六十律，衍之以三百六十律、八十四調。何古人之樂明白簡徑，而後世
translation_en:
…His imperial counsels and sagely insights surpass those of all preceding ages. Indeed, the transmission of the legitimate imperial succession and the succession of the Way was first renewed under the sagely founder and has become still more glorious under our Emperor. You assembled scholars were born in this age and are steeped in its transforming moral influence: can this not be called a great blessing? I hope you will together expound and celebrate these achievements fully, omitting nothing.
Question: Music calms the heart and spreads moral transformation; it represents virtue and makes achievements manifest. Great indeed is its usefulness. Since the decline of the Zhou, music has fallen into disuse, and successive ages have introduced new sounds, while the musical systems of Ying and Jing have grown ever more remote. Yet some traces survive among the records in the classics and other writings. Can their subtle teachings and surviving purport be explained? Commentators say that restoring ancient music requires first investigating and establishing the pitches of bells and pitch pipes, and that Huangzhong is the source of the yin and yang pitch standards. Can this be discussed in detail? The account of the Three Systems and Three First Months in the treatise in the History of the Han seems to place the pitches Linzhong and Taicu alongside Huangzhong. Is this really so? Do earlier Confucian scholars’ theories of generating pitches from one another by reduction and augmentation, and their systems of altered pitch standards and half-length pitches, truly accord with the natural numerical relations of creation, and do they shed light on music? The ancients, in making music, used only five notes and twelve pitch standards. Later generations increased these to sixty pitch standards and further expanded them to three hundred and sixty pitch standards and eighty-four modes. Why was the music of the ancients clear and straightforward, whereas that of later generations…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
繁瑣若是歟至於術家制尺較黍之類
其言不一而足不知亦可用之今日否
歟茲欲審聲以和律定律以正音用復
古樂之盛爾諸士必有定見也盍相與
講明之
問穆叔有言太上立德其次立功其次立
言士微此三者無以垂不朽然嘗稽之
古昔禹皐陶伊傅周召之徒以德稱而
未嘗無功亦未嘗無言孔孟有德無位
===
始以言爲訓而昔人謂孔子賢于堯舜
孟子功不在禹下是又未可以立言槩
之也然則立德立功立言之分何所始
乎豈春秋之時已有不能兼者而穆叔
言之乎嗣後立言之士代不乏人類湮
沒而名不稱宋蘇軾謂孟子之後五百
餘年而得韓愈愈之後三百餘年而得
歐陽子盖將推韓歐以附孔孟也然而
君子不與焉則士之勤一世以用心于

punctuated:
繁瑣若是歟？至於術家制尺較黍之類，其言不一而足，不知亦可用之今日否歟？茲欲審聲以和律，定律以正音，用復古樂之盛，爾諸士必有定見也，盍相與講明之？
問：穆叔有言：「太上立德，其次立功，其次立言。」士微此三者，無以垂不朽。然嘗稽之古昔，禹、皐陶、伊、傅、周、召之徒，以德稱，而未嘗無功，亦未嘗無言。孔孟有德無位，始以言爲訓，而昔人謂孔子賢于堯舜，孟子功不在禹下，是又未可以立言槩之也。然則立德、立功、立言之分，何所始乎？豈春秋之時已有不能兼者，而穆叔言之乎？嗣後立言之士，代不乏人，類湮沒而名不稱。宋蘇軾謂孟子之後五百餘年而得韓愈，愈之後三百餘年而得歐陽子，盖將推韓歐以附孔孟也。然而君子不與焉，則士之勤一世以用心于
translation_en:
…so complicated and cumbersome? As for the technical specialists’ methods of making measuring rules and comparing millet grains, their accounts are too numerous to enumerate. Could these also be put to use today? We now wish to examine sounds so as to harmonize the pitch standards, and establish those standards so as to correct musical tones, thereby restoring the flourishing music of antiquity. You gentlemen must have settled views on this. Why not discuss and elucidate the matter together?
Question: Mu Shu said: “Highest is establishing virtue; next is establishing meritorious achievements; next is establishing enduring words.” Without these three, a scholar has no means of securing an imperishable legacy. Yet, examining antiquity, we find that such men as Yu, Gao Yao, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao were renowned for virtue, but were never without achievements, nor without words. Confucius and Mencius possessed virtue but held no position, and only then made their words a vehicle for instruction. Yet men of former times said that Confucius surpassed Yao and Shun in worthiness, and that Mencius’s achievements were no less than Yu’s. Thus they, too, cannot be characterized simply as having established enduring words. Where, then, did the distinction between establishing virtue, establishing achievements, and establishing words originate? Could it be that already in the Spring and Autumn period there were men unable to combine all three, prompting Mu Shu’s statement? Thereafter, no generation lacked scholars who sought to establish enduring words, yet for the most part they sank into oblivion and their names went uncelebrated. Su Shi of the Song said that more than five hundred years after Mencius there appeared Han Yu, and more than three hundred years after Han Yu there appeared Master Ouyang. Presumably he intended to exalt Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu by placing them alongside Confucius and Mencius. Yet gentlemen do not assent to this. Thus, as for scholars who labor all their lives, devoting their minds to …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
文字者果可以垂不朽否也修之言曰
聖賢之異于眾人不朽而存者修之于
身施之于事見之于言所以能不朽而
存也施于事矣不見于言可也修于身
矣不施于事不見于言亦可也夫修固
喜為文辭者而其言如此然則言固不
足恃乎諸士挟策而來盖將以言進者
試為我折衷之母曰是亦空言也
問黃河為患所從來久矣其决不常故其
===
策亦靡定即如漢世文武哀成之間相
去未百年而或塞或不塞何其異歟其
時言不塞者或稱之或謂其未便何歟
今徐房之决或言新安可開而諸决口
必可塞或言河乃天變非人力所為不
若舍故道而別圖之其說孰當歟萬世
言治河者莫如神禹其事有可施於今
者否歟
明興河之諸道皆已非古二百年間往往數

punctuated:
文字者，果可以垂不朽否也？修之言曰：「聖賢之異于眾人，不朽而存者，修之于身，施之于事，見之于言，所以能不朽而存也。施于事矣，不見于言，可也；修于身矣，不施于事，不見于言，亦可也。」夫修固喜為文辭者，而其言如此，然則言固不足恃乎？諸士挟策而來，盖將以言進者，試為我折衷之，母曰是亦空言也。
問：黃河為患，所從來久矣。其决不常，故其策亦靡定。即如漢世文武哀成之間，相去未百年，而或塞或不塞，何其異歟？其時言不塞者，或稱之，或謂其未便，何歟？今徐房之决，或言新安可開，而諸决口必可塞；或言河乃天變，非人力所為，不若舍故道而別圖之。其說孰當歟？萬世言治河者，莫如神禹，其事有可施於今者否歟？
明興，河之諸道皆已非古，二百年間，往往數
translation_en:
…those who devote themselves to literary writing: can they truly secure an enduring name? Ouyang Xiu said: “What distinguishes sages and worthies from ordinary people, allowing them to endure without perishing, is that they cultivate it in themselves, put it into practice in affairs, and manifest it in words. This is how they endure without perishing. If they have put it into practice in affairs, it is acceptable not to manifest it in words. If they have cultivated it in themselves, it is also acceptable neither to put it into practice in affairs nor to manifest it in words.” Xiu was certainly fond of literary composition, yet this is what he said. Does this mean that words alone cannot be relied upon? You gentlemen have come bearing your writings, presumably seeking advancement through words. Try to weigh these views and reach a sound judgment for me; do not [?] say that this too is merely empty talk.
Question: The Yellow River has caused calamities for a very long time. Its breaches are unpredictable, and therefore the policies for dealing with them have likewise lacked consistency. Take, for example, the reigns of Wen, Wu, Ai, and Cheng of the Han: though separated by fewer than a hundred years [?], breaches were sometimes closed and sometimes left open. Why such differences? As for those who advocated leaving breaches open at that time, some praised them, while others considered their proposals impracticable. Why? Concerning the present breaches at Xu and Fang [?], some say that a channel can be opened at Xin’an and that all the breaches can certainly be closed. Others say that the river’s behavior is a portentous change wrought by Heaven, beyond human power to control, and that it would be better to abandon the old course and devise another plan. Which view is correct? Among all who have addressed river control through the ages, none has equaled the divine Yu. Are any of his measures applicable today?
When the Ming arose, the river’s various courses were already different from those of antiquity. Over the ensuing two hundred years, time and again, repeatedly…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
决能知諸道所從又知决之之故則可
與言治河矣今聞徐房之上流有所謂
孫繼口趙皮寨諸河議者以為必先治
此而或又言當急治安東其說孰是歟
夫一時而舉諸役恐非所以惜財而體
國者且罷民不可以重勞灾地不可以
處衆宜如何而可今所以進諸士將實
求可行之道幸毋以陳言對
問大學論平天下以理財與用人並言則
===
理財之道固為治者所不可不講也况
在司農告匱之時耶然嘗觀於今日國
無不耕之民野無失時之農則所謂生
之為之者既已衆且疾矣獨食之者或
未寡用之者或未舒故論者謂冗官當
革冗兵當汰力役當罷工作當止而有
司又謂
國家之制率以一官任一事去其人則事遂
廢是官本未嘗冗而難革也
