國家之制率以一官任一事去其人則事遂
廢是官本未嘗冗而難革也
punctuated:
决，能知諸道所從，又知决之之故，則可與言治河矣。今聞徐房之上流，有所謂孫繼口、趙皮寨諸河，議者以為必先治此，而或又言當急治安東，其說孰是歟？夫一時而舉諸役，恐非所以惜財而體國者。且罷民不可以重勞，灾地不可以處衆，宜如何而可？今所以進諸士，將實求可行之道，幸毋以陳言對。

問：大學論平天下，以理財與用人並言，則理財之道固為治者所不可不講也，况在司農告匱之時耶？然嘗觀於今日，國無不耕之民，野無失時之農，則所謂生之為之者，既已衆且疾矣。獨食之者或未寡，用之者或未舒。故論者謂冗官當革，冗兵當汰，力役當罷，工作當止。而有司又謂：國家之制，率以一官任一事，去其人則事遂廢，是官本未嘗冗而難革也。
translation_en:
…breaches. Only someone who understands the courses followed by the various channels, and also the reasons for their breaching, can be consulted about managing the Yellow River. We now hear that upstream of Xu and Fang are the waterways known as Sunjikou and Zhaopizhai. Those discussing the matter believe that these must be dealt with first, while others say that urgent attention should be given to Andong. Which view is correct? Undertaking all these works at once would, I fear, hardly conserve resources or show proper concern for the state. Moreover, exhausted people must not be subjected to further toil, and disaster-stricken areas cannot accommodate large workforces. What, then, would be an appropriate course? Our purpose in bringing you candidates forward now is earnestly to seek practicable measures. Please do not answer with stale formulas.

Question: In discussing bringing peace to all under Heaven, the Great Learning treats managing wealth alongside employing men. The principles of managing wealth are therefore certainly something those who govern must study—how much more so when the Minister of Revenue reports that the treasury is depleted! Yet, observing conditions today, one finds no people in the realm who do not cultivate the land, and no farmers in the countryside who miss the proper seasons. Thus, those who, in the text’s words, produce wealth and work to create it are already numerous and swift. It may only be that those who consume it are not yet few, and those who spend it are not yet restrained. Commentators therefore argue that superfluous officials should be dismissed, superfluous troops discharged, labor service suspended, and manufacturing and construction halted. The responsible officials, however, say: Under the state’s institutions, each official is generally entrusted with a particular duty. Remove the person, and the duty is consequently left unfulfilled. These officials were therefore never superfluous in the first place, and their posts are difficult to abolish.

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
國家承平日久尺伍消耗過半去之則勢益
以弱是兵本未嘗冗而難汰也王公設
險以守其國今城堡之築皆守國所不
容巳者是力役欲罷而不能也先王以
弧矢威天下如戎器之除皆威天下所
不容無者是工作欲止而不能也然則
將遂付之無可柰何而巳乎諸士子明
於先王之道當世之務必有以處此矣
願聞其說

punctuated: 國家承平日久，尺伍消耗過半，去之則勢益以弱，是兵本未嘗冗而難汰也。王公設險以守其國，今城堡之築，皆守國所不容巳者，是力役欲罷而不能也。先王以弧矢威天下，如戎器之除，皆威天下所不容無者，是工作欲止而不能也。然則將遂付之無可柰何而巳乎？諸士子明於先王之道、當世之務，必有以處此矣。願聞其說。
translation_en: The state has long enjoyed peace, and the ranks of its soldiers [?] have dwindled by more than half. To dismiss them would further weaken its strength. Thus the troops were never actually redundant, and reducing them is difficult. Kings and dukes establish defenses at strategic points to protect their states. The construction of fortresses today is likewise indispensable to defending the state; thus, even if one wishes to discontinue corvée labor, one cannot. The former kings used bows and arrows to overawe all under Heaven. Such undertakings as the provision [?] of military equipment are indispensable to overawing all under Heaven; thus, even if one wishes to halt manufacturing, one cannot. Are we, then, simply to leave matters as they are, resigned to being unable to do anything? You candidates understand the Way of the former kings and the affairs of the present age, and surely have some means of addressing this. I wish to hear your explanations.

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Great indeed was Yao as a ruler! How lofty! Heaven alone is great, and Yao alone took it as his model. How boundless! The people could find no words to describe him.”

Feng Ye

Comment by Associate Examiner Xie, Left Supervising Secretary: This elucidates how Yao took Heaven as his model. The wording is economical, yet the meaning is fully expressed.

Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Chief Supervising Secretary: The Sage’s praise of Yao’s greatness is fully expressed in the first two sentences. The words about the people finding no words to describe him merely complete the preceding thought. This essay’s exposition captures the essential meaning. Select it for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhu, Examining Editor: The inability to describe him is precisely where his taking Heaven as his model is manifest. This essay grasps that point.

Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, Examining Editor: It fully elucidates the meaning of Yao’s matching Heaven in just a few phrases. It merits selection.

Comment by Associate Examiner Qu, Compiler: Yao’s taking Heaven as his model and his being beyond description become misrepresented the moment one puts them into words. This essay understands that, and is therefore selected for inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Ao, Expositor-in-waiting: It explains very clearly the inability to describe him.

Comment by Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary: It sensitively grasps Zhu Xi’s commentary and develops it into an essay.

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
聖人賛前聖君德之大與天為一焉盖大而不
可名者天也堯之德能與之一此其所以為大
歟想吾夫子賛堯之意盖曰君天下者繼天以
為治則必憲天以為德使其德與天有間未足
以言大也吾甞稽古帝王大矣哉堯之為君乎
巍巍乎天之高大物莫過焉而唯堯也俊德之
克明有以格于上下盖其首出庶物者於天之
高獨能凖焉而不可踰也帝德之廣運有以被
於四表盖其覆冒天下者於天之大獨能凖焉
===
而不可量也故其德之蕩蕩不特後之人莫能
名也當堯之時為堯之民覿德於聖作之際亦
惟有胥戴焉已爾如欲從而名之則其廣也猶
之天然非有局於方體也而何以能為之形容
耶仰德於君臨之下亦惟有相忘焉已爾如欲
即而名之則其遠也猶之天然非有滯於形器
也而又何以能為之擬議耶故曰大哉堯之為
君也知天則知堯矣善觀堯者觀之於天斯可
矣雖然天之生人其所賦予非有異於堯而與

translation_en:
The sage praises the greatness of an earlier sage ruler’s virtue, which was one with Heaven. For that which is great beyond description is Heaven; Yao’s virtue could be one with it. Was this not what made him great? I imagine that our Master’s intention in praising Yao was to say: “One who rules all under Heaven carries on Heaven’s work in governing and must therefore take Heaven as the model for his virtue. If his virtue falls short of Heaven, it cannot yet be called great. I have examined the emperors and kings of antiquity: how great was Yao as a ruler! Lofty indeed is Heaven: nothing surpasses its height and greatness. Yao alone could make his eminent virtue shine forth, reaching above and below. In standing foremost among all beings, he alone could match Heaven’s height and could not be surpassed. His imperial virtue, vast and far-reaching, extended to the four outer bounds. In sheltering all under Heaven, he alone could match Heaven’s greatness and could not be measured.

“Thus, in the boundlessness of his virtue, it was not merely later generations who could find no words to describe him. Those who lived in Yao’s time as his people, witnessing his virtue as the sage acted, could only join together in reverently upholding him. If they wished then to describe it, its breadth was like Heaven itself, confined to no defined shape. How could they give it expression? Looking up to his virtue under his sovereign rule, they could only live in mutual unawareness of it. If they wished to approach and describe it, its far-reaching extent was like Heaven itself, restricted to no material form. How, then, could they frame a comparison or discussion of it? Hence the saying: ‘Great indeed was Yao as a ruler!’ To know Heaven is to know Yao. Those who would rightly contemplate Yao need only contemplate Heaven.”

translation_en:
…unite his virtue with Heaven: why was Yao alone able to do this? In the nature conferred by Heaven, Yao was the same as other people. Yet in faithfully holding fast to the Mean, and thus fully realizing his nature, Yao differed from them. Thus, fully realizing his nature was how Yao united with Heaven; failing to realize their nature fully is why ordinary people do not resemble Heaven. This is broadly the meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean’s discussion of utmost sincerity and participation in assisting Heaven and Earth. Students should consider these teachings together.

“Sincerity does not merely perfect oneself; it is also the means of perfecting other things. Perfecting oneself is benevolence; perfecting other things is wisdom. These are the virtues of one’s nature, the Way that unites the external and the internal. Thus, their application is appropriate to the occasion.”

Zhuang Shiyuan.

Associate Examiner Yang, Acting Bureau Director, comments: “Its elucidation of application according to the occasion is markedly different from other compositions. Include it in the record.”

Associate Examiner Hu, Compiler, comments: “Pure and orthodox, grounded in the classics and substantial: it sweeps away the defects of current literary habits.”

Associate Examiner Kang, Compiler, comments: “Its understanding is intimate and direct, and its language precise and apt. Only someone deeply versed in principle could achieve this.”

Associate Examiner Zhang, Compiler, comments: “By explaining how what is inherent in human nature comes into operation, it shows an understanding of that nature.”

Examiner Ao, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “Free of excessive elaboration [?]; worthy of selection.”

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
考試官大學士徐批典雅不類時作
中庸論誠之及物一性之所有而為用焉盖性
者萬物之一原也君子能誠於己則夫所以成
物者寧外是乎宜中庸言之以明人道也盖謂
君子所性根於心而其道貴於誠夫苟誠矣則
不惟誠之立於我者有以自成而道之行於彼
者自然及物以成己言之妄復無妄渾然全體
之不息非仁而何以成物言之物各付物燦然
妙用之顯行非知而何曰仁與知本諸吾性之
===
固有而為吾心之實德仁非在内也知非在外
也不貳之貞裕吾内者所以致用于外也不測
之化利吾外者所以致養乎内也由是天德妙
道合同而化無適而無莫者與時偕行以盡利
也誠精神應流而不息不習無不利者隨時變
易以盡能也凡所以範圍曲成之道而致彌綸
輔賛之功亦舉此而措之爾大哉誠乎其冒天
下之道者乎君子思誠之功至矣盡矣抑考之
經曰物有本末於此又曰不誠無物然則誠也

中庸論誠之及物，一性之所有而為用焉。盖性者，萬物之一原也。君子能誠於己，則夫所以成物者，寧外是乎？宜中庸言之以明人道也。盖謂君子所性根於心，而其道貴於誠。夫苟誠矣，則不惟誠之立於我者有以自成，而道之行於彼者，自然及物。以成己言之，妄復無妄，渾然全體之不息，非仁而何？以成物言之，物各付物，燦然妙用之顯行，非知而何？曰仁與知，本諸吾性之固有，而為吾心之實德。仁非在内也，知非在外也。不貳之貞，裕吾内者，所以致用于外也；不測之化，利吾外者，所以致養乎内也。由是天德妙道，合同而化，無適而無莫者，與時偕行以盡利也；誠精神應，流而不息，不習無不利者，隨時變易以盡能也。凡所以範圍曲成之道，而致彌綸輔賛之功，亦舉此而措之爾。大哉誠乎！其冒天下之道者乎！君子思誠之功，至矣，盡矣！抑考之經，曰：「物有本末。」於此又曰：「不誠無物。」然則誠也

Examiner Grand Secretary Xu comments: “Refined and classical, unlike the compositions of the day.”

When the Doctrine of the Mean discusses sincerity extending to things, it takes all that is inherent in human nature and brings it into operation. For nature is the single source of the myriad things. If the gentleman can be sincere in himself, could that by which he brings things to fulfillment lie outside this? It is fitting that the Doctrine of the Mean speaks of this to illuminate the human Way. Its meaning is that what belongs to the gentleman’s nature is rooted in his heart, and that sincerity is paramount in his Way. If he is indeed sincere, then sincerity established within him not only enables him to fulfill himself: the Way operating in other things naturally extends to them as well. In terms of fulfilling oneself, falsity returns to freedom from falsity, and the undivided whole operates without ceasing. What is this if not benevolence? In terms of fulfilling things, each thing is accorded what belongs to it, and wondrous activity manifests itself brilliantly. What is this if not wisdom? Benevolence and wisdom are rooted in what is inherent in our nature and constitute the substantial virtues of our hearts. Benevolence is not confined to the inner realm, nor wisdom to the outer. Unwavering constancy enriches us inwardly and thereby enables us to act outwardly; unfathomable transformation benefits us outwardly and thereby nourishes us inwardly. Thus heavenly virtue and the wondrous Way unite and transform: having neither fixed preferences nor fixed rejections, they move with the times to realize benefit fully. Sincerity is refined and spirit responds [?], flowing without cease: needing no practice yet leaving nothing unbenefited, they change with the times to exercise their capacities fully. All the means by which the Way encompasses things and brings them to fulfillment in every particular, accomplishing the work of comprehensively ordering and assisting transformation, consist simply in taking this and putting it into practice. Great indeed is sincerity! Does it not encompass all the ways of the world? The gentleman’s work of seeking sincerity is ultimate and complete! Yet, examining the classics, we find it said: “Things have roots and branches.” Here it is also said: “Without sincerity there are no things.” Thus sincerity…

The great worthy recounted in succession those through whom the Way was transmitted; in doing so, he expressed his intention to take its transmission upon himself. For from Yao and Shun down to Confucius, although knowing through seeing and knowing through hearing differed, the Way transmitted was one and the same. How fitting that Mengzi should recount this succession to convey his intention to assume that responsibility! Now, the Way has never disappeared from the world, and therefore the succession of those who transmit it has never been broken. Among the sages and worthies of antiquity, some lived at the same time, giving and receiving instruction face to face within a single hall, and thus came to know through seeing. Others lived in different ages, yet their minds accorded with those of men several hundred years before them, and thus they came to know through hearing.
Thus, from the time when Yao and Shun initiated the transmission of this Way, more than five hundred years passed before Tang. Yu and Gao Yao knew it through seeing; Tang knew it through hearing. translation_en:
…and the Way embodied in King Wen was thus entrusted to a successor once again. Those who knew it through seeing could await a future sage, unhindered by the great distance between their ages; those who knew it through hearing could carry on the legacy of former sages, unobstructed by the difficulty of being born in time to encounter them. Such is how the Way has been transmitted without interruption. Could it be that Confucius alone had no successor? Ah! Mencius surely meant to take this responsibility upon himself as successor to those several sages.

Yet observe that, before and including King Wen, those who transmitted the Way all occupied high positions; only with Confucius did its transmitter occupy a lowly station. When sages and worthies are born, if they attain office and occupy high positions, the Way is put into practice; if they remain straitened and in lowly stations, the Way is elucidated. Although this neither adds to nor detracts from their endowed nature, their people are fortunate or unfortunate accordingly. This chapter of Mencius certainly shows the weight of the responsibility he assumed; does it not also express a profound lament?

The four virtues reside in human beings, but without utmost vigor they cannot be put into practice. Can their meaning not be discerned by considering the words that the sage attached to Qian? The Wenyan uses the four virtues to disclose Qian’s underlying meaning. At this point, it is essentially saying: the four virtues are ordained by Heaven and fully present in human beings; why is it that only the gentleman can realize them completely? Because, with a mind intent on unceasing self-strengthening, the gentleman reaches the utmost degree of sustained purity and unity. Energetic, strong, firm, and resolute, he accords with Heaven’s movement and remains constant; firm and vigorous, centered and correct, he matches Heaven’s course without interruption. Thus his virtuous nature operates and material desires gain no sway. Benevolence and ritual propriety become perfected virtues, through which he leads others and brings them together in fitting harmony: it is entirely his unceasing mind that puts them into operation. Luminous yang prevails, unmixed with yielding yin. Righteousness and wisdom become established in his nature, through which he benefits things and manages affairs: these proceed entirely from his enduring purity. Without the gentleman’s utmost vigor, how could he embody together the four virtues ordained by Heaven and remain unencumbered?
Thus, when the sage appended words to the Changes, there was significance in his not merely saying “origination, flourishing, benefit, and firmness,” but necessarily associating them with Qian. This is indeed because the gentleman’s vigor is precisely Qian, and his practice of the four virtues is precisely Qian’s origination, flourishing, benefit, and firmness. 同考試官編修胡批：「神易通於造化，此徹上徹下之理，然非聖人用易之功不可見也。是作融會傳義，而詞不煩，殆究心于易者。」
translation_en:
…and it is through Qian’s pure yang and utmost strength that the virtues of origination, flourishing, benefit, and constancy are united. Otherwise, with both yin and yang among the lines, these virtues would be mixed in some cases and pure in others; how could they all be fully present like this? It was because the sage contemplated the image in Qian that he attached to it the words “origination, flourishing, benefit, and constancy.” Otherwise, he might have presented only some of these words, or let their meanings appear across different hexagrams; why would he have assigned them exclusively to this one? Ah, how profound is the meaning of the sage’s attaching statements to the Changes! Generally speaking, Qian is the image of the ruler, and origination, flourishing, benefit, and constancy are the ruler’s virtues. Among a ruler’s virtues, none surpasses firmness and strength. Thus, when the Master supplied the Wings to the Changes, he treated the meaning of Qian with particular fullness. Only after possessing the unceasing virtue that matches Heaven can one exercise the transforming power of governing Heaven by mounting at the proper times. His bringing this out through mutually illuminating explanations in the Commentary on the Judgments and the Commentary on the Images therefore had a purpose. A Song Confucian said: “Once one possesses Heaven’s virtue, one can speak of the Kingly Way.” Surely he understood the Changes!

“Encompassing the transformations of Heaven and Earth without exceeding them, bringing the myriad things to completion in all their particularities without omitting any, and comprehending the way of day and night and knowing it: thus the numinous has no fixed location, and the Changes has no fixed form.”

Wu Kexing.

Associate Examiner Yang, Acting Bureau Director, comments: “Precisely where yin and yang transform and are rooted in one another are the numinous and the Changes; fundamentally, these are not two separate things. This composition succeeds in expressing this and merits inclusion.”

Associate Examiner Hu, a Compiler, comments: “The numinous and the Changes pervade the processes of creation and transformation. This principle extends throughout both the higher and lower realms, yet it cannot be perceived apart from the sage’s achievement in applying the Changes. This composition integrates the interpretations of the Commentary and the Original Meaning, while avoiding verbosity. Its author has surely devoted careful thought to the Changes.”

The Great Commentary elaborates on how the sage uses the Changes to reach an understanding of Heaven’s decree, thereby revealing the subtle workings of the numinous and of change. To reach Heaven’s decree through the Changes is the sage’s highest accomplishment. How could those subtle workings fail to become apparent here? Such is the intention of the Great Commentary in praising the Changes. Now, the Changes accords with Heaven and Earth. Once the sage has used it to fathom principle and fully realize nature, what does his reaching Heaven’s decree entail?
The transformations of Heaven and Earth are the flowing operation of Heaven’s decree. Through the Changes, the sage encompasses and regulates them. The movement of transformation is inexhaustible, yet he has a way to shape and complete it: how could there be any excess? The birth of the myriad things is the bestowal of Heaven’s decree. Through the Changes, the sage brings each to completion in accordance with its particular circumstances. Though the kinds of things are many, he embodies them all alike: how could anything be omitted? As for the Way of day and night, it is the ceaseless cycling of Heaven’s decree. Through the Changes, the sage comprehends and knows it. His mind shares the beginnings and endings of day and night, silently accordant with the incipient workings of movement and stillness, which have no beginning. What, then, could he fail to know?
Such is the sage’s reaching Heaven’s decree through the Changes. Can the subtle workings of the Way of the Changes not be seen in this? The Way of the Changes is simply yin and yang. Insofar as they are rooted in yin and rooted in yang, uniting as one and not …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
測者謂之神凡天地之化萬物之理晝夜之道
舉於是乎出焉本無方也使其有方則物而已
爾何以周聖人無方之用耶故觀於至命而所
謂神者可見矣自其陽變陰化而變動不居者
謂之易凡天地之化萬物之理晝夜之道皆相
為流通焉本無體也使其有體則器而已爾又
何以資聖人無體之用耶故觀於至命而所謂
易者可見矣大哉易也斯其至乎雖然聖人有
心易焉洗心退藏而神易之妙一以貫之是故
===

則索之卦爻適以為鑿烏足以語聖人之極功
哉故曰神而明之存乎其人

測者謂之神。凡天地之化、萬物之理、晝夜之道，舉於是乎出焉，本無方也。使其有方，則物而已爾，何以周聖人無方之用耶？故觀於至命，而所謂神者可見矣。自其陽變陰化而變動不居者謂之易。凡天地之化、萬物之理、晝夜之道，皆相為流通焉，本無體也。使其有體，則器而已爾，又何以資聖人無體之用耶？故觀於至命，而所謂易者可見矣。大哉易也，斯其至乎！雖然，聖人有心易焉，洗心退藏，而神易之妙一以貫之。是故窮理、盡性、至命，一事也；易與聖人，一道也。不然，則索之卦爻，適以為鑿，烏足以語聖人之極功哉？故曰：「神而明之，存乎其人。」

帝庸作歌曰：「勅天之命，惟時惟幾。」乃歌曰：「股肱喜哉，元首起哉，百工熈哉！」皐陶拜手稽首，颺言曰：「念哉！率作興事，慎乃憲，欽哉！屢省乃成，欽哉！」乃賡載歌曰：「元首明哉，股肱良哉，庶事康哉！」
translation_en:
…unfathomable is called the numinous. The transformations of Heaven and Earth, the principles of the myriad things, and the course of day and night all issue from this; fundamentally, it has no fixed direction. If it had a fixed direction, it would merely be a thing. How could it encompass the sage’s activity, which has no fixed direction? Thus, by considering the attainment of Heaven’s mandate, we can discern what is called the numinous. Insofar as yang changes and yin transforms, shifting without remaining fixed, it is called change. The transformations of Heaven and Earth, the principles of the myriad things, and the course of day and night all flow through one another; fundamentally, change has no fixed form. If it had a fixed form, it would merely be an implement. How, then, could it sustain the sage’s activity, which has no fixed form? Thus, by considering the attainment of Heaven’s mandate, we can discern what is called change. Great indeed are the Changes! Is this not their utmost reach? Nevertheless, the sage holds the Changes in his heart [?], cleansing his heart and withdrawing into concealment; a single principle runs through the subtle workings of the numinous and of change. Therefore, fathoming principle, fully realizing one’s nature, and attaining Heaven’s mandate are one undertaking; the Changes and the sage follow one Way. Otherwise, searching for it in the hexagrams and their lines merely produces forced interpretations. How could this suffice to discuss the sage’s ultimate achievement? Thus it is said: “Making it numinous and illuminating it depends upon the person.”

Book of Documents

The emperor thereupon composed a song, saying: “In attending to Heaven’s mandate, consider the proper timing and the first stirrings of events.” Then he sang: “When the limbs rejoice, the head rises to action, and the hundred officers flourish!” Gao Yao bowed with his hands joined and knocked his head to the ground, then declared aloud: “Keep this in mind! In leading undertakings and initiating affairs, be attentive to your established standards. Be reverent! Repeatedly examine your accomplishments. Be reverent!” Then he continued the song: “When the head is enlightened and the limbs are worthy, all affairs prosper!”

===
下之治致之固難而保之尤難也有虞君臣作
歌以責難如此此其所以不可及歟昔帝舜當
至治之時懷惕厲之心用是以作歌曰天命靡
常至可畏也其可以不敕哉殆必謹畏之恒存
幾微之畢察而無有弗戒焉斯則帝之不自恃
而有望於其臣也乃歌曰股肱喜哉元首起哉

謹於時幾而奮庸熙載矣則君之治有不興而
百官之功有不廣乎是保治之道在臣君特責

Associate Examiner Zhang, a Supervising Secretary, comments: “It captures the purport of the admonitions at the court of Yu. Record it as a model for the many candidates.”
Associate Examiner Dong, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “The language is concise, yet the meaning is complete.”
Associate Examiner Quan, a Hanlin Senior Compiler, comments: “Concise and weighty; worthy of selection.”
Examiner Ao, a Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Rigorous and orderly.”
Examiner Xu, a Grand Secretary, comments: “Refined and precise.”

When we consider the meaning of the songs composed by ruler and ministers in the age of the sages, their concern to preserve good government becomes apparent. For although achieving order throughout the realm is difficult, preserving it is harder still. The ruler and ministers of Yu composed songs in this way to demand of one another what was difficult: was this not why they could not be equaled?

In former times, Emperor Shun, living in an age of consummate order, maintained a vigilant and cautious heart. Thus he composed a song, saying: “Heaven’s mandate is not constant and is greatly to be feared. How could we fail to be watchful? Surely we must keep caution and awe constantly in our hearts, examine every subtle sign, and leave nothing unguarded against.” This shows that the emperor did not rely upon himself alone, but held expectations of his ministers. He then sang: “When the limbs rejoice, the head rises, and all offices flourish!”

The ministers are the limbs upon which the ruler depends for assistance in government. Once they have attended carefully to the times and their incipient signs, exerted themselves in service, and brought their undertakings to fruition, how could the ruler’s government fail to prosper, or the achievements of the hundred officials fail to expand? Thus the way to preserve good government rests with the ministers; the ruler merely holds them responsible …

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
成焉耳帝之所以儆之臣者蓋如此皐陶承儆
戒之命懷忠愛之心致敬以颺言曰天位維艱
不可忽也其可以不念哉殆必率作而愼其憲
屢省以考其成而無有弗敬焉斯則臣之有所
感而致望於其君也乃賡載歌曰元首明哉股
肱良哉庶事康哉蓋君為元首臣所仰以主治
者夫旣勤於綜覈而明庶以功矣則臣之職有
弗良而庶政之績有弗康乎是保治之本在君
臣特效法焉耳皐陶之所以儆之君者蓋如此
===
是則于賡歌而見其上下之和焉于交儆而見
其上下之敬焉虞廷明良相遇之盛可以想見
其氣象矣自是而後及于有周鹿鳴諸詩君之
所以貺其臣也天保諸詩臣之所以答其君也
其交相酬和庶幾虞廷之遺響焉噫唐虞之際
于周為盛其信矣哉
嚴惟丕式克用三宅三俊其在商邑用協
于厥邑其在四方用丕式見德

punctuated:
成焉耳。帝之所以儆之臣者，蓋如此。皐陶承儆戒之命，懷忠愛之心，致敬以颺言曰：「天位維艱，不可忽也，其可以不念哉？」殆必率作而愼其憲，屢省以考其成，而無有弗敬焉。斯則臣之有所感而致望於其君也。乃賡載歌曰：「元首明哉，股肱良哉，庶事康哉！」蓋君為元首，臣所仰以主治者。夫旣勤於綜覈，而明庶以功矣，則臣之職有弗良，而庶政之績有弗康乎？是保治之本在君，臣特效法焉耳。皐陶之所以儆之君者，蓋如此。
是則于賡歌而見其上下之和焉，于交儆而見其上下之敬焉。虞廷明良相遇之盛，可以想見其氣象矣。自是而後，及于有周，《鹿鳴》諸詩，君之所以貺其臣也；《天保》諸詩，臣之所以答其君也。其交相酬和，庶幾虞廷之遺響焉。噫！唐虞之際，于周為盛，其信矣哉！
嚴惟丕式，克用三宅三俊。其在商邑，用協于厥邑；其在四方，用丕式見德。
張誼
translation_en:
…for the results, that is all. Such was the emperor’s admonition to his ministers. Gao Yao received this admonitory charge with loyal affection in his heart, and respectfully proclaimed: “The throne of Heaven is difficult to occupy and must not be treated lightly. How could one fail to keep this in mind?” Surely the ruler must lead the work and exercise care over its standards, repeatedly inspecting it to assess its accomplishments, leaving nothing unattended with reverence. Thus the minister, moved by the admonition, expressed his expectations of his ruler. He then continued the song: “When the head is enlightened, the limbs are worthy, and all affairs prosper!” For the ruler is the head, to whom the ministers look to preside over government. Once he diligently oversees and examines everything, judging the many officials by their achievements, how could the ministers fail to perform their duties well, or the various branches of government fail to prosper? Thus the foundation for preserving good government lies with the ruler; the ministers simply follow his example. Such was Gao Yao’s admonition to his ruler.
In their answering songs we see the harmony between sovereign and ministers; in their mutual admonitions we see their reverence. We can thus imagine the splendid atmosphere at the court of Shun, where an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers met. Thereafter, in the Zhou dynasty, “The Deer Call” (Lu ming) and the associated poems were the means by which the ruler honored his ministers; “Heaven Protects” (Tian bao) and the associated poems were the means by which the ministers responded to their ruler. Their exchanges and answering songs came close to preserving an echo of Shun’s court. Ah! The saying that the flourishing of the age of Yao and Shun found its fullest expression in Zhou is indeed true!
“Reverently he followed the great model and was able to employ those occupying the three principal offices and the outstanding men suited to them. Those in the capital of Shang brought harmony to that capital; those throughout the four quarters greatly followed his example and manifested virtue.”
Zhang Yi

translation_en:
Associate Examiner Chen, a Bureau Director, comments: “An essay that can explain the substance of Cheng Tang’s understanding of his responsibilities deserves to be recorded as a model.”
Associate Examiner Zhang, a Left Supervising Secretary, comments: “Concise in expression and clear in reasoning: this is the only essay of its kind I have seen.”
Associate Examiner Dong, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “It explains Cheng Tang’s way of employing men to put the illustrious Mandate fully in order. Its conclusion brings the argument back to governing the mind, showing especially that it has a firm foundation. Accept it.”
Associate Examiner Tong, a Hanlin Senior Compiler, comments: “Its elucidation of the meaning of reflection and emulation is most pertinent and correct. Accordingly, it is selected for inclusion.”
Examiner Ao, a Hanlin Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “It grasps the purport.”
Examiner Xu, a Grand Secretary, comments: “Plain and substantial.”

When a sage ruler fully realizes the way of employing the worthy, good government throughout the realm is achieved. In governing, nothing takes precedence over employing the worthy. That a sage ruler can fully realize this way and thereby achieve good government reveals the substance of his understanding of his responsibilities. Fittingly, the Duke of Zhou cited this to instruct King Cheng. The meaning is that, when an enlightened king establishes government, his desire to fulfill the way of serving Heaven must be founded upon sincerity in employing the worthy. How did Tang deal with those occupying office and those of outstanding talent?

When reflection falls short, doubts arise. Tang, however, earnestly cherished the resolve to follow and ponder their counsel; his spiritual energies were concentrated upon it, without any gap between naming and speaking [?]. When emulation is incomplete, counsels become divided. Tang, however, embodied the benefits of learning from others as teachers and took their plans as his standard, without the slightest wavering between following and rejecting them. Thus, moved by his sincerity, those occupying office were enabled to fulfill their duties, sparing no effort in carrying out the tasks of the illustrious Mandate. Loyalty…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
信所勸有以著其俊者之才而耿命之陳也無
餘蘊矣吾見賢知有奮庸之美天下登至治之
休以商邑言之未易以協也今則政教施而漸
摩洽有孚惠德有孚惠心翕然習俗之化也情
之難齊者于是乎齊矣不謂純之至乎以四方
言之未易以式也今則章軌立而觀法同會其
有極歸其有極沛然聲教之訖也德之難徧者
于是乎徧矣不謂大之至乎此成湯之知恤而
耿命之不釐也有由然矣抑觀之仲虺之誥曰
===
以義制事以禮制心則知湯之所以克用三宅
三俊者實本於治心以立取人之則也雖然豈
惟湯哉有敬德之禹而後有迪知忱恂之臣有
丕顯丕承之文武而後有克知灼見之臣此周
公之所以告君惓惓而三代有道之長可見矣
詩
維此文王小心翼翼昭事上帝聿懷多福
厥德不回以受方國
張書紳

三俊者實本於治心以立取人之則也雖然豈
惟湯哉有敬德之禹而後有迪知忱恂之臣有
丕顯丕承之文武而後有克知灼見之臣此周
公之所以告君惓惓而三代有道之長可見矣
詩
維此文王小心翼翼昭事上帝聿懷多福
厥德不回以受方國

punctuated:
信所勸，有以著其俊者之才，而耿命之陳也無餘蘊矣。吾見賢知有奮庸之美，天下登至治之休。以商邑言之，未易以協也，今則政教施而漸摩洽，有孚惠德，有孚惠心，翕然習俗之化也。情之難齊者，於是乎齊矣，不謂純之至乎？以四方言之，未易以式也，今則章軌立而觀法同，會其有極，歸其有極，沛然聲教之訖也。德之難徧者，於是乎徧矣，不謂大之至乎？此成湯之知恤，而耿命之不釐也，有由然矣。抑觀之《仲虺之誥》曰：「以義制事，以禮制心。」則知湯之所以克用三宅三俊者，實本於治心以立取人之則也。雖然，豈惟湯哉？有敬德之禹，而後有迪知忱恂之臣；有丕顯丕承之文武，而後有克知灼見之臣。此周公之所以告君惓惓，而三代有道之長可見矣。
詩
維此文王，小心翼翼，昭事上帝，聿懷多福。厥德不回，以受方國。
張書紳
translation_en:
…encouraged by loyalty and trustworthiness, the outstanding men could display their talents, leaving nothing of their abilities unexpressed in carrying forth the luminous mandate. I see the worthy and wise achieving distinction through vigorous service, and all under Heaven attaining the blessings of perfect government. As for the capital of Shang, harmony was not easily achieved. Now, however, government and instruction were put into effect, and their gradual influence permeated everywhere: with sincere benevolence in virtue and sincere benevolence of heart, habits and customs were transformed in unison. Human dispositions, so difficult to bring into accord, were thereby brought into accord. Could this not be called the utmost purity? As for the four quarters, bringing them to follow a common model was not easy. Now, however, regulations and standards were established, and all looked to the same example: they gathered around the supreme standard and returned to it, as the ruler’s influence and instruction spread everywhere in abundance. Virtue, so difficult to extend everywhere, thereby reached everywhere. Could this not be called the utmost greatness? Thus there was a reason why Cheng Tang understood what required his concern and why his luminous mandate was not cut off.
Moreover, consider what the Announcement of Zhonghui says: “Regulate affairs by righteousness; regulate the heart by ritual propriety.” From this we know that Tang’s ability to employ men in the three offices and the three classes of outstanding talent was indeed rooted in governing his own heart, thereby establishing a standard for selecting men. Yet was this true only of Tang? Only with a Yu who revered virtue were there ministers who practiced wisdom and were sincere and trustworthy. Only with Kings Wen and Wu, who grandly manifested and inherited virtue, were there ministers capable of understanding and clear discernment. This is why the Duke of Zhou admonished his sovereign so earnestly; here we can see the enduring strength of the Three Dynasties when they possessed the Way.
Book of Odes
“This King Wen was circumspect and reverent. He illustriously served the Lord on High, thereby securing manifold blessings. His virtue did not deviate, and thus he received the states of the four quarters.”
Zhang Shushen

Associate Examiner Jiang, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “King Wen won Heaven and the people through reverence alone. This essay elucidates the point with precision, profoundly grasping the poet’s intent. It should be recorded as a model.”

Associate Examiner Zhu, Hanlin Examining Editor, comments: “Heaven’s favor and the people’s allegiance are very easy to elaborate upon, so contemporary essays often become prolix and diffuse. This essay alone grounds its argument in the learning of the mind; its author evidently possesses cultivated understanding.”

Associate Examiner Sun, Hanlin Examining Editor, comments: “The discussion of King Wen’s reverent cultivation of virtue is exceptionally clear [?]. This is someone with whom one can discuss the learning of the mind.”

Examiner Ao, Hanlin Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Clear and fluent.”

Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: “It portrays King Wen’s reverent cultivation of virtue well.”

A great minister points to the reality of a former king’s abundant virtue and receipt of the Mandate: profound indeed is his intention in thereby enlightening a succeeding king. For Heaven to favor him and the people to turn to him would be impossible without virtue of the highest excellence. Was this not how King Wen received the Mandate and founded Zhou? It was fitting that the Duke of Zhou should recount it to admonish King Cheng. His meaning was this: the Mandate of our Zhou dynasty truly began with King Wen’s virtue. And what was that virtue like? This King Wen held solemn reverence within…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
蘊天命之顧諟者不以一息而有懈敬畏中存
帝則之默順者不以幾微而有忽齊明以澄其
心既已退藏於密矣視之若猶未也而不顯亦
臨焉緝熈以持其敬既已安於所止矣視之若
猶未也而無射亦保焉其翼翼小心有如此故
以此心而事帝也則為事天之明對越在下秉
精白以承休德者豈有意於徼福哉然天之所
親者敬也其敬不已自足以懷多福而天亦不
能違之矣以此心而治民也則為皇極之建大
===
觀在上履中正而無畔援者豈有意於求媚哉
然民之所懷者德也其德不回自足以受方國
而人亦不能外之矣夫以文王之德始於一敬
而終於天人之相與如此為後王者可不知所
務乎抑祗台德先禹以王夏聖敬日躋湯以王
商然則敬也者非傳心之要王天下之本乎盖
不獨周之世德為然也使其子孫能守而勿失
則周之祚寧有窮乎成王以冲年撫成業其心
易以肆者此周公所以惓惓也卒之基命宥密

punctuated: 蘊，天命之顧諟者，不以一息而有懈；敬畏中存，帝則之默順者，不以幾微而有忽。齊明以澄其心，既已退藏於密矣，視之若猶未也，而不顯亦臨焉；緝熈以持其敬，既已安於所止矣，視之若猶未也，而無射亦保焉。其翼翼小心有如此。故以此心而事帝也，則為事天之明，對越在下，秉精白以承休德者，豈有意於徼福哉？然天之所親者敬也，其敬不已，自足以懷多福，而天亦不能違之矣。以此心而治民也，則為皇極之建，大觀在上，履中正而無畔援者，豈有意於求媚哉？然民之所懷者德也，其德不回，自足以受方國，而人亦不能外之矣。夫以文王之德，始於一敬，而終於天人之相與如此，為後王者，可不知所務乎？抑「祗台德先」，禹以王夏；「聖敬日躋」，湯以王商。然則敬也者，非傳心之要、王天下之本乎？盖不獨周之世德為然也。使其子孫能守而勿失，則周之祚寧有窮乎？成王以冲年撫成業，其心易以肆者，此周公所以惓惓也。卒之基命宥密
translation_en:
…held within, he kept Heaven’s mandate constantly in view, never relaxing for a single breath. Reverence and awe abiding in his heart, he silently followed the Supreme Lord’s rules, neglecting not even the slightest detail. Through purification and clarity he made his heart lucid and had already withdrawn into its hidden depths; yet he regarded this as still insufficient, and even where nothing was visible, he acted as though in the divine presence. Through continuing illumination he sustained his reverence and had already found repose in his proper place; yet he regarded this as still insufficient, and preserved it without weariness. Such was his cautious and attentive heart.

Thus, when he served the Supreme Lord with this heart, he manifested an enlightened service to Heaven. Responding reverently from below, he maintained perfect purity in receiving Heaven’s gracious virtue: could he have intended thereby to solicit blessings? Yet what Heaven draws close to is reverence. His unceasing reverence was itself sufficient to attract manifold blessings, and Heaven could not turn against him. When he governed the people with this heart, he established the august standard. Standing above as a great exemplar, he followed the central and correct course without deviation or grasping ambition: could he have intended thereby to court favor? Yet what the people cherish is virtue. His undeviating virtue was itself sufficient to win the allegiance of the regional states, and the people could not hold themselves apart from him.

Now King Wen’s virtue began in reverence alone and culminated in such support from Heaven and humankind. Could later kings fail to know what they should strive for? Moreover, by “reverently putting my virtue first,” Yu became king of Xia; through “sagely reverence increasing daily,” Tang became king of Shang. Is reverence, then, not the essential principle in transmitting the heart’s teaching, and the foundation for ruling all under Heaven? Surely this was true not only of Zhou’s virtue transmitted through the generations. If its descendants could preserve it without loss, how could Zhou’s allotted tenure ever come to an end? King Cheng inherited an established dominion while still young, and his heart was readily susceptible to self-indulgence. This was why the Duke of Zhou was so earnestly concerned. In the end, he laid the foundation of the mandate in profound tranquility…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
所永賴歟商人之頌高宗若曰我高宗之中興
也表極建而聲威振夫既極一時之盛矣是豈
惟增前人之光哉一德之格天有以凝保定之
命多方之助順有以斂和平之福以總萬幾則
之綱之紀者久而彌見其精明也年所之多歷
有迓續于天者矣以御萬邦則君之宗之者久
而益見其尊安也福履之交綏有獨厚于天者
矣我高宗之壽考且寧如此施之後世不有以
保我後生哉蓋其經營之勤固將以貽燕也而
===
化成於悠久則其本固者其廕遠自衍夫宗社
之休興復之勞固將以垂裕也而治隆於熈洽
則其源深者其澤長自篤夫邦家之祜皇圖永
奠而一統之盛猶夫肇域之初也人心永戴而
四海之假猶夫撻武之日也威德之所留豈有
窮哉吁此高宗之功所以當百世祀也抑考高
宗之中興在此詩既稱其不僭不濫不敢怠遑
而監成憲師甘盤相傅說載諸書者又不一而
足蓋其所以成外攘之績實本乎内修而所謂

translation_en:
…on which later generations could forever depend? The Shang people’s praise of Gaozong seems to say: In the restoration under our Gaozong, the supreme standard was established and his renown and authority spread. He had already brought his age to the height of prosperity. Could this merely have added to his predecessors’ glory? His unwavering virtue reached Heaven and thereby secured its mandate of protection and stability; the many regions supported his righteous rule and thereby gathered the blessings of peace and harmony. In overseeing the myriad affairs of government, his ordering and regulation of them showed ever greater discernment as time passed. Through his many years on the throne, he received Heaven’s continuing favor. In governing the myriad states, those who acknowledged him as sovereign and revered him as their chief increasingly manifested his honored and secure position. In the blessings that together brought him peace, he enjoyed Heaven’s exceptional generosity. With such longevity and tranquility, could our Gaozong fail, by extending their benefits to later ages, to protect our descendants? His diligent labors in managing the realm were indeed intended to bequeath ease to posterity. As his transforming influence reached fulfillment over the long years, his firm roots afforded far-reaching shade, naturally extending the blessings of the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain. His labors of restoration were indeed intended to leave abundance to posterity. As his government flourished in harmony, his deep source sent forth an enduring stream of beneficence, naturally enriching the blessings of the state and royal house. The royal dominion was established forever, and the splendor of its unity remained as it had been when its territories were first founded. The people’s hearts upheld him forever, and those within the Four Seas came in allegiance as they had in the days of vigorous martial conquest. Could the enduring influence of his authority and virtue ever be exhausted? Ah! Such were Gaozong’s achievements, which entitled him to receive sacrifices for a hundred generations.
Furthermore, when we examine Gaozong’s restoration, this ode already praises him for neither erring in rewards nor exceeding proper bounds in punishments, and for never daring to indulge in idleness or ease. His taking established statutes as his model, adopting Gan Pan as his teacher, and appointing Fu Yue as his chief minister are also recorded in the Documents, along with more deeds than can readily be enumerated. text:
負之以為固舊矣兹而俛首以聽于齊承寡君
之願若恐後者齊何以得此哉良由陘亭之次
桓責之以義耳盖惟義可以服人楚恃其強卑
周而廢職貢非義也于時齊桓申先君之命聲
罪討之徵包茅之不入問王祭之不供齊有詞
矣楚安得不畏而服哉故夫按兵不動以數千
里之強夷帖然而請盟者非中國之力能制之
也義有出於人心之同然耳聖人樂與人為善
者也故特書曰来盟序桓績也不然則後此國
===
佐袁婁之盟耳要之而至豈仗義執言之功哉
齊人曷為歸地乎謝魯過也夫東方之國莫強
於齊鄆讙龜陰之地侵之以為利舊矣兹而藉
手以委于魯聽賢臣之言若弗遑者魯何以得
此哉良由夾谷之會孔子責之以禮耳盖惟禮
可以化人齊逞其詐弱魯以干盟好非禮也于
時仲尼相两君之好馳詞當之拒兵車之命罷
宴享之設我有禮矣齊安得不感而化哉故夫
歷階一對以數十年之侵疆幡然而效順者非

負之以為固舊矣。兹而俛首以聽于齊，承寡君之願，若恐後者，齊何以得此哉？良由陘亭之次，桓責之以義耳。盖惟義可以服人。楚恃其強，卑周而廢職貢，非義也。于時齊桓申先君之命，聲罪討之，徵包茅之不入，問王祭之不供，齊有詞矣。楚安得不畏而服哉？故夫按兵不動，以數千里之強夷帖然而請盟者，非中國之力能制之也，義有出於人心之同然耳。聖人樂與人為善者也，故特書曰「来盟」，序桓績也。不然，則後此國佐袁婁之盟耳，要之而至，豈仗義執言之功哉？

齊人曷為歸地乎？謝魯過也。夫東方之國莫強於齊，鄆、讙、龜陰之地，侵之以為利舊矣。兹而藉手以委于魯，聽賢臣之言，若弗遑者，魯何以得此哉？良由夾谷之會，孔子責之以禮耳。盖惟禮可以化人。齊逞其詐，弱魯以干盟好，非禮也。于時仲尼相两君之好，馳詞當之，拒兵車之命，罷宴享之設，我有禮矣。齊安得不感而化哉？故夫歷階一對，以數十年之侵疆幡然而效順者，非
translation_en:
…had long relied upon these as secure defenses. Now, however, Chu bowed its head and obeyed Qi, carrying out its lord’s wishes as though afraid of falling behind. How did Qi achieve this? It was simply because, when he encamped at Xingting, Duke Huan called Chu to account on grounds of righteousness. For righteousness alone can bring people into submission. Chu relied on its strength, treated Zhou with contempt, and neglected its prescribed tribute: this was unrighteous. At that time, Duke Huan of Qi invoked the mandate received by his predecessor, proclaimed Chu’s offenses, and proceeded against it. He demanded an explanation for its failure to deliver the bundled mao grass and questioned its failure to supply the royal sacrifices. Qi thus had a just case. How could Chu fail to submit in fear? Thus, while Qi held its troops motionless, a powerful non-Chinese state extending several thousand li submitted meekly and requested a covenant. This was not because the power of the central states could subdue it, but because righteousness arises from what human hearts acknowledge in common. The Sage delighted in helping others do good. He therefore specifically wrote, “came to make a covenant,” recording Duke Huan’s achievement. Otherwise, this would merely have been like Guo Zuo’s later covenant at Yuanlou: he came under coercion. How could that count as an achievement won by upholding righteousness and speaking for a just cause?

Why did the people of Qi return the territory? To make amends for their offense against Lu. Among the eastern states, none was stronger than Qi. It had long seized the territories of Yun, Huan, and Guiyin for its own advantage. Now, however, it offered them back to Lu, heeding the words of a worthy minister as though it could not act quickly enough. How did Lu achieve this? It was simply because, at the meeting at Jiagu, Kongzi called Qi to account on grounds of ritual propriety. For ritual propriety alone can transform people. Qi practiced deception, treating Lu as weak and violating their covenant of friendship: this was contrary to ritual propriety. At that time, Zhongni assisted in the friendly meeting between the two rulers. He responded with forceful words, rejected the demand concerning war chariots, and caused the planned banquet to be canceled. We had ritual propriety on our side. How could Qi fail to be moved and transformed? Thus, with an ascent of the steps and a single reply, Qi abruptly changed course and demonstrated submission by returning territory it had occupied for several decades. This was not…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
魯之力能及此也禮有出於人心之同然耳聖
人以天自處者也故亦書曰来歸自序績也不
然則前此齊惠濟西之歸耳請之而得豈過化
存神之妙哉雖然齊之服楚非心服也以力假
仁者也若孔子之化齊則心服也使桓微八國
江黃之助楚肯為齊下乎嗣而圍許敗徐桓蓋
不能終抑之矣仲尼試于齊三田歸焉試于魯
三都墮焉使其得邦家綏和動来之效當何如
也女樂歸不稅冕而行天也此固王伯之辨世

translation_en:
…Lu’s strength could not have accomplished this. Ritual propriety springs from what human hearts share in common. The sage takes Heaven as his own standard; thus he also wrote, “came to return,” recording his own achievement. Otherwise, this would merely have been like the earlier return of Jixi by Duke Hui of Qi: something obtained by asking. How could that embody the wonder of the sage’s transforming influence wherever he passes and spiritual efficacy wherever he abides? Yet Qi’s subjugation of Chu did not secure heartfelt submission: it relied on force under the guise of benevolence. Confucius’s transformation of Qi, by contrast, secured heartfelt submission. Had Duke Huan lacked the assistance of the eight states and of Jiang and Huang, would Chu have consented to submit to Qi? Subsequently, Chu besieged Xu 許 and defeated Xu 徐; Duke Huan evidently could not keep it in check to the end. When Zhongni [Confucius] put his abilities to the test in dealing with Qi, the three territories were returned; when he did so in Lu, the walls of the three strongholds were demolished. Had he obtained a state or a noble domain to govern, how great would have been his achievements in bringing peace through reassurance and attracting people through action! When the female musicians were presented, he departed without even removing his ceremonial cap: this was Heaven’s will. Surely herein lies the distinction between true kingship and hegemony, and the pivotal point in the rise and decline of the moral order!
In winter, the duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi 杞, the Viscount of Lesser Zhu, and Guang, heir apparent of Qi 齊, in attacking Zheng. In the twelfth month, on the yihai [?] day, they jointly covenanted at Xi. 〔Ninth year of Duke Xiang.〕
Sun Mingshi.
Comment by Associate Examiner Bi, Secretary: 〔He succeeds in explaining the sage’s intention in commending Jin for not fighting.〕
Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Examining Editor: 〔He grasps the purport of the Spring and Autumn Annals in approving Jin. Clear and fluent; worthy of inclusion.〕

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
考試官侍講學士敖批以謀取勝於此可見
考試官大學士徐批善發揮
伯主用善勝之謀以敝外春秋所以予之也夫
善勝敵者以謀也悼之敝楚進于是矣春秋得
不予之乎且晉悼帥列國之師以伐鄭而為戲
之盟焉固未能即得鄭也春秋遽予之何哉誠
以善用兵者非能戰之貴而能謀之貴非勝敵
之難而不戰以屈人之難晉楚爭鄭為日久矣
方鄟門之師而鄭人請成也使悼違知罃而用
===
荀偃以與楚戰豈計之得乎幸而有見于此以
為逞吾之眾以禦楚則我勞而敵未可以力爭
分吾之兵以敝楚則敵勞而我可以坐勝寧還
師養銳不徼乎一勝之捷修德息民不必其一
時之從人徒見反覆之鄭而晉許之盟其成未
可知也而不知所以服鄭者此也以全取勝蓋
無遺策矣人徒見陸梁之楚而晉避其鋒其勢
若少懦也而不知所以屈楚者此也以靜制動
蓋有成算矣卒之蕭魚之會良霄之執鄭不敢

punctuated:
考試官侍講學士敖批：以謀取勝，於此可見。
考試官大學士徐批：善發揮。
伯主用善勝之謀以敝外，春秋所以予之也。夫善勝敵者，以謀也。悼之敝楚，進于是矣，春秋得不予之乎？且晉悼帥列國之師以伐鄭，而為戲之盟焉，固未能即得鄭也，春秋遽予之，何哉？誠以善用兵者，非能戰之貴，而能謀之貴；非勝敵之難，而不戰以屈人之難。晉楚爭鄭，為日久矣。方鄟門之師，而鄭人請成也，使悼違知罃而用荀偃，以與楚戰，豈計之得乎？幸而有見于此，以為逞吾之眾以禦楚，則我勞而敵未可以力爭；分吾之兵以敝楚，則敵勞而我可以坐勝。寧還師養銳，不徼乎一勝之捷；修德息民，不必其一時之從。人徒見反覆之鄭，而晉許之盟，其成未可知也，而不知所以服鄭者此也。以全取勝，蓋無遺策矣。人徒見陸梁之楚，而晉避其鋒，其勢若少懦也，而不知所以屈楚者此也。以靜制動，蓋有成算矣。卒之蕭魚之會，良霄之執，鄭不敢
translation_en:
Examiner Ao, Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Here one can see victory achieved through strategy.”
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: “An excellent exposition.”
The hegemon employed a strategy adept at securing victory to wear down his external opponent: this is why the Spring and Autumn Annals approves of him. For those skilled at defeating an enemy do so through strategy. Duke Dao’s wearing down of Chu attained this level. Could the Spring and Autumn Annals withhold its approval? Duke Dao of Jin led the armies of the various states against Zheng and concluded the covenant at Xi. Certainly, he had not yet secured Zheng’s allegiance immediately. Why, then, did the Spring and Autumn Annals so readily approve of him? It is because, in one skilled at employing troops, what deserves esteem is the ability to plan rather than merely to fight; the difficult achievement is to subdue others without battle rather than merely to defeat the enemy. Jin and Chu had long contended over Zheng. During the campaign at Zhuanmen, when the people of Zheng requested peace, had Duke Dao rejected Zhi Ying’s advice and followed Xun Yan in fighting Chu, could this have been sound strategy? Fortunately, he understood this point, reasoning: “If we deploy our full strength to resist Chu, we shall exhaust ourselves, while the enemy will still be beyond overcoming by force. If we divide our troops to wear down Chu, the enemy will become exhausted, while we can win without exertion.” He preferred to withdraw his army and replenish its vigor, rather than gamble on a single victory; to cultivate virtue and give the people rest, rather than insist upon Zheng’s immediate submission. People saw only that Jin allowed the vacillating Zheng to enter a covenant, whose success remained uncertain. They did not understand that this was precisely the means of bringing Zheng into submission. By securing victory while preserving his strength intact, he left no strategic provision wanting. People saw only that Jin avoided the onslaught of unruly Chu, appearing somewhat timid in its posture. They did not understand that this was precisely the means of subduing Chu. By controlling movement through stillness, he already possessed a settled plan. Finally, with the meeting at Xiaoyu and the seizure of Liang Xiao, Zheng did not dare…

text:

知其不可與爭久矣豈待力屈而後服哉鄭有

叛，楚不能爭者，豈非其好謀而成者耶？君子曰：「晉悼之復伯也，宜哉！其臣能明於善陣之法以佐其君，而其君能用其善勝之術以駕乎敵。自齊桓晉文以来，未有得志於楚如今日者也。故《春秋》下書蕭魚之會以美之，而聖人慎用兵之情見矣。抑悼之所以勝楚者，不獨一罃也。魏絳、祁奚諸臣相與左右之，舉不失選，敵國謀臣已知其不可與爭久矣，豈待力屈而後服哉？鄭有一子産，不能用也，而晉楚交伐，犧牲玉帛待于二境，其能國乎？噫！用人之有關於人國也如此，可不鑒哉？」

禮記

translation_en:
…rebel, and Chu could not contend: was this not because he delighted in planning and brought his plans to fruition? The gentleman says: “How fitting that Duke Dao of Jin restored his state’s hegemony! His minister understood the methods of skillful deployment and thereby assisted his ruler, while the ruler employed his minister’s techniques for securing victory to master the enemy. Since Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin, no one had achieved such success against Chu as on this occasion. Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals subsequently records the meeting at Xiaoyu to praise him, revealing the Sage’s concern for caution in the use of arms.

“Yet Duke Dao’s victory over Chu was not due to Ying alone. Wei Jiang, Qi Xi, and the other ministers together assisted him, and his appointments never failed to select suitable men. The counselors of the rival state had long known that they could not contend with him. Why would they have needed to wait until their strength was exhausted before submitting? Zheng had a Zichan but could not employ him. Jin and Chu attacked it in turn, and sacrificial animals, jade, and silk were kept ready at both borders. Could it sustain itself as a state? Alas! Such is the importance of employing men to the fortunes of a state. Can we fail to take heed?”

Book of Rites
“The Son of Heaven then, on the auspicious first day, prays to the Lord on High for grain.”
Luo Liang

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, a Hanlin Compiler: “This brings out almost fully the intentions of the former kings in attending to the foundation of livelihood and benefiting the people. Its language is also striking and vigorous. It can serve as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, a Hanlin Compiler: “The topic itself is clear, but most writers treat it vaguely and superficially. This essay alone is precise in both language and meaning. I select it.”

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
考試官侍講學士敖批明健
考試官大學士徐批説得先王勤民之意出
王者因時以祈農事勤民之意至矣盖民生所
資以養者穀也先王於元日而預以祈之其知
所重者乎記者之意盖曰天之立君以養民為
職而君之為政以順時為先彼孟春之月農祥
正矣土脉膏矣耕籍之典欲舉於東郊布農之
命將申於田畯於此而祈年之禮其容後乎先
王以為及時而耕者農也而所以使之耕而必
===
穫者則有賴於天之降康生百穀以利民者地
也而所以使之生而必成者則有資乎神之垂
佑于焉值上辛之吉以祗修祀事而一念之精
禋有以孚諸冥漠際發生之候以殷薦明神而
内心之誠敬有以見之禱祠奉帝以祀於郊而
天神於是乎格也推稷以配乎帝而人鬼於是
乎歆也假祝史之薦辭以達有秋之望冀神功
之默相以慰三農之求盖祭非徼福而享獻妥
侑之勤不以為褻志實在民而陶匏藁靿之陳

天神於是乎格也推稷以配乎帝而人鬼於是
乎歆也假祝史之薦辭以達有秋之望冀神功
之默相以慰三農之求蓋祭非徼福而享獻妥

translation_en:
Examiner Ao, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “Clear and vigorous.”
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: “It brings out the former kings’ intention to exert themselves for the people.”
When a true king follows the seasons in praying for the work of farming, his concern for the people reaches its utmost expression. Grain is what sustains the people’s lives. By praying for it beforehand on the auspicious opening day, did not the former kings show that they understood what deserved priority? The meaning of the compiler of the Record of Rites is presumably this: Heaven establishes rulers with the duty of nourishing the people, and rulers, in conducting government, give first priority to following the seasons. In the first month of spring, the constellation that heralds farming has reached its proper position, and the soil is rich and moist. The ceremony of plowing the imperial field is about to be performed in the eastern suburbs, and commands initiating farm work are about to be conveyed to the field overseers. At such a time, could the rite of praying for a fruitful year be delayed? The former kings considered that farmers plow at the proper time, but ensuring that their plowing yields a harvest depends upon Heaven’s bestowal of well-being. The earth produces the many grains to benefit the people, but ensuring that what it produces reaches maturity depends upon the spirits’ protection. Thus, on the auspicious first xin day, the king reverently performs the sacrifices, and the purity of his single-minded offering reaches the unseen realm. At the season when things begin to grow, he makes abundant offerings to the luminous spirits, expressing his inward sincerity and reverence through prayers and sacrifices. He honors the Supreme Lord with sacrifice in the suburbs, and the celestial spirits arrive; he exalts Hou Ji as the Supreme Lord’s associate in worship, and the ancestral spirit accepts the offering. Through the invocations presented by the invocators and scribes, he conveys his hope for an autumn harvest; he hopes that the spirits’ power will secretly assist, fulfilling the wishes of farmers of all three kinds. Sacrifice is not an attempt to solicit blessings, and the painstaking rites of presenting offerings, settling the spirits, and urging them to partake are not regarded as importunate. His purpose truly lies with the people, and the setting out of earthenware vessels, gourd vessels, and straw footwear [?] …

translation_en:
…why would they shrink from the trouble? This was one aspect of the former kings’ policies of attending to the foundation of livelihood and benefiting the people. That they performed it first, on the initial auspicious day, shows that they understood the urgency of attending to first things. Moreover, the Zhou founded their state upon agriculture; hence the Zhou institutions recorded in the Monthly Ordinances give particularly detailed attention to sowing and reaping. Prayers to the celestial powers, sacrifices to mountains, rivers, and the sources of streams, and rain sacrifices to former lords and ministers are all instances of this. With rulers directing their attention in this way, there was surely a reason why no farmer left the fields untilled and successive years brought the joy of abundant harvests! Alas, in later ages this intention faded, and there were even those who encroached upon the farmers’ working time, leaving their fields eventually overgrown.

“When applied to victory in battle, it makes one invincible; when applied to ritual and rightness, it brings harmonious order. Invincibility abroad and harmonious order at home: this is called abundant virtue.”

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
德其孰能之記聘義者盖以天下之事非有勇
者固不足以任重而非善用其勇者亦不足以
成功君子之以禮自養也而豈徒哉自其有事
而用之戰勝也則謀猷壯而聲威振盖不假於
兵革之強而天下自畏矣孰有抗之者乎自其
無事而用之禮義也則彝倫敘而教本端盖不
出乎揖讓之間而禮俗自刑矣有弗順治者乎
夫戡亂者武也而至於無敵則威加于外者遠
矣附衆者文也而至於順治則化被于內者深
===
矣非君子之盛德孰能與於此乎盖其浩然之
氣得之于天者足以配道義而不餒義理之勇
素豫吾內者足以當大任而不懼夫是以積之
深者用之利而靖內靖外固其優為者矣否則
器有所拘而何以勝天下之重耶蓄之厚者發
之遠而允文允武皆其時出者矣否則才有所
偏而何以成天下之功耶君子用勇之效如此
然則聖王之貴之也豈徒尚其力也哉噫吾于
是而知禮之不可已也夫一勇力也君子用之

translation_en:
…virtue—who could accomplish this without it? The author of “The Meaning of Diplomatic Visits” (Pin yi) held that, in the affairs of the world, those without courage certainly cannot bear heavy responsibilities, while those unable to use their courage well likewise cannot achieve success. How, then, could the gentleman’s cultivation of himself through ritual be without purpose? When affairs require action and he employs it to gain victory in battle, his plans are bold and his martial prestige resounds. Without relying on the strength of weapons and armor, he naturally inspires awe throughout the world. Who could resist him? When affairs are tranquil and he employs it in ritual and righteousness, the enduring human relationships are ordered and the foundations of moral teaching are set right. Without going beyond the exchange of bows and gestures of deference, rituals and customs naturally take proper form. Could any fail to become obedient and well governed?

It is martial prowess that quells disorder; when it reaches the point where none can oppose it, its authority extends far abroad. It is civil virtue that draws the multitude into allegiance; when it brings obedience and good order, its transforming influence penetrates deeply within. Who but a gentleman of abundant virtue could attain this? His vast, flowing vital force, received from Heaven, suffices to accord with the Way and righteousness without flagging. His courage grounded in moral principle, long nurtured within, suffices to shoulder great responsibilities without fear. Thus, what is deeply accumulated is effective in use, and bringing peace both within and without is assuredly something he accomplishes with ease. Otherwise, if his capacity were constrained, how could he bear the weight of the world’s responsibilities? What is richly stored has far-reaching effects when released, and both his true civil virtue and his true martial prowess emerge as the occasion demands. Otherwise, if his abilities were one-sided, how could he accomplish the work of the world?

Such are the results when the gentleman employs courage. Then, when the sage king prizes him, can it be merely his physical strength that he esteems? Ah! From this I understand that ritual must never be abandoned. Courage and strength are the same in themselves; the gentleman employs them…

…to accomplish worthwhile deeds, while the petty man relies upon it to fight and contend. The difference lies simply in whether it has been properly nurtured. The sages established ritual so that people might bow a hundred times throughout the day without finding it burdensome. Was this from a fondness for complexity? This composition fully explains the principles by which the sages acted as rulers and teachers of all under Heaven, as though its author had personally witnessed the transforming guidance of those times. 考試官大學士徐批：以三重為治，而本於教民寡過之心，此所以為王道也。子能識此意，而文足以發之，佳士！佳士！
聖人有所以治天下之具，而必本其有教天下之心，而後其治成。夫聖人之有天下，固將範圍之以統于一。而天下若是其廣，其情若是其不齊，其習若是其異，而聖人無所以治之之具以為之法守，則天下各以其情之所安、習之所便，而日蹈于過。聖人閔天下之人，以為其性本同，而其情與習不能以無異。顧吾未有以示之法守，以一其趨，而先責其過，則是不究其本，而強之以所不能從也。故制一代之典章，以為治之之具者甚備，而特自其性之所同，約而趨之，以歸于一，漸摩成就，優柔而不迫，此聖人所以教
translation_en:
…the intention to teach all under Heaven: this essay alone apprehends it truly and precisely. Moreover, its style is elegant and ample. It does not strive for the extraordinary or eccentric, yet its bearing is naturally beyond others’ reach. It deserves to rank first among the candidates.
Examiner Ao, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: It has argument and thoughtful insight. Only someone who comprehends the fundamental source of governance and instruction could achieve this.
Examiner Xu, Grand Secretary, comments: To govern through the three weighty matters, grounding this in the desire to teach the people to commit fewer errors—this is what constitutes the kingly Way. You have grasped this meaning, and your writing adequately expresses it. A fine scholar! A fine scholar!
The sage possesses the means to govern all under Heaven, but he must ground their use in his desire to teach all under Heaven; only then does his governance succeed. When the sage possesses all under Heaven, he indeed intends to bring it within an encompassing order and unite it as one. Yet the realm is so vast, its people’s dispositions so uneven, and their habits so different. If the sage lacked the instruments of government that could provide them with rules to observe, everyone would follow what suited their dispositions and what their habits made convenient, falling into error day after day. The sage has compassion for the people of the realm, considering that their nature is originally the same, while their dispositions and habits cannot be without differences. He reflects: “If I have not yet shown them rules to observe so as to give their inclinations a common direction, but first blame them for their errors, then I am failing to investigate the root of the matter and forcing upon them what they cannot follow.” Thus he establishes the statutes and institutions of an era, providing a full complement of instruments for governing them. Drawing specifically upon what their nature shares in common, he regulates and guides them toward unity, gradually cultivating and perfecting them, gently and without pressure. This is how the sage teaches…

title: 嘉靖三十二年會試錄
text:
天下之心也天下感于其心而又有典章以為
之法守故其從之也其勢順且易相率以遠于
過而不自知而後聖人之治成子思曰王天下
有三重焉其寡過矣乎三重者何也議禮也制
度也考文也自夫天下之有父子君臣夫婦長
幼朋友相與之節也而禮所由始焉自夫天下
之有車輿宮室服飾器用之等也而度所由始
焉自夫天下之有形聲點畫文字之體也而文
所由始焉此其本之天地自然之理根諸人性
===
所同宜民之皆得以與能而不免于過何也盖
天下之人可以使之共由而不可使之自治五
方之風氣不同相沿于俗其習之所以異宜也
民之氣禀剛柔通蔽不同相限于質其情之所
以異趣也以其異趣之情而施之異宜之習而
聖人無典章以為之治則將安于情而志益流
便于習而俗益散彼縱欲恣惡喪失其心迷而
不復者固已不少然其天性之良終不泯絕一
觸其機未有不興起焉者而其間亦有稍知其

盖天下之人，可以使之共由，而不可使之自治。五方之風氣不同，相沿于俗，其習之所以異宜也；民之氣禀剛柔通蔽不同，相限于質，其情之所以異趣也。以其異趣之情，而施之異宜之習，而聖人無典章以為之治，則將安于情而志益流，便于習而俗益散。彼縱欲恣惡、喪失其心、迷而不復者，固已不少；然其天性之良，終不泯絕，一觸其機，未有不興起焉者。而其間亦有稍知其
translation_en:
…the intention with which the sage teaches all under Heaven. All under Heaven are moved by his intention and also have statutes and institutions to observe as their standards. Thus, following him is naturally smooth and easy: they lead one another away from wrongdoing without even realizing it, and only then is the sage’s governance accomplished. Zisi said: “In ruling all under Heaven, there are three weighty matters. With these, surely faults will be few!” What are these three weighty matters? Deliberating on rites, establishing standards, and examining written forms. Rites originate in the proper ways of interaction between fathers and sons, rulers and ministers, husbands and wives, elders and juniors, and friends throughout the world. Standards originate in the gradations governing carriages, palaces and dwellings, clothing and adornments, and implements and utensils throughout the world. Written forms originate in the structures of writing and characters, their forms and sounds, dots and strokes. These are based on the natural principles of Heaven and Earth and rooted in what human nature holds in common. The people should therefore all be able to participate in their practice. Why, then, do they fail to avoid wrongdoing?

The people of the world can be made to follow a common path, but they cannot be left to regulate themselves. The prevailing influences of the five regions differ and are perpetuated in local customs; this explains why people’s habits differ in what they find fitting. People’s endowments of vital energy differ in firmness and softness, understanding and obtuseness, and each is constrained by their innate constitution; this explains why their dispositions tend in different directions. If they apply these divergent dispositions to habits that differ in what they find fitting, and the sage has no statutes and institutions with which to govern them, they will settle comfortably into their dispositions, and their aspirations will drift ever further; they will find ease in their habits, and their customs will become increasingly unrestrained. There are already many who indulge their desires, give free rein to evil, lose their original heart, and go astray without returning. Yet the goodness of their innate nature is never wholly extinguished. Once its impulse is stirred, there are none in whom it does not awaken. Among them there are also those who begin to recognize their …

text:
非欲反情以振習而拘于其故厥路無繇然則
斯民之過未必盡皆其罪也聖人所以惻然閔
之而思其治之之具者深有所不能自已矣故
夫民之不知禮之有節也或失則簡或失則瀆
簡者闕恩瀆者渝義而民親疎貴賤之間其過
多矣聖人不以為民之過而曰吾禮有未議也
民之不知度之有等也或失則侈或失則儉侈
者偪上儉者病下而民尊卑隆殺之間其過多
矣聖人不以為民之過而曰吾度有未制也民

亂正詭者失真而民象形轉聲之間其過多矣

非，欲反情以振習，而拘于其故，厥路無繇。然則斯民之過，未必盡皆其罪也。聖人所以惻然閔之，而思其治之之具者，深有所不能自已矣。
故夫民之不知禮之有節也，或失則簡，或失則瀆。簡者闕恩，瀆者渝義，而民親疎貴賤之間，其過多矣。聖人不以為民之過，而曰：「吾禮有未議也。」民之不知度之有等也，或失則侈，或失則儉。侈者偪上，儉者病下，而民尊卑隆殺之間，其過多矣。聖人不以為民之過，而曰：「吾度有未制也。」民之不知文之有體也，或失則俚，或失則詭。俚者亂正，詭者失真，而民象形轉聲之間，其過多矣。聖人不以為民之過，而曰：「吾文有未考也。」
聖人視民之有過也，常若在我，而其率民以寡過也，常始于身。故其明物察倫，經禮三百，曲禮三千，而身有其禮矣；制節謹度，周旋中規，折旋中矩，而身有其度矣；仰觀于天，俯察于地，中觀于人，其聲為律，其辭為經，而身有其文矣。此其折衷古今前後聖人之道，體備陰陽造化之理，於辰
translation_en:
…their error and wish to turn their dispositions around and reform their habits, yet are constrained by their established ways and have no path by which to proceed. Thus, the faults of these people are not necessarily all their own blame. The sages therefore feel compassion for them and ponder the means of bringing them into good order, moved by a profound impulse they cannot restrain.
When the people do not understand that ritual has its proper limits, some err through perfunctoriness and others through excessive familiarity. Perfunctoriness leaves affection unexpressed; excessive familiarity violates righteousness. Thus, in relations between close and distant kin, and between the noble and the lowly, the people commit many faults. The sage does not regard these as the people's fault, but says: “There are matters of ritual that I have yet to deliberate upon.” When the people do not understand that standards have their proper gradations, some err through extravagance and others through excessive frugality. Extravagance encroaches upon superiors; excessive frugality brings hardship upon inferiors. Thus, in distinctions between high and low, and in the greater or lesser elaboration appropriate to each, the people commit many faults. The sage does not regard these as the people's fault, but says: “There are standards that I have yet to establish.” When the people do not understand that writing has its proper forms, some err through vulgarity and others through eccentricity. Vulgarity confounds what is correct; eccentricity loses what is genuine. Thus, in representing forms and conveying sounds through written characters [?], the people commit many faults. The sage does not regard these as the people's fault, but says: “There are matters of writing that I have yet to examine.”
When the sage sees the people's faults, he always regards the responsibility as resting with himself; in leading the people to reduce their faults, he always begins with his own person. Thus, he understands things and discerns human relationships: the three hundred major rules of ritual and the three thousand detailed observances are embodied in his own person. He establishes limits and carefully observes standards: his circling movements conform to the compass, and his angular turns conform to the square. Thus, the standards are embodied in his own person. He looks upward to observe Heaven, downward to examine Earth, and between them to observe humanity. His sounds become tonal standards, and his words become canonical texts. Thus, writing is embodied in his own person. In this way, he reconciles the Way of the sages of antiquity and the present, of earlier and later times, and fully embodies the principles of yin and yang and of creation and transformation; with regard to [the people's?] …

text:
性之所同者已貫徹而無不盡矣由是即以其
所貫徹者通于制作之原察之天下而見其情
之異趣習之異尚皆深得其故而明其所以反
異為同之義是以為之議禮焉自然之節性之
所同也為之制度焉自然之等性之所同也為
之考文焉自然之體性之所同也本其所同者
以先盡于己而達之于人故上不必于強而下
不待于強其一切禁令法制所以強民之術與
夫懲膚及體所以強民之事皆無所施獨率三
===

能行而訓之行有勸導而無操切有寬裕而無
督促假典章一定之則以寓長養造就之仁故

成也如此其殷勤委曲懇切詳備勞于民而為
之立法守也如此又莫不曰吾昔之迷于習溺
于情自陷于過而今恍然有悟戚戚然得其本

translation_en:
…what is common to human nature he has already comprehended thoroughly, leaving nothing unexplored. From this, he draws on what he has comprehended to penetrate the source of institutional creation. Examining the world, he sees the divergent tendencies of people's feelings and the differing preferences of their customs; he fully grasps their causes and understands the principle by which such differences may be brought back into unity. Thus he deliberates on rites for them: their natural articulations are common to human nature. He establishes regulations for them: their natural gradations are common to human nature. He examines written forms for them: their natural configurations are common to human nature. Taking what they share as his foundation, he first realizes it fully in himself and then extends it to others. Thus those above need not resort to coercion, and those below need not await coercion. All the techniques for compelling the people through prohibitions, commands, laws, and regulations, together with the acts of compulsion that punish their skin and bodies, have no occasion for use. He relies solely on these three things to bring order among the people. Pitying their inability to understand, he teaches them to understand; pitying their inability to act, he teaches them to act. There is encouragement and guidance without harsh constraint, generosity and forbearance without pressure and haste. Through the fixed standards of institutions and ordinances, he embodies the benevolence that nurtures people and brings them to fulfillment. Thus it is said: “This is the intention with which the sage teaches the people to have few faults.”
At this point, all under Heaven rely upon his institutions and ordinances as means of sustaining order, and are transformed by the intention underlying his teaching. Everyone says: “Such is the sage's compassion for what we have yet to attain; such is his refusal to compel us or hasten our fulfillment; such is his tireless solicitude, attentive to every circumstance, earnest and thorough, as he labors for the people and establishes laws for them to observe.” Everyone also says: “Formerly, we were bewildered by habit and submerged in our feelings, entangling ourselves in faults; now we suddenly awaken to understanding and feel an intimate recognition of our original…”

心也如此。」又莫不曰：「其道之簡易，率而由之，本于吾性，其可從也如此。」故其親疎貴賤之相與，莫不曰：「有聖人之禮焉，不簡且瀆也。」其尊卑隆殺之相辨，莫不曰：「有聖人之度焉，不侈而儉也。」其象形轉聲，莫不曰：「有聖人之文焉，凡俚者、訛者，不得干其間也。」過者俯而就之，不及者跂而及之，懽欣鼓舞于其範圍之中，合天下以趨于一，而歸其治之極焉。故曰：「教行而治成也。」《書》有云：「天降下民，作之君，作之師，亶聰明，作元后。」王天下而為元后者，固無有君師之責者哉？唐虞三代帝王之盛，率皆由是。及秦，盡裂先王為治之具而棄之，殊不足道。至于漢唐，其最上者，法令禁制亦畧備矣，而不可與語至治，則以本無教天下之心故也。嗟乎！非有聖人之德卓越古今者，其孰與此？

表

擬宋司馬光進資治通鑑表〔元豐七年〕
祝世廉
translation_en:
…thus have we recovered our original heart.” All likewise say: “How simple and easy this Way is! Following it is rooted in our own nature; thus readily can we comply with it.” Hence, in dealings between those close and distant, noble and humble, all say: “Here are the sage’s rites; we must not be negligent or disrespectful.” In distinguishing the honored from the lowly and greater from lesser degrees of ceremony, all say: “Here are the sage’s measures; we must be frugal rather than extravagant.” Regarding pictographic forms and changes of sound, all say: “Here is the sage’s writing; nothing vulgar or erroneous may intrude upon it.” Those who exceed the standard bend down to meet it; those who fall short stand on tiptoe to reach it. Joyfully inspired within its bounds, all under Heaven are brought together to advance toward unity and attain the utmost perfection of government. Thus it is said: “When teaching is put into practice, good government is achieved.”

The Book of Documents says: “Heaven brought forth the common people and established rulers and teachers for them. Only one truly discerning and wise becomes their sovereign.” Could one who rules all under Heaven as sovereign indeed be without the responsibilities of ruler and teacher? The flourishing rule of the emperors and kings of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties all followed this course. When Qin arose, it utterly destroyed and discarded the means by which the former kings had governed; it scarcely merits discussion. As for Han and Tang, under their best rulers, laws, ordinances, prohibitions, and regulations were fairly complete. Yet their rule cannot be spoken of as perfect government, because fundamentally they lacked the intention to teach all under Heaven. Alas! Who could attain this unless endowed with a sage’s virtue, surpassing past and present?

Memorial

Memorial in the Voice of Sima Guang of the Song Dynasty, Presenting the Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government (Zizhi tongjian)〔Seventh year of Yuanfeng [1084]〕
By Zhu Shilian.

translation_en:
Associate Examiner Zhang, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “Its allusions and phrasing are richly ornamented, restrained, and rigorous. It achieves the proper manner for a subject addressing his sovereign.”

Associate Examiner Wang, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: “The exposition is appropriate, and the language is also richly elegant: an excellent example of four-and-six parallel prose.”

Examiner Ao, a Hanlin Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “Dignified, weighty, and classically correct.”

Examiner Xu, a Grand Secretary, comments: “Through four-and-six parallel prose, it brings out Sima Guang’s loyal devotion. It may well be said to supply what was lacking in his expression of it. Include it.”

Your servant Sima Guang, holding the requisite official titles, respectfully submits the completed Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government (Zizhi tongjian).

An enlightened king, seeking good government, draws upon written records to find instruction; a subject, offering loyal service, conveys admonition through compilation. The purpose lies in providing a mirror for guidance; the aspiration is to assist Your Majesty’s grand designs. Your servant, truly trembling and fearful, bows his head to the ground and repeatedly knocks his forehead upon it.

I humbly consider that the sages’ teachings concerning the mind are fully embodied in the Classics, while the deeds of successive ages are comprehensively recorded in the histories. Since the Spring and Autumn Annals, no age has lacked men of broad learning; from Sima Qian and Ban Gu onward, every era has produced officials who took up the historian’s brush. Yet thousands of years have passed, and the accounts of a hundred schools are intermingled. Even a Confucian scholar cannot traverse all the waves of this ocean of learning; how could a sovereign have leisure to explore the silk-bound volumes in this forest of letters? I therefore considered that these materials should be condensed into a book, so as to facilitate consultation of antiquity. Without properly measuring my own ignorance and inadequacy, I began compiling a chronological history; if granted recognition [?] …

punctuated: 遇於先朝，俾終緒業。暨遭逢於聖主，荐被殊恩，書局仍許自隨，經筵常令進讀。嘉名豫錫，榮逾華衮之褒；冠序親裁，寵溢奎章之爛。既切私心之感激，復縁散地之優閒，博采舊聞，旁搜小說。始於七國之際，上下千三百年；訖乎五季之間，後先一十六姓。凡朝廷之舉措及廊廟之謀謨，言切民生，微無不錄；事關君德，動則必書。頗摘隱而鉤深，爰刪繁而舉要。彚次幾三百卷之富，囊括靡遺；校讎積十九載之勤，管窺畧效。昔唐帝興思於三鑑，而張相寓意於千秋。祇仰前修，愧追隨之弗逮；恭承聖志，幸纂輯之粗成。謹齋沐以上陳，冀清閒而賜省。恭惟
translation_en:
…received favor under the former emperor and was enabled to complete the undertaking. Then, upon encountering Your Sacred Majesty, I repeatedly received extraordinary grace: I was still permitted to take the compilation bureau with me, and was regularly commanded to present readings at the Classics Colloquium. You bestowed an auspicious title in advance—an honor surpassing the commendation conveyed by a splendid ceremonial robe—and personally composed the prefatory introduction, a favor radiant with the brilliance of imperial writing.

Deeply moved with gratitude in my heart, and also enjoying the leisure of an unburdened post, I gathered widely from earlier accounts and searched incidental narratives as well. Beginning in the age of the Seven States and ending in the era of the Five Dynasties, the work spans thirteen hundred years and sixteen successive ruling houses. Among the court’s actions and the deliberations of its chief ministers, whenever words bore upon the people’s livelihood, none were too slight to record; whenever affairs concerned the ruler’s virtue, every action was set down. I sought to uncover what was hidden and probe what was profound, eliminating excessive detail and presenting the essentials. Arranged in nearly three hundred juan, the compilation embraces its material without omission. Nineteen years of painstaking collation have yielded some modest results from my limited perspective.

In former times, a Tang emperor reflected upon the three mirrors, while Chief Minister Zhang embodied his purpose in a work concerning a thousand autumns. Reverently looking up to these predecessors, I am ashamed that I cannot match them; respectfully carrying out Your Majesty’s sacred intent, I am fortunate to have brought the compilation to a rough completion. Having reverently fasted and bathed, I submit it for presentation, hoping that in a moment of leisure you will graciously examine it. I reverently reflect that…
